mangal-state.t: One of the tiniest of the Simla Hill States, a chiefship of a few villages on the Sutlej side of the Shimla hills.
mangal-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins.
mangal-state.r: Mangal had a very small population and revenue, making it one of the smallest [[e:princely-state|princely states]] in [[e:india|India]]. It was restored under British protection after the [[e:anglo-nepalese-war|Anglo-Nepalese War]]. Its history is poorly recorded.
mangal-state.e: Mangal merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948.

merkit-confederation.t: A confederation of forest-steppe tribes south of Lake Baikal, sworn enemies of Genghis Khan after they kidnapped his wife Börte.
merkit-confederation.o: The Merkits lived along the lower Selenga river south of Lake Baikal, on the edge of the Siberian forest. They are known from the 12th century as three allied tribes, the Uduyit, Uwas and Qa'at, speaking a Mongolic language.
merkit-confederation.r: Merkit society combined herding with hunting and forest resources, under tribal chiefs with no permanent central government; [[e:toqtoa-beki|Toqto'a Beki]] of the Uduyit was their most powerful leader. According to the [[e:secret-history-of-the-mongols|Secret History of the Mongols]], [[e:genghis-khan|Temüjin's]] father Yesügei had stolen his wife Hö'elün from a Merkit, and in revenge the Merkits abducted Temüjin's bride Börte, who was rescued with help from Toghrul of the [[s:keraite-khanate|Keraite Khanate]] and Jamukha.
merkit-confederation.e: [[e:genghis-khan|Temüjin]] defeated the Merkits repeatedly from 1204. [[e:toqtoa-beki|Toqto'a Beki]] was killed on the Irtysh in 1208, and his sons fled west towards the Qipchaks. Mongol forces under [[e:subutai|Subutai]] and Jochi destroyed the last Merkit groups in 1217 to 1218, absorbing the survivors into the [[s:mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]].

mangyul-gungthang.t: A Tibetan kingdom on the Nepal border, ruled by descendants of the old emperors, which guarded the main trade route between Lhasa and Kathmandu.
mangyul-gungthang.o: Gungthang, around Dzongkha and the Kyirong valley in south-western [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]], was ruled by a branch of the royal line descended from the emperors of the [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]]. It became a recognised principality in the 1260s, when the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] and the [[s:sakya-regime|Sakya regime]] reorganised [[e:tibet|Tibet]] into administrative units.
mangyul-gungthang.r: The kings controlled the Kyirong pass, the easiest route between [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] and the Kathmandu valley, and profited from trade in salt, grain, wool and metalwork. They built fortresses and temples at Dzongkha, patronised scholars and [[e:printing-press|printing]], and stayed close to the [[s:sakya-regime|Sakya]] and later the [[s:phagmodrupa-dynasty|Phagmodrupa dynasty]], while ruling with a court of local nobles.
mangyul-gungthang.e: Gungthang declined in the 16th century amid struggles among central Tibetan powers. Around 1620 it was conquered by the [[s:tsangpa-dynasty|Tsangpa dynasty]], and the area later came under the [[s:ganden-phodrang|Ganden Phodrang]]. Sources on its later rulers are limited.

mazrui-sultanate.t: The rule of the Omani Mazrui family over Mombasa, which broke away from Oman and resisted its sultans for nearly a century.
mazrui-sultanate.o: After [[e:oman|Oman]] captured [[e:fort-jesus|Fort Jesus]] from [[s:portuguese-mombasa|Portuguese Mombasa]] in 1698, it appointed governors from the Mazrui clan. When the Ya'rubid dynasty of Oman fell in 1741, the governor [[e:muhammad-ibn-uthman-al-mazrui|Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Mazrui]] refused to recognise the new Busaidi rulers and made [[s:mombasa|Mombasa]] independent.
mazrui-sultanate.r: The Mazrui ruled from [[e:fort-jesus|Fort Jesus]] as governors-turned-sovereigns, allied with the twelve [[e:swahili|Swahili]] clans of [[s:mombasa|Mombasa]] and with mainland Mijikenda communities. At their height they controlled the coast from Pemba to Pate. Facing the Busaidi, they sought British protection, and Captain William Owen declared a short-lived [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1824 that [[e:london|London]] disowned in 1826.
mazrui-sultanate.e: [[e:said-bin-sultan|Sayyid Said of Oman]] conquered [[s:mombasa|Mombasa]] in 1837 and deported leading Mazrui. Branches of the family moved to Gazi and Takaungu on the Kenyan coast, and some rebelled against British rule in 1895 to 1896.

medulli.t: Alpine people of the Maurienne valley, among the mountain peoples finally subdued by Augustus.
medulli.o: Strabo places the Medulli on the highest mountains above the confluence of the Isère and the Rhône, and they are generally located in the Maurienne, the valley of the Arc in [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]]. They controlled routes towards the passes into [[e:italy|Italy]].
medulli.r: Almost nothing is known of their society beyond their mountain economy of herding and pass trade. They appear among the communities of the [[e:cottian-alps|Cottian Alps]].
medulli.e: Their name is listed among the Alpine peoples conquered by Augustus on the [[e:tropaeum-alpium|Tropaeum Alpium]] at La Turbie, erected in 7 to 6 BCE. Their land was divided between the [[e:cottian-alps|Cottian Alps]] and neighbouring districts.

mamunid-khwarazm.t: A brief Khwarazmian dynasty whose court at Gurganj gathered scholars such as al-Biruni and Ibn Sina before Mahmud of Ghazni absorbed it.
mamunid-khwarazm.o: The Ma'munids were rulers of [[e:gurganj|Gurganj]], the rising commercial city of northern [[e:khwarazm|Khwarazm]]. In 995 [[e:mamun-ibn-muhammad|Ma'mun ibn Muhammad]] defeated and killed the last Afrighid shah of Kath, uniting Khwarazm and taking the title Khwarazmshah.
mamunid-khwarazm.r: Ma'mun's sons Ali and [[e:abul-abbas-mamun|Ma'mun II]] made [[e:gurganj|Gurganj]] a centre of learning, hosting al-Biruni, [[e:avicenna|Ibn Sina]] and the mathematician Abu Nasr Mansur at a gathering later called the 'Academy of Ma'mun'. [[e:khwarazm|Khwarazm]] prospered on trade with the [[e:volga|Volga]] and the steppe. The Ma'munids balanced between the [[s:kara-khanid-khanate|Kara-Khanid Khanate]] and the rising [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavid Empire]], and Ma'mun II married a sister of [[e:mahmud-of-ghazni|Mahmud of Ghazni]].
mamunid-khwarazm.e: In 1017 [[e:abul-abbas-mamun|Ma'mun II]] was killed by his own troops, who resented Ghaznavid influence. [[e:mahmud-of-ghazni|Mahmud of Ghazni]] invaded, annexed [[e:khwarazm|Khwarazm]] and took al-Biruni to Ghazni. Khwarazm was then ruled by Ghaznavid and later Seljuk governors.

military-government-of-santo-domingo.t: The US occupation of the Dominican Republic from 1916 to 1924, which modernised roads and built the National Guard from which Rafael Trujillo rose.
military-government-of-santo-domingo.o: After years of civil war and default on foreign debt, President [[e:woodrow-wilson|Woodrow Wilson]] sent Marines to [[e:santo-domingo|Santo Domingo]] in May 1916. When the Dominican congress refused American conditions, Captain Harry Shepard Knapp proclaimed a military government in November 1916, ending the [[s:second-dominican-republic|Second Dominican Republic]].
military-government-of-santo-domingo.r: US naval officers ruled by decree, with Dominican ministers replaced by Americans. They disarmed the population, censored the press, built highways linking the main towns, expanded schools and reorganised finances. A land law favoured [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] companies, many of them American. In the eastern provinces peasant [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrillas]] called gavilleros resisted until 1922 and were met with harsh repression. A new [[e:national-guard-dominican-republic|National Guard]] was trained, in which [[e:rafael-trujillo|Rafael Trujillo]] rose quickly.
military-government-of-santo-domingo.e: Under the Hughes-Peynado plan of 1922, a provisional Dominican government was installed. [[e:horacio-vasquez|Horacio Vásquez]] won elections in 1924, and the Marines left in September 1924, creating the [[s:third-dominican-republic|Third Dominican Republic]].

morioka-domain.t: The domain of the Nanbu family in northern Honshu, known for its horses and for the frequent famines and peasant uprisings of its cold lands.
morioka-domain.o: The Nanbu were an old warrior family of northern Mutsu. [[e:nanbu-nobunao|Nanbu Nobunao]] was confirmed in his lands by [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] in 1590, though he lost the Tsugaru region to a breakaway [[e:vassal|vassal]]. He moved his seat to Morioka, where the castle was built in stages over several decades.
morioka-domain.r: Assessed at 100,000 koku, later raised to 200,000 in 1808 to pay for guarding Ezo, the domain had poor [[e:rice|rice]] yields and suffered repeated famines. It was famed for Nanbu horses and later for ironware. Heavy taxes provoked many peasant uprisings, culminating in the great Sanhei uprising of 1853, when thousands fled to the [[s:sendai-domain|Sendai Domain]]. The feud with the Tsugaru of Hirosaki lasted the whole period.
morioka-domain.e: Morioka joined the [[s:ouetsu-reppan-domei|Ouetsu Reppan Domei]] in 1868 and surrendered; it was briefly transferred and reduced. After abolition in 1871 it became part of Iwate Prefecture.

muli-state.t: A small Parmar Rajput state in the Jhalawad region of Saurashtra, one of the minor states of the Kathiawar Agency.
muli-state.o: The ruling [[e:parmar-rajputs|Parmar Rajputs]], by tradition, came to Saurashtra from Sindh and established themselves at Muli in the late 15th century.
muli-state.r: Muli was a small, dry agricultural state in the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]]. The temple of Mandavrayji, family deity of its Parmar rulers, stands in the town. Little detail of its history is recorded.
muli-state.e: Muli joined the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and is now in Surendranagar district, [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

maukharis.t: The dynasty that made Kannauj an imperial city in the 6th century, contesting the Gupta legacy before passing its throne to Harsha.
maukharis.o: Maukhari chiefs are known from inscriptions in Rajasthan and Bihar from earlier centuries. The line that ruled Kannauj began as feudatories of the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]] in the early 6th century. As Gupta power faded, Ishanavarman took the imperial title maharajadhiraja around 554.
maukharis.r: Ishanavarman claimed victories over the [[s:satavahana-dynasty|Andhras]], the Gaudas and the [[e:huns|Huns]], and the Maukharis fought a long rivalry with the [[s:later-guptas|Later Guptas]] for control of the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges plain]]. They ruled the Doab and Awadh from Kannauj, which began its rise as the leading city of northern [[e:india|India]]. They issued [[e:silver|silver]] coins modelled on Gupta issues and supported Vedic and Shaiva traditions.
maukharis.e: The last king, Grahavarman, married Rajyashri, sister of [[e:harsha|Harsha]], but was killed around 606 by the king of [[e:malwa|Malwa]]. Harsha of the [[s:pushyabhuti-dynasty|Pushyabhuti dynasty]] then took over the Maukhari kingdom and ruled from Kannauj.

mohanpur-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Mahi Kantha country in northern Gujarat, one of dozens of small Rajput holdings under British protection.
mohanpur-state.o: Mohanpur was one of the many petty estates of the [[e:mahi-kantha-agency|Mahi Kantha]] region, held by a [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] family whose origins are recorded mainly in local tradition. It emerged as a separate holding by around 1600.
mohanpur-state.r: The Thakor ruled a handful of villages, paying tribute to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads of Baroda]] and, after the early 19th century settlements, coming under the supervision of the [[e:mahi-kantha-agency|Mahi Kantha Agency]]. Few details of its rulers or internal affairs appear in standard references.
mohanpur-state.e: In 1948 Mohanpur was merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]], and its villages became part of Sabarkantha district in [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960.

moldavian-democratic-republic.t: Short-lived republic of Bessarabia proclaimed after the Russian Revolution, which voted for union with Romania in 1918.
moldavian-democratic-republic.o: After the fall of the Russian monarchy in 1917, Bessarabia's Romanian-speaking majority organised politically. A regional council, the [[e:sfatul-tarii|Sfatul Țării]], met in Chișinău and on 2 December 1917 proclaimed the Moldavian Democratic Republic as an autonomous member of a planned Russian federation, with [[e:ion-inculet|Ion Inculeț]] as president.
moldavian-democratic-republic.r: The council, elected by soldiers' congresses, peasants and national groups, struggled to govern amid deserting soldiers, peasant land seizures and Bolshevik agitation. In January 1918 Romanian troops entered Bessarabia, invited by part of the leadership, and drove out Bolshevik units. The republic proclaimed full independence on 24 January 1918, and land reform was a central issue.
moldavian-democratic-republic.e: On 27 March 1918 the [[e:sfatul-tarii|Sfatul Țării]] voted for union with the [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Kingdom of Romania]], under Romanian military presence. [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]] never recognised the union, and the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] annexed Bessarabia in 1940; much of it is now Moldova.

mandara-kingdom.t: Sultanate of the Wandala people at the foot of the Mandara mountains, which long held off both Bornu and the Fulani jihad.
mandara-kingdom.o: The Wandala kingdom developed on the plains north of the Mandara mountains, on the borderlands of present-day [[e:cameroon|Cameroon]] and [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]]. It was established by the 16th century, when [[e:bornu|Bornu]] sources mention it, and its capital moved between Keroua, Doulo and later Mora.
mandara-kingdom.r: Mandara's ruler, the tlikse, became a Muslim sultan in the early 18th century. The kingdom worked iron from the mountains and raided the non-Muslim mountain communities for slaves. It alternated between war and alliance with the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]], and in the 19th century fought off the [[e:fula|Fulani]] of the [[s:adamawa-emirate|Adamawa Emirate]], though it lost territory.
mandara-kingdom.e: German forces occupied Mandara around 1902, and it became part of [[s:kamerun|German Kamerun]] and later [[s:french-cameroon|French Cameroon]], with a small portion in [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]]. The sultan of Mandara remains a traditional ruler at Mora.

melingoi.t: Slavic tribe of the Taygetus mountains in the Peloponnese that kept a semi-independent life under Byzantine and Frankish rule for centuries.
melingoi.o: The Melingoi were descendants of [[e:slavs|Slavs]] who settled in the Peloponnese in the late 6th and 7th centuries. By the 9th century they lived on the slopes of Mount Taygetus, west of [[s:sparta|Sparta]]. [[e:constantine-vii|Constantine VII's]] De Administrando Imperio describes their revolt and subjugation by the general [[e:theoktistos-bryennios|Theoktistos Bryennios]] in the 840s.
melingoi.r: Living in mountain villages under their own leaders, the Melingoi paid the Byzantine state a small fixed tribute, 60 gold coins a year according to [[e:constantine-vii|Constantine VII]], rather than ordinary taxes. They revolted again in the 920s and had their tribute raised before it was reduced once more. The Chronicle of the Morea shows them still distinct in the 13th century.
melingoi.e: After the Frankish conquest, William of Villehardouin built Mistras and other castles in 1249 partly to control them; they later served as soldiers for both [[s:franks|Franks]] and [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]]. Gradually Christianised and Hellenised, they disappear as a separate group by the late [[e:middle-ages|Middle Ages]].
melingoi.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

malaysia.t: Federal constitutional monarchy formed in 1963, uniting the Malay Peninsula with Sabah and Sarawak in northern Borneo.
malaysia.o: Malaysia was formed on 16 September 1963 by joining the [[s:federation-of-malaya|Federation of Malaya]] with [[s:singapore|Singapore]], the [[s:crown-colony-of-north-borneo|Crown Colony of North Borneo]] (Sabah) and the [[s:crown-colony-of-sarawak|Crown Colony of Sarawak]]. [[s:brunei-sultanate|Brunei]] declined to join. [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]] opposed the federation in the Confrontation of 1963 to 1966, and tensions with [[e:singapore|Singapore]] led to its expulsion in 1965.
malaysia.r: Malaysia is a federation of thirteen states and federal territories with a parliamentary system and a king elected every five years from the nine hereditary Malay rulers. After the race riots of 13 May 1969 the New Economic Policy favoured the Malay and indigenous majority. Under Mahathir Mohamad from 1981 to 2003 it industrialised rapidly, exporting electronics, [[e:palm-oil|palm oil]] and petroleum.
malaysia.e: The ruling Barisan Nasional coalition, in power since independence, lost the 2018 election after the 1MDB scandal. Several changes of government followed, and [[e:anwar-ibrahim|Anwar Ibrahim]] became prime minister in 2022.

min-ten-kingdoms.t: A kingdom in Fujian under the Wang family, which opened the province to overseas trade before tearing itself apart in dynastic feuds.
min-ten-kingdoms.o: The brothers Wang Chao and [[e:wang-shenzhi|Wang Shenzhi]], leaders of a band of soldiers from Henan, conquered Fujian in the 890s. After Wang Chao's death in 898 Wang Shenzhi ruled from Changle (Fuzhou), and in 909 the [[s:later-liang|Later Liang]] named him Prince of Min.
min-ten-kingdoms.r: [[e:wang-shenzhi|Wang Shenzhi]] governed frugally, lightened taxes, promoted schools and welcomed foreign merchants to the ports of Fuzhou and [[e:quanzhou|Quanzhou]], laying the base for Fujian's later maritime prosperity. He was a generous patron of Buddhist monasteries. His successors were less able: [[e:wang-yanjun|Wang Yanjun]] proclaimed himself emperor in 933, and later rulers murdered each other in a series of coups.
min-ten-kingdoms.e: In 943 Wang Yanzheng founded a rival state, Yin, at Jianzhou, and civil war followed. [[s:southern-tang|Southern Tang]] conquered most of Min in 945; Fuzhou passed to [[s:wuyue|Wuyue]] in 947 and [[e:quanzhou|Quanzhou]] to local commanders who submitted to the [[s:song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]] in 978.

madhya-bharat.t: The union of Gwalior, Indore and the smaller Malwa states, an Indian state from 1948 to 1956 with Gwalior and Indore as twin capitals.
madhya-bharat.o: In 1948 the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] states of [[s:gwalior-state|Gwalior State]] and [[s:indore-state|Indore State]] joined with more than twenty smaller states of [[e:malwa|Malwa]], including Dhar, [[s:dewas-senior|Dewas Senior]], [[s:dewas-junior|Dewas Junior]], [[s:ratlam-state|Ratlam]] and [[s:jaora-state|Jaora]], to form the United State of Gwalior, Indore and Malwa, known as Madhya [[s:republic-of-india|Bharat]].
madhya-bharat.r: [[e:jivajirao-scindia|Jivajirao Scindia]] of [[s:gwalior-state|Gwalior]] served as Rajpramukh and [[e:yashwant-rao-holkar-ii|Yashwant Rao Holkar II]] as Uprajpramukh. Gwalior was the winter capital and [[s:indore-state|Indore]] the summer capital. It became a Part B state of [[e:india|India]] in 1950, with an elected government; Indore's textile mills and the rich black-soil farmland of [[e:malwa|Malwa]] were its economic base.
madhya-bharat.e: Under the States Reorganisation Act Madhya [[s:republic-of-india|Bharat]] was merged into Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 1956, except Sunel, transferred to Rajasthan.

muang-sua.t: The early Tai-Lao principality at the meeting of the Mekong and Nam Khan, the site of Luang Prabang and the cradle of the kingdom of Lan Xang.
muang-sua.o: Lao chronicles say [[e:khun-lo|Khun Lo]], a son of the mythical [[e:khun-borom|Khun Borom]], took Muang Sua from its earlier inhabitants and founded a dynasty there, traditionally in the 8th century. The town, also called Xieng Dong Xieng Thong, occupied the site of present-day [[s:kingdom-of-luang-phrabang|Luang Prabang]], which had earlier been settled by Mon-[[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] peoples.
muang-sua.r: Muang Sua was a Tai muang, a valley principality ruled by a chief whose authority rested on [[e:rice|rice]] lands, river trade and ties to other Tai rulers. Lao tradition records a long line of rulers, but few are attested outside the chronicles. In the late 13th century it seems to have come under the influence of [[s:sukhothai-kingdom|Sukhothai]].
muang-sua.e: In 1353 [[e:fa-ngum|Fa Ngum]], a Lao prince raised at the [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] court, captured Muang Sua with Khmer support and made it the capital of his new kingdom of [[s:lan-xang|Lan Xang]]. The city was renamed [[s:kingdom-of-luang-phrabang|Luang Prabang]] after the [[e:phra-bang|Phra Bang]] Buddha image was installed there in the 16th century.

mahra-sultanate.t: The sultanate of the Mahra people, ruling the far east of Yemen and the island of Socotra until the British withdrawal in 1967.
mahra-sultanate.o: The Mahra, a people speaking a Modern [[e:south-arabia|South Arabian]] language rather than Arabic, lived in the far east of [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] and on Socotra. In the 15th century the Afrar family established a sultanate ruling Qishn on the mainland and the island of Socotra, with a seat at Tamrida (modern Hadibu).
mahra-sultanate.r: The sultanate was loose, depending on tribal loyalty and revenues from frankincense, aloes, livestock and ship traffic. In 1507 the Portuguese seized Socotra and held it until 1511. In 1886 the sultan signed a protection treaty with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], and the sultanate became part of the [[s:aden-protectorate|Aden Protectorate]], with Socotra valued for its position on shipping routes. Mehri and Soqotri are still spoken.
mahra-sultanate.e: After the National Liberation Front took over the region in 1967, the sultanate was abolished and incorporated into [[s:south-yemen|South Yemen]], later the [[s:republic-of-yemen|Republic of Yemen]].

mediomatrici.t: Gallic people of the Moselle valley whose chief town Divodurum became the city of Metz.
mediomatrici.o: The Mediomatrici held the middle Moselle and Seille valleys in [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]]. Caesar notes that their territory once reached the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], before [[e:germanic-peoples|Germanic peoples]] such as the [[s:triboci|Triboci]] settled on its left bank.
mediomatrici.r: Little is known of their rulers. Their territory lay on the trade routes linking the Rhône and Saône with the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and the Moselle, and their oppidum at Divodurum controlled the Moselle crossing.
mediomatrici.e: They sent five thousand men to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] Divodurum became a major town on the road from Lyon to [[e:trier|Trier]], known in late antiquity as Mettis after the people, from which comes Metz, later capital of [[s:austrasia|Austrasia]].

maedi.t: Thracian tribe of the middle Strymon valley that raided Macedon for centuries and fought Philip II, Alexander and Rome.
maedi.o: The Maedi lived along the middle Strymon (Struma) in modern south-western [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] from at least the 5th century BCE, as independent Thracian highlanders.
maedi.r: Known mainly from Greek and Roman accounts of war, the Maedi were a tribal people of hill country, often raiding Macedonia. In 340 BCE the young Alexander, regent for [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II]], defeated them and founded Alexandroupolis in their land. Some scholars read Plutarch as saying that Spartacus was a Maedian.
maedi.e: After [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]] became a Roman province in 146 BCE, the Maedi raided it repeatedly; Roman commanders including Sulla fought them in the 80s BCE. They were later absorbed into the Roman province of Thrace.

manavadar-state.t: A small Babi Pathan state in Kathiawar whose ruler, like his kinsman of Junagadh, tried to join Pakistan in 1947.
manavadar-state.o: Manavadar was held by a branch of the Babi family, the Pathan dynasty that ruled [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh State]]. It became a separate chiefship in the 18th century and, together with Bantva, formed a small Muslim-ruled holding in western Saurashtra.
manavadar-state.r: The Khan of Manavadar governed a largely [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] farming population under the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]] and later the [[e:western-india-states-agency|Western India States Agency]]. It was a minor state with no gun salute and little recorded political history.
manavadar-state.e: In 1947 the Khan, [[e:ghulam-moinuddin-khanji|Ghulam Moinuddin Khanji]], acceded to [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] along with [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]]. [[e:india|India]] took control in October 1947, and in 1948 Manavadar was merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]]; it now lies in Junagadh district of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

malaka.t: A Phoenician harbour on the Costa del Sol that grew into Málaga, one of Iberia's oldest cities.
malaka.o: [[e:phoenicians|Phoenicians]] settled the bay of Málaga in the 8th century BCE, first at Cerro del Villar on an island in the mouth of the Guadalhorce, and then on the hill below the later Alcazaba, where Malaka grew into the main settlement by the 6th century BCE.
malaka.r: Malaka traded with the Iberian peoples of the interior and lived from fishing, fish salting and crafts. It was later drawn into the Carthaginian sphere, and its coins with Punic legends showed a smith god with tongs. Strabo described it as a market for the nomads of the opposite African coast.
malaka.e: After 206 BCE Malaka came under [[e:rome|Rome]] as an allied city. As Malaca it received municipal status under the Flavian emperors, recorded in the bronze Lex Flavia Malacitana, and continued as a major port of [[s:hispania-baetica|Hispania Baetica]].

mirdasid-emirate.t: A Bedouin dynasty of the Banu Kilab that ruled Aleppo for half a century, balancing between Byzantium and the Fatimids.
mirdasid-emirate.o: [[e:salih-ibn-mirdas|Salih ibn Mirdas]], chief of the Banu Kilab who dominated the steppe of northern [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]], joined the 1024 Bedouin alliance against the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] and captured [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] from its Fatimid governor, becoming its emir.
mirdasid-emirate.r: [[s:salihids|Salih]] was killed in 1029 at al-Uqhuwana, but his son [[e:shibl-al-dawla-nasr|Shibl al-Dawla Nasr]] defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos III near Azaz in 1030 and then accepted Byzantine protection. The Mirdasids relied on tribal horsemen and the city's Shi'i notables, alternated between Fatimid and Byzantine alliances, and under Thimal ruled a wide area of northern [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. Family quarrels repeatedly divided the [[e:emirate|emirate]].
mirdasid-emirate.e: In 1070 Mahmud ibn Nasr switched allegiance to the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] to placate the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]]. Weakened by internal feuds and [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] pressure, the dynasty lost [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] in 1080 to the Uqaylid Muslim ibn [[e:quraysh|Quraysh]], and the city soon passed to the [[s:seljuk-sultanate-of-syria|Seljuk Sultanate of Syria]].

maqpon-dynasty.t: The long-ruling dynasty of Baltistan, whose rajas governed Skardu high in the Karakoram for six centuries until the Dogra conquest.
maqpon-dynasty.o: Maqpon tradition holds that the dynasty was founded around 1190 by [[e:ibrahim-shah|Ibrahim Shah]], a foreign prince who married into the local ruling house of Skardu. The early centuries are known only from later Balti chronicles and genealogies, which present the line as continuous rulers of the [[e:indus|Indus]] valley around Skardu.
maqpon-dynasty.r: [[e:ali-sher-khan-anchan|Ali Sher Khan Anchan]], in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, was the most famous ruler: he campaigned into [[s:kingdom-of-ladakh|Ladakh]] and Gilgit and is credited with building the Skardu fort and with polo's spread in the region. The population converted to [[e:islam|Islam]], mainly Noorbakhshi and [[e:shia-islam|Shia]], from the 14th century. The rajas traded and intermarried with Ladakh and acknowledged Mughal suzerainty for a time.
maqpon-dynasty.e: In 1840 the [[e:dogras|Dogra]] general [[e:zorawar-singh|Zorawar Singh]], serving [[e:gulab-singh|Gulab Singh of Jammu]], conquered Baltistan and deposed the last Maqpon raja, Ahmad Shah. The region became part of [[s:jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state|Jammu and Kashmir]] and since 1948 has been administered by [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] as part of Gilgit-Baltistan.

mississippi-in-africa.t: A short-lived colony on the Sinoe river in Liberia, settled by freed slaves from Mississippi plantations, which merged into Liberia in 1842.
mississippi-in-africa.o: The [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] Colonization Society, founded by planters in the 1830s, established a colony at the mouth of the Sinoe river in 1835. Its first town was Greenville. The best-known emigrants, people freed under the will of the planter Isaac Ross, could leave only after his heirs had fought the will in court for years, and reached Greenville in the late 1840s, after the colony had joined [[s:liberia|Liberia]].
mississippi-in-africa.r: The colony was small and poorly supplied, run by agents of the society with settler leaders. Settlers farmed and traded with the Kru people of the coast, but disease, shortages and conflict with local communities made life hard, and the colony depended on help from other settlements.
mississippi-in-africa.e: In 1842 Mississippi-in-[[e:africa|Africa]], unable to survive alone, joined the [[s:colony-of-liberia|Commonwealth of Liberia]], and it later became Sinoe County of the [[s:liberia|Republic of Liberia]], with Greenville as its capital, a name the county seat still bears.

mahlog-state.t: A small Rajput hill state in the lower Shimla hills, ruled from Patta, one of the Simla Hill States.
mahlog-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins.
mahlog-state.r: Mahlog was a small state of hill villages near the edge of the plains. It was occupied by the Gurkhas of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]] in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. Its history is poorly recorded.
mahlog-state.e: Mahlog merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Solan district.

melos.t: Dorian island of the Cyclades whose refusal to join Athens ended in the massacre of 416 BCE described in Thucydides's Melian Dialogue.
melos.o: Melos was famous from the Neolithic for its obsidian and had an important [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] town at Phylakopi. In the early [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] it was settled by [[e:dorians|Dorians]] who claimed Spartan descent. The city grew on the bay of Klima, on the north side of the island's great natural harbour.
melos.r: Melos was a small oligarchic state that sent ships to Salamis in 480 BCE but, like Dorian [[s:thera|Thera]], stayed outside the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]]. [[s:athens|Athens]] attacked it in 426 BCE and besieged it in 416 BCE. Thucydides's Melian Dialogue presents the debate over power and justice before the siege.
melos.e: After the city surrendered in 416 BCE, [[s:athens|Athens]] killed the men, enslaved the women and children and settled 500 colonists. Lysander restored surviving Melians in 405 BCE. The later town produced the Aphrodite of Milos, the Venus de Milo.

manteno-huancavilca.t: Seafaring chiefdoms of the Ecuadorian coast whose balsa rafts carried spondylus shell and trade goods along the Pacific from Mexico to Peru.
manteno-huancavilca.o: The Manteño and Huancavilca peoples developed from earlier coastal traditions in present-day Manabí, Guayas and Santa Elena from around 800. The Manteño occupied the central coast, with Jocay, near modern Manta, as a main port, while the Huancavilca lived to the south around the Gulf of Guayaquil.
manteno-huancavilca.r: The coastal chiefdoms formed a league of lordships under several chiefs. They were skilled sailors: in 1526 the Spanish pilot Bartolomé Ruiz met a large sailing balsa raft loaded with trade goods off the coast. Spondylus shell, prized in Andean ritual, was a key export. The Manteño carved U-shaped stone seats and stelae, and built settlements with stone foundations on hills such as Cerro de Hojas-Jaboncillo.
manteno-huancavilca.e: The coastal peoples largely avoided [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] rule. Spanish conquest after 1534, followed by epidemics, devastated the population, and Portoviejo and Guayaquil were founded in their lands. Descendant communities on the Santa Elena peninsula have revived Manteño and Huancavilca identity.

munqidhite-emirate-of-shaizar.t: A small Arab emirate on the Orontes that survived between Crusaders and Muslim powers and produced the memoirist Usama ibn Munqidh.
munqidhite-emirate-of-shaizar.o: The Banu Munqidh, an Arab family of the Kinana, held lands near Shaizar on the Orontes. In 1081 [[e:ali-ibn-munqidh|Ali ibn Munqidh]] acquired the fortress of Shaizar from its Byzantine-appointed [[e:bishop|bishop]] and made it the seat of a family [[e:emirate|emirate]].
munqidhite-emirate-of-shaizar.r: Shaizar's castle on a ridge above the Orontes was its strength. The [[e:emir|emirs]] paid tribute or fought as needed against the [[s:principality-of-antioch|Principality of Antioch]], the [[e:nizari-ismailism|Nizari Ismailis]] and Turkish rulers of [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], and withstood a siege by the Byzantine emperor John II Komnenos and Frankish allies in 1138. Usama ibn Munqidh, born there in 1095, wrote the Kitab al-I'tibar, vivid memoirs of hunting, war and Frankish customs.
munqidhite-emirate-of-shaizar.e: In 1157 a great earthquake destroyed the citadel during a family celebration and killed nearly all the Munqidhites. [[e:nur-al-din|Nur al-Din]] of the [[s:zengid-dynasty|Zengid dynasty]] took the ruins and rebuilt the fortress.

monte-alban.t: The Zapotec capital on a levelled mountain above the Valley of Oaxaca, one of the earliest cities and states of Mesoamerica.
monte-alban.o: Around 500 BCE communities of the [[e:valley-of-oaxaca|Valley of Oaxaca]] founded a new centre on a defensible hilltop where the valley's three arms meet. The move, probably by an alliance led from San José Mogote, created a capital that soon dominated the valley.
monte-alban.r: The Main Plaza was framed by temples, palaces and a ballcourt. The early Danzantes carvings show slain or sacrificed captives, and Building J lists conquered places, among the earliest evidence of Zapotec writing and expansion. Monte Albán controlled the valley and areas beyond, kept diplomatic ties with [[s:teotihuacan|Teotihuacan]], and buried its nobles in painted tombs.
monte-alban.e: Monte Albán's population and authority declined between about 700 and 850 CE, and power passed to smaller valley centres such as [[s:zaachila|Zaachila]], Lambityeco and [[s:mitla|Mitla]]. Mixtec nobles later reused its tombs, including the famous Tomb 7 treasure.

muang-phuan.t: A Tai Phuan principality on the Plain of Jars in north-eastern Laos, caught for centuries between Lan Xang, Vietnam and Siam.
muang-phuan.o: Muang Phuan, centred on Xieng Khouang, emerged among the Tai Phuan people of the high plateau; Lao chronicles link its ruling house to [[e:khun-borom|Khun Borom]] and date its founding to the 14th century, when it was brought into [[e:fa-ngum|Fa Ngum's]] [[s:lan-xang|Lan Xang]]. The plateau is famous for the much older stone jars of the Plain of Jars.
muang-phuan.r: Its rulers governed a strategic upland crossroads between the [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]] valley and [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]], paying tribute to [[s:lan-xang|Lan Xang]] and later to [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Vientiane]] and [[e:luang-prabang|Luang Phrabang]], while often sending tribute to [[s:later-le-dynasty|Dai Viet]] as well. Buddhist temples and stupas filled the capital. Its position made it a frequent battlefield and source of forced [[e:deportation|deportations]].
muang-phuan.e: Siam deported much of the Phuan population across the [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]] in the 1830s, and the [[s:nguyen-dynasty|Nguyen dynasty]] briefly annexed Xieng Khouang as Tran Ninh. Chinese Haw bands ravaged it in the 1870s. Under the French it became part of [[e:laos|Laos]], and its ruler lost power by 1899.

monastic-community-of-mount-athos.t: Self-governing Orthodox monastic republic on the Athos peninsula in northern Greece, continuously inhabited by monks for over a thousand years.
monastic-community-of-mount-athos.o: Hermits lived on the mountainous Athos peninsula from at least the 9th century. In 963 [[e:athanasios-the-athonite|Athanasios the Athonite]], with the backing of his friend the general and future emperor [[e:nikephoros-ii-phokas|Nikephoros Phokas]], founded the Great Lavra, the first large monastery. The first charter, the Tragos, issued under John Tzimiskes around 972, organised the community under a Protos at Karyes.
monastic-community-of-mount-athos.r: Twenty ruling monasteries, Greek, Serbian (Hilandar), Russian (Saint Panteleimon), Bulgarian (Zograf) and others, own the land and send representatives to the Holy Community at Karyes. Women have been excluded since the [[e:middle-ages|Middle Ages]]. Life follows the Byzantine liturgical calendar and day, and the monasteries hold great libraries of [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]] and icons.
monastic-community-of-mount-athos.e: Athos kept its autonomy under Byzantine, Serbian and Ottoman rulers. Greek forces took it in 1912, and the [[e:treaty-of-lausanne|Treaty of Lausanne]] and the Greek constitution of 1927 confirmed its self-government under Greek [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], with a civil governor. It is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

morvi-state.t: A Jadeja Rajput state of Kathiawar founded by a displaced heir of Kutch, later known for its railways, port and tile and clock industries.
morvi-state.o: Morvi was founded in 1698 by Kanyoji, the eldest son of the Rao of [[s:cutch-state|Kutch]], who had been passed over for the Kutch throne. He established himself on the Machhu river in northern Kathiawar.
morvi-state.r: The Thakore Sahibs ruled a territory of [[e:cotton|cotton]] farms with a port on the Gulf of [[s:cutch-state|Kutch]]. Waghji and Lakhdhirji in the late 19th and early 20th centuries built a light railway, tramway and Navlakhi port and fostered local industry. It was an eleven-gun salute state.
morvi-state.e: Morvi merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960. Morbi is now a centre of ceramic tiles and clocks.

mutawakkilite-kingdom-of-yemen.t: The Zaydi kingdom of the Hamid al-Din imams, which held North Yemen in deliberate isolation from 1918 until the 1962 revolution.
mutawakkilite-kingdom-of-yemen.o: [[e:imam|Imam]] Yahya Muhammad Hamid al-Din had led the Zaydi resistance against the [[s:yemen-vilayet|Yemen Vilayet]] and gained autonomy in 1911. When the Ottoman garrisons left after the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] in 1918, he entered Sanaa as ruler of an independent state, taking the title al-Mutawakkil.
mutawakkilite-kingdom-of-yemen.r: The [[e:imam|imams]] ruled as religious and political heads, with power concentrated in the family and in hostages taken from the tribes to guarantee loyalty. Yahya kept [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] isolated, built a small army and claimed the [[e:aden-protectorate|British Aden Protectorate]]. A war with [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]] in 1934 lost Asir, Jizan and Najran under the [[e:treaty-of-taif|Treaty of Ta'if]]. Yahya was assassinated in 1948, and his son Ahmad ruled from Ta'izz.
mutawakkilite-kingdom-of-yemen.e: Ahmad died in September 1962. A week later army officers led by [[e:abdullah-al-sallal|Abdullah al-Sallal]] overthrew his son [[e:muhammad-al-badr|Muhammad al-Badr]] and proclaimed the [[s:yemen-arab-republic|Yemen Arab Republic]]. Royalists backed by [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]] fought republicans backed by [[e:egypt|Egypt]] until a settlement in 1970.

margraviate-of-baden.t: A south-west German margraviate on the upper Rhine, divided for two centuries, reunited in 1771 and later the Grand Duchy of Baden.
margraviate-of-baden.o: Hermann II, of the Zähringen family, first called himself margrave of Baden in 1112, after the castle of Baden near [[s:margraviate-of-baden-baden|Baden-Baden]]. The title derived from his family's claim to the [[s:march-of-verona|March of Verona]]. The margraves built lands in the upper [[e:rhine|Rhine]] plain and the northern [[e:black-forest|Black Forest]].
margraviate-of-baden.r: In 1535 Baden split into Catholic [[s:margraviate-of-baden-baden|Baden-Baden]] and Protestant [[s:margraviate-of-baden-durlach|Baden-Durlach]]. [[e:louis-william-margrave-of-baden-baden|Louis William of Baden-Baden]], the 'Turkish Louis', fought the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] and built Rastatt Palace. [[e:charles-iii-william-margrave-of-baden-durlach|Charles III William]] of Baden-Durlach founded Karlsruhe in 1715, a planned city radiating from the palace. [[e:charles-frederick-grand-duke-of-baden|Charles Frederick]], an enlightened ruler, abolished [[e:serfdom|serfdom]] in 1783.
margraviate-of-baden.e: The two lines reunited under [[e:charles-frederick-grand-duke-of-baden|Charles Frederick]] in 1771. [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] reorganisation tripled Baden's size: it became an electorate in 1803 and a grand duchy in 1806. Today it forms part of Baden-Württemberg.

march-of-ivrea.t: March in north-western Italy whose Anscarid rulers, Berengar II and Arduin, both seized the Italian crown.
march-of-ivrea.o: Around 888–891 [[e:guy-iii-of-spoleto|Guy of Spoleto]], contending for the Italian crown, created a march around Ivrea for his Burgundian ally Anscar, guarding the Alpine passes of the Aosta valley and the western Po plain. Anscar's descendants, the Anscarids, held it for more than a century.
march-of-ivrea.r: The margraves of Ivrea controlled a large area of Piedmont and [[e:lombardy|Lombardy]]. Anscar's grandson [[e:berengar-ii-of-italy|Berengar II]], after exile in [[e:germany|Germany]], made himself King of [[e:italy|Italy]] in 950 with his son Adalbert, until [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] forced him to submit in 952 and deposed him in 961. A later margrave, Arduin, was elected king in 1002 in opposition to the German emperor [[e:henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor|Henry II]].
march-of-ivrea.e: [[e:henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor|Henry II]] defeated Arduin, who retired to the monastery of Fruttuaria and died in 1015. The march was then broken up, its lands divided among [[e:bishop|bishops]] and other families, notably the Arduinici of Turin.

mauretania-caesariensis.t: The Roman province of western and central Algeria, governed from Juba II's former capital at Caesarea.
mauretania-caesariensis.o: Claudius created Mauretania Caesariensis in 42 CE from the eastern part of the [[s:kingdom-of-mauretania|Kingdom of Mauretania]], after the murder of [[e:ptolemy-of-mauretania|King Ptolemy]]. Its capital was [[s:lordship-of-caesarea|Caesarea]] (Cherchell), the former royal city of [[e:juba-ii|Juba II]], and it was governed by an equestrian procurator with [[e:auxilia|auxiliary troops]].
mauretania-caesariensis.r: Roman towns grew along the coast and fertile valleys, with veteran colonies and estates producing grain and [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]], while [[e:berbers|Berber]] tribes held the mountains. Frontier forts gradually moved south. [[e:diocletian|Diocletian]] divided off [[s:kingdom-of-mauretania|Mauretania]] Sitifensis in the east. [[e:christianity|Christianity]], and the Donatist movement, spread widely. The revolts of the Berber princes Firmus around 372 to 375 and his brother Gildo showed the power of local dynasts.
mauretania-caesariensis.e: The [[e:vandals|Vandals]] overran the province from 429, and by treaty in 435 [[e:rome|Rome]] conceded control. As Roman authority faded, [[e:berbers|Berber]] leaders such as Masuna created the [[s:kingdom-of-the-moors-and-romans|Kingdom of the Moors and Romans]] in the western part.

myus.t: The smallest of the twelve Ionian cities, near the mouth of the Maeander, eventually abandoned as silt turned its harbour into marsh.
myus.o: Myus was founded, by tradition, by Cydrelus, a son of [[e:codrus|Codrus of Athens]], c. 1000 BCE on the Latmian Gulf near the mouth of the Maeander. Though small, it ranked as one of the twelve members of the [[s:ionian-league|Ionian League]].
myus.r: Myus lived from fishing and the farmland of the Maeander valley. It sent three ships to the [[e:battle-of-lade|Battle of Lade]] in 494 BCE. Later the Persian king Artaxerxes I granted the exiled Themistocles the revenues of Myus to supply him with relish. It then paid tribute in the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]].
myus.e: The silting of the Maeander turned the gulf into a lake and marsh, and Pausanias says mosquitoes drove the people to move to [[s:miletus|Miletus]], which absorbed the city by c. 200 BCE. Only a temple of Dionysus and scattered ruins remain.

military-frontier.t: Habsburg defensive belt along the Ottoman border, where soldier-settlers held land in return for military service and lived under army rule.
military-frontier.o: After Mohács the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] organised the Croatian and Slavonian border into fortified captaincies, formalised around 1553 with funds from the Austrian estates. Karlovac was founded in 1579 as a frontier fortress. [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Vlach and Serb refugees from Ottoman lands were settled as Grenzer, receiving land and freedom from [[e:serfdom|serfdom]] in return for service.
military-frontier.r: The frontier was run by army officers answering to the War Council in [[e:vienna|Vienna]] and Graz, not to the Croatian ban or Hungarian diet. Grenzer families lived in communal households, zadrugas, and owed lifelong military service. The 1630 Statuta Valachorum confirmed their privileges. In the 18th century the system was extended to Banat and [[s:principality-of-transylvania|Transylvania]], guarding against plague as well as raids.
military-frontier.e: With the Ottoman threat gone, the frontier was dissolved between 1871 and 1881 and reattached to [[s:kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia|Croatia-Slavonia]] and [[e:hungary|Hungary]]. It left large Serb communities in Croatia, whose Krajina later became the base of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the 1990s.

marca-hispanica.t: The Carolingian frontier zone south and east of the Pyrenees, the cradle of the Catalan counties and of Catalonia itself.
marca-hispanica.o: After failing at [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] in 778, [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] forces built a buffer zone against [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]]. Girona submitted in 785, and [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious]], king of [[s:duchy-of-aquitaine|Aquitaine]], took Barcelona in 801. The resulting counties, among them Barcelona, Girona, Urgell, Cerdanya, Osona, Empúries and Roussillon, became known as the Spanish March.
marca-hispanica.r: It was never a single state but a group of counties under counts appointed by the Frankish kings, sometimes grouped under one marquis such as [[e:bernard-of-septimania|Bernard of Septimania]]. The Gothic population kept the Visigothic law code. Revolts such as Aissó's in 826 and Muslim raids made it unstable. From 878 the counts, led by [[e:wilfred-the-hairy|Wilfred the Hairy]], made their offices hereditary.
marca-hispanica.e: Frankish authority faded through the 10th century. When the [[e:caliphate|Caliphate's]] general Almanzor sacked Barcelona in 985 no help came, and in 988 Count [[e:borrell-ii-of-barcelona|Borrell II]] did not renew homage to the new Capetian king, a step later seen as the birth of Catalan independence.

march-of-verona.t: Imperial march in north-eastern Italy created by Otto I in 952, which joined Verona, Friuli and Istria to the German duchies until the Veronese cities rose against Barbarossa.
march-of-verona.o: In 952 [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] forced [[e:berengar-ii-of-italy|Berengar II]], King of [[e:italy|Italy]], to cede [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]], Friuli, Aquileia and [[s:histria|Istria]]. Otto attached these lands to the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria|Duchy of Bavaria]] under his brother Henry, creating a march that secured the Brenner and eastern Alpine routes between [[e:germany|Germany]] and Italy. In 976 it passed with the new [[s:duchy-of-carinthia|Duchy of Carinthia]].
march-of-verona.r: The march was held by German dukes and margraves who rarely resided there, among them Henry I of Bavaria, dukes of Carinthia and Berthold of Zähringen; Hermann I, margrave of [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]] in the 1060s, passed the title to his heirs, the margraves of Baden. Real power in the region shifted to [[e:bishop|bishops]], the patriarchs of Aquileia and the growing city of Verona.
march-of-verona.e: In 1164 [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]], [[s:commune-of-vicenza|Vicenza]], [[s:commune-of-padua|Padua]] and [[s:commune-of-treviso|Treviso]] formed the [[s:veronese-league|Veronese League]] against [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]], and the league later merged into the [[s:lombard-league|Lombard League]]. The march ceased to function, and Verona became a self-governing commune. The margraves of Baden kept the title.

marabout-state-of-al-ayyashi.t: The holy-war state of the marabout Muhammad al-Ayyashi, who led Moroccan resistance to Spanish coastal forts from Salé.
marabout-state-of-al-ayyashi.o: [[e:spain|Spain]] took Larache in 1610 and [[e:mehdya|La Mamora]] in 1614 as the [[s:saadi-sultanate|Saadi Sultanate]] fell apart. [[e:muhammad-al-ayyashi|Muhammad al-Ayyashi]], a [[e:sufism|Sufi]] disciple appointed as governor near Azemmour, broke with the weak Saadi court and around 1614 began leading tribal holy war against the Christian forts, based at Salé.
marabout-state-of-al-ayyashi.r: Al-Ayyashi's authority rested on religious charisma and the tribes of the Atlantic plains rather than formal institutions. He besieged [[e:mehdya|La Mamora]] and Spanish and Portuguese positions, and controlled the region of Salé, clashing with the [[e:moriscos|Morisco]] settlers of the [[s:republic-of-sale|Republic of Salé]], whom he suspected of dealing with [[e:spain|Spain]].
marabout-state-of-al-ayyashi.e: In 1641 al-Ayyashi was defeated and killed by forces allied with the [[s:dilaiyya|Dila'iyya]], whose zawiya then took over his territory and influence over Salé.

myanmar.t: Independent Burma, renamed Myanmar in 1989, a union of many peoples whose history since 1948 has been dominated by ethnic conflict and military rule.
myanmar.o: [[e:burma|Burma]] became independent from [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] on 4 January 1948 as the Union of Burma, after [[e:aung-san|Aung San]] negotiated with the British and agreed at the Panglong Conference with Shan, Kachin and Chin leaders to form a union. Aung San was assassinated in 1947, and U Nu became the first prime minister.
myanmar.r: Communist and ethnic insurgencies, including the Karen, began almost immediately. General Ne Win seized power in 1962 and pursued the Burmese Way to [[e:socialism|Socialism]], isolating and impoverishing the country. After the 1988 uprising a new junta renamed the country Myanmar and ignored the 1990 election won by [[e:aung-san|Aung San]] Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy. The capital moved from Yangon to Naypyidaw in 2005 to 2006.
myanmar.e: A partial transition after 2011 brought an NLD government in 2016, but the military expelled over 700,000 Rohingya in 2017 and seized power again in February 2021. The coup sparked a nationwide armed resistance, and the conflict continues.

marrucini.t: Small Sabellic people on the Adriatic coast around Teate (Chieti), allies of Rome from 304 BCE and rebels in the Social War.
marrucini.o: The Marrucini occupied a narrow strip between the Aterno river and the Foro, inland of the Adriatic coast in modern Abruzzo, with Teate as their main town. They were counted among the Sabellian peoples and spoke a dialect close to Oscan.
marrucini.r: Little is known of their organisation beyond a single community centred on Teate. A bronze inscription from Rapino, the Tabula Rapinensis, records a sacred regulation in their dialect. Like their neighbours, they lived by farming and herding.
marrucini.e: The Marrucini made an alliance with [[e:rome|Rome]] in 304 BCE with the [[s:marsi|Marsi]] and [[s:paeligni|Paeligni]] and fought for Rome against [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]]. In the Social War they joined the rebels; their commander [[e:herius-asinius|Herius Asinius]] was killed in 90 BCE. They gained citizenship afterwards, and Teate became a Roman municipium.

massylii.t: The eastern Numidian kingdom of Gaia and Masinissa, whose cavalry helped decide the Second Punic War.
massylii.o: The Massylii were a [[e:berbers|Berber]] people of eastern [[e:algeria|Algeria]] and western [[e:tunisia|Tunisia]], bordering Carthaginian territory. By the 3rd century BCE they were ruled by kings, and they long fought for [[e:carthage|Carthage]] as allies and [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:punic-empire|Punic Empire]], supplying its famous Numidian cavalry.
massylii.r: The kingdom was a federation of tribes under a royal clan, with succession often passing between brothers, which caused disputes. King Gaia sent his son [[e:masinissa|Masinissa]] to fight for [[e:carthage|Carthage]] in [[e:spain|Spain]]. After Gaia's death the throne passed through Oezalces, Capussa and Lacumazes amid civil war, while Syphax of the [[s:masaesyli|Masaesyli]] seized Massylian lands. Masinissa switched sides to [[e:rome|Rome]] in 206 BCE.
massylii.e: With Roman help [[e:masinissa|Masinissa]] recovered his father's kingdom, defeated Syphax in 203 BCE and fought at Zama in 202 BCE. He then united the Massylii and [[s:masaesyli|Masaesyli]] into [[s:numidia|Numidia]], with Cirta as its capital.

marashi-dynasty.t: A dynasty of Shia sayyids that ruled Mazandaran on the Caspian for over two centuries, linked by marriage to the Safavid shahs.
marashi-dynasty.o: [[e:qavam-al-din-marashi|Sayyid Qavam al-Din Mar'ashi]], known as Mir-i Buzurg, was a Twelver [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] [[e:sufism|Sufi]] teacher whose dervish followers grew powerful in [[e:mazandaran|Mazandaran]]. In 1359 they defeated the [[s:afrasiyabids-of-mazandaran|Afrasiyabids of Mazandaran]], and Qavam al-Din's sons established a theocratic principality based at Amol and Sari.
marashi-dynasty.r: The Mar'ashis ruled as religious leaders as well as princes, spreading Twelver [[e:shia-islam|Shia Islam]] in the Caspian lands and backing the [[s:karkiya-dynasty|Karkiya dynasty]] in [[e:gilan|Gilan]]. [[e:timur|Timur]] conquered [[e:mazandaran|Mazandaran]] in 1392 and deported the family, but [[e:shah-rukh|Shah Rukh]] restored them. Later rulers were often divided among rival branches. The [[e:safavid-empire|Safavids]] married into the family: Khayr al-Nisa Begum, mother of [[e:abbas-i-of-persia|Shah Abbas I]], was a Mar'ashi.
marashi-dynasty.e: Despite these ties, [[e:abbas-i-of-persia|Shah Abbas I]] annexed [[e:mazandaran|Mazandaran]] in 1596, ending Mar'ashi rule and making the province a royal domain.

messapians.t: Iapygian people of the Salento peninsula in Apulia, long-time rivals of Greek Taras, with their own language, fortified towns and kings.
messapians.o: The Messapians emerged in the heel of [[e:italy|Italy]] in the early 1st millennium BCE as one of three Iapygian peoples, with the [[s:daunians|Daunians]] and [[s:peucetians|Peucetians]]. Ancient writers traced them to Illyria or [[e:crete|Crete]]; modern scholars note links across the Adriatic but see a largely local formation. Their main centres included Uria (Oria), Rudiae, Manduria, Cavallino and Egnatia.
messapians.r: Messapian towns had massive stone walls, chamber tombs and painted trozzella vases. They wrote Messapic, an Indo-European language, in an alphabet borrowed from the [[e:greeks|Greeks]] of [[s:taras|Taras]], and their many inscriptions are a key source. Kings are mentioned occasionally, like Artas, who supplied javelin-men to [[s:athens|Athens]] in 413 BCE. They inflicted a heavy defeat on [[e:tarentum|Taras]] and [[s:rhegion|Rhegion]] around 473 BCE, and at Manduria in 338 BCE they killed the Spartan king Archidamus III.
messapians.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] defeated the Messapians and their Sallentini neighbours in 267–266 BCE, and their towns became allies and later municipia. Messapic was still written into the 1st century BCE before giving way to [[e:latin|Latin]]. The poet Ennius, born at Rudiae, was of Messapian background.
