malwa-sultanate.t: A central Indian sultanate whose hilltop capital at Mandu is famed for its palaces, mosques and the romance of Baz Bahadur and Rupmati.
malwa-sultanate.o: Dilawar Khan Ghuri, appointed governor of [[e:malwa|Malwa]] by the Tughluqs in 1392, ruled independently after [[e:timur|Timur's]] [[e:sack-of-delhi|sack of Delhi]] in 1398 and formally declared independence around 1401. His son [[e:hoshang-shah|Hoshang Shah]] moved the capital from Dhar to the plateau fortress of Mandu, which he fortified and adorned.
malwa-sultanate.r: [[e:mahmud-khalji|Mahmud Khalji]], who seized the throne in 1436 and founded the Khalji line of [[e:malwa|Malwa]], made it a major power, fighting [[s:udaipur-state|Mewar]], [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] and the [[s:bahmani-sultanate|Bahmani Sultanate]]; he built a victory tower at Mandu. Mandu's Jahaz Mahal, Hindola Mahal, Jama Masjid and [[e:hoshang-shah|Hoshang Shah's]] marble tomb show a distinctive Afghan style. The plateau's wealth came from agriculture and trade routes to Gujarat.
malwa-sultanate.e: The [[s:gujarat-sultanate|Gujarat Sultanate]] conquered [[e:malwa|Malwa]] in 1531, and [[e:sher-shah-suri|Sher Shah Suri]] later took it. [[e:baz-bahadur|Baz Bahadur]], the last independent ruler, was defeated by [[e:akbar|Akbar's]] general Adham Khan in 1561, and Malwa was incorporated into the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] by 1562.

mpondo-kingdom.t: The kingdom of Pondoland on the Wild Coast, the last independent African state south of Natal to be annexed by the Cape in 1894.
mpondo-kingdom.o: The Mpondo were a southern [[e:nguni|Nguni]] people whose royal genealogy reaches back many generations, settled between the Mtata and Mtamvuna rivers by the 17th century. The Mpondo grew powerful in the early 19th century under Faku, who survived raids by Shaka's [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zulu Kingdom]] and absorbed refugees from the wars of that era.
mpondo-kingdom.r: Kings ruled through royal kin and councillors over [[e:cattle|cattle]]-keeping and farming homesteads, and the Great Place was the centre of justice and ritual. Faku signed a treaty with the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]] in 1844 recognising his rule over a large territory. After his death in 1867 the kingdom divided into Eastern Pondoland under Mqikela and Western Pondoland under Ndamase.
mpondo-kingdom.e: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] pressed for control of Port St Johns and the Pondoland coast. In 1894 Mqikela's successor Sigcawu was compelled to accept annexation to the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]]. Pondoland was the scene of a major revolt against apartheid policies in 1960.

margraviate-of-austria.t: The Babenberg march on the Danube, first named Ostarrîchi in 996, from which the Duchy of Austria and the Habsburg state grew.
margraviate-of-austria.o: After [[e:otto-i|Otto I's]] victory over the [[e:magyars|Magyars]] at the Lechfeld in 955, a march was established on the [[e:danube|Danube]] east of Bavaria. In 976 [[e:otto-ii-holy-roman-emperor|Otto II]] gave it to Leopold of Babenberg. A document of [[e:otto-iii-holy-roman-emperor|Otto III]] in 996 names the area 'Ostarrîchi', the earliest form of the name [[e:austria|Austria]].
margraviate-of-austria.r: The Babenberg margraves pushed the frontier east to the March and the Leitha, encouraging settlement and founding monasteries. Their seat moved from Melk to Tulln, Klosterneuburg and finally [[e:vienna|Vienna]] around 1145. [[e:leopold-iii-margrave-of-austria|Leopold III]], founder of Klosterneuburg and Heiligenkreuz, was later canonised and became [[e:austria|Austria's]] patron saint.
margraviate-of-austria.e: In 1156 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] raised the margraviate to the [[s:duchy-of-austria|Duchy of Austria]] by the [[e:privilegium-minus|Privilegium Minus]], compensating [[e:henry-ii-duke-of-austria|Henry II Jasomirgott]] for giving up Bavaria. The new duchy, with special rights of inheritance, formed the nucleus of [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] power.

megiddo.t: Megiddo, a fortified Canaanite city guarding a key pass into the Jezreel Valley, scene of Thutmose III's famous victory and origin of the name Armageddon.
megiddo.o: [[e:battle-of-megiddo|Megiddo]] had been a walled town since the [[e:early-bronze-age|Early Bronze Age]]. Its [[e:middle-bronze-age|Middle Bronze Age]] kingdom, rebuilt with massive ramparts and a palace in the early 2nd millennium BCE, controlled the route through the Carmel ridge along which armies and caravans travelled between [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]].
megiddo.r: Kings ruled from a palace near the city gate, alongside a temple to Canaanite gods. In c. 1457 BCE [[e:thutmose-iii|Thutmose III]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] defeated a coalition led by the king of [[s:kadesh|Kadesh]] outside the city and besieged it for seven months. Afterwards [[e:battle-of-megiddo|Megiddo]] was an Egyptian [[e:vassal|vassal]]; its ruler Biridiya wrote several [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]].
megiddo.e: The Canaanite city was destroyed in the 12th century BCE as Egyptian power in [[e:canaan|Canaan]] collapsed. A later town became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Kingdom of Israel]], and the hoard of carved [[e:battle-of-megiddo|Megiddo]] [[e:ivory-trade|ivories]] survives from its last Canaanite palace.

meshwesh.t: A Libyan tribal confederation that raided New Kingdom Egypt, settled in the Delta as soldiers and produced a line of pharaohs.
meshwesh.o: The Meshwesh, often shortened to Ma in Egyptian texts, were a Libyan people living west of the [[e:nile-delta|Nile Delta]]. They appear in Egyptian records from the reign of [[e:amenhotep-iii|Amenhotep III]] and became prominent in the 13th century BCE, when drought and movements of peoples around the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] pushed them towards the Delta.
meshwesh.r: They were pastoralists organised under hereditary chiefs, whose feathered headdresses and long cloaks are shown in Egyptian reliefs. [[e:ramesses-iii|Ramesses III]] defeated them in his fifth and eleventh years, capturing their chief Meshesher, son of Kapur, and thousands of [[e:cattle|cattle]]. Large numbers were settled as military colonists around Herakleopolis and in the Delta, where their leaders took the title 'Great Chief of the Ma' and kept their tribal identity for centuries.
meshwesh.e: From these settlers came [[e:shoshenq-i|Sheshonq I]], who founded the [[s:twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt]] around 943 BCE. Chiefs of the Ma went on ruling Delta towns such as Mendes and Busiris until the [[s:kushite-empire|Kushite Empire]] and later the Saite kings ended their independence by around 700 BCE.

marwanid-badajoz.t: The autonomous muwallad lordship founded by the rebel Ibn Marwan, who built the city of Badajoz and defied the emirs of Córdoba.
marwanid-badajoz.o: Abd al-Rahman ibn Marwan, known as al-Jilliqi, 'the Galician', was a muwallad leader from Mérida who rebelled against the [[s:emirate-of-cordoba|Emirate of Córdoba]]. After a period of revolt and an alliance with [[e:alfonso-iii-of-asturias|Alfonso III of Asturias]], the emir Muhammad I allowed him in about 875 to settle at [[e:badajoz|Badajoz]], which he fortified as his capital.
marwanid-badajoz.r: Ibn Marwan and his descendants ruled the lower Guadiana as virtually independent lords, drawing support from muwallads and Christians and shifting between [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] and the Christian north. Their lordship was one of several autonomous states that split [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] during the fitna of the late 9th century.
marwanid-badajoz.e: As [[e:abd-al-rahman-iii|Abd al-Rahman III]] restored central authority, he took [[e:badajoz|Badajoz]] in 929 or 930 and ended the Marwanid lordship. Badajoz remained an important city and later became the capital of the [[s:taifa-of-badajoz|Taifa of Badajoz]].

mpezenis-ngoni-kingdom.t: The Ngoni kingdom of Mpezeni in eastern Zambia, conquered by the British South Africa Company in 1898.
mpezenis-ngoni-kingdom.o: After the death of [[e:zwangendaba|Zwangendaba]] around 1848, his son Mpezeni led one branch of the [[e:ngoni|Ngoni]] through the lands west of [[e:lake-malawi|Lake Malawi]]. After years of migration and warfare, in the 1860s they settled on the plateau of what is now eastern [[e:zambia|Zambia]], near modern [[e:chipata|Chipata]].
mpezenis-ngoni-kingdom.r: Mpezeni ruled a regimental society in the [[e:nguni|Nguni]] pattern, drawing tribute and captives from the [[e:chewa|Chewa]], Nsenga and others. His people were noted [[e:cattle|cattle]] herders, and his court received traders and concession hunters as European interest grew in the region's supposed gold.
mpezenis-ngoni-kingdom.e: Disputes with a company holding a concession on his land led to war with the [[e:british-south-africa-company|British South Africa Company]] in 1898. Mpezeni was captured and his son Nsingu executed, and the territory became part of [[s:north-eastern-rhodesia|North-Eastern Rhodesia]], run from [[e:chipata|Fort Jameson]]. His successors remain paramount chiefs.

massina-empire.t: A Fulbe Islamic state in the inner Niger delta, ruled from Hamdullahi, which tried to build a model Muslim society under a council of scholars.
massina-empire.o: In 1818 [[e:seku-amadu|Seku Amadu]], a Fulbe preacher in the Massina region of the inner [[e:niger-river|Niger]] delta, led a revolt against the Fulbe ardo chiefs and their Bambara overlords of the [[s:bamana-empire|Bamana Empire]], winning a battle at Noukouma. He proclaimed a [[e:caliphate|caliphate]], the Diina, and around 1820 founded a new capital, Hamdullahi, the House of Praise.
massina-empire.r: [[e:seku-amadu|Seku Amadu]] ruled with a Great Council of forty scholars, imposed strict Islamic law, banned tobacco and dancing, and built schools. The state regulated the seasonal movements of Fulbe herds through the delta, settling pastoral life into a code that endured long after. Massina took Djenne and, from 1826, controlled [[e:timbuktu|Timbuktu]]. His son [[e:amadu-seku|Amadu Seku]] and grandson [[e:amadu-amadu|Amadu Amadu]] succeeded him.
massina-empire.e: Rivalry with [[e:el-hadj-umar-tall|Umar Tall]], a Tijani rather than a Qadiri, led to war. In 1862 Umar took Hamdullahi and had [[e:amadu-amadu|Amadu Amadu]] executed, and Massina became part of the [[s:toucouleur-empire|Toucouleur Empire]], though Fulbe resistance killed Umar in 1864.

margraviate-of-lower-lusatia.t: The march of Lusatia between the Elbe and the Oder, a homeland of the Sorbs passed between Germany, Poland and Bohemia before Prussia took it in 1815.
margraviate-of-lower-lusatia.o: After Gero died in 965, [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] made the [[s:marca-geronis|Saxon Eastern March]], later called the March of Lusatia, a separate margraviate. In 1002 the Polish ruler Bolesław I seized it, and [[e:poland|Poland]] held it until 1031. From 1136 it was held mainly by the Wettin margraves of Meissen.
margraviate-of-lower-lusatia.r: The land around Lübben, Cottbus and Guben was largely rural, with a strong Sorbian-speaking population. Lordship changed often: [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] held it from 1304, and in 1367 [[e:charles-iv|Emperor Charles IV]] bought it for the Bohemian crown. The estates of the land kept substantial self-government under these distant rulers.
margraviate-of-lower-lusatia.e: The Peace of [[e:prague|Prague]] of 1635 transferred [[e:lower-lusatia|Lower Lusatia]] from [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] to the [[s:electorate-of-saxony|Electorate of Saxony]]. After Saxony sided with [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] gave it to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1815, and it became part of the province of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]]. The Lower Sorbian language is still spoken around Cottbus.

moesi.t: Thracian people of the Danube plain who gave their name to the Roman province of Moesia.
moesi.o: Known mainly from Roman sources, the Moesi lived along the right bank of the [[e:danube|Danube]] in modern [[s:serbia|Serbia]] and northern [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]], probably related to the Mysians of [[e:asia-minor|Asia Minor]]. They appear as a distinct people from the late centuries BCE.
moesi.r: Little is recorded of their institutions. They lived in tribal communities of farmers and herders in the valleys south of the [[e:danube|Danube]], neighbours of the [[s:triballi|Triballi]] and the [[s:scordisci|Scordisci]], and resisted Roman advances from Macedonia.
moesi.e: [[e:marcus-licinius-crassus|Marcus Licinius Crassus]] defeated them in his campaign of 29 BCE, and their land was organised as the province of Moesia early in the 1st century CE. The province became a key [[e:danube|Danube]] frontier with [[e:legion|legionary]] bases at Singidunum, Viminacium and Novae.

mekhtuli-khanate.t: A small khanate of the Kumyk-Avar borderland in Dagestan, ruled by a branch of the shamkhal family until Russia abolished it.
mekhtuli-khanate.o: The Mekhtuli Khanate formed around the 17th century in the foothills of central [[e:dagestan|Dagestan]], between the Kumyk plain and the [[e:avars|Avar]] mountains, with its seat at Dzhengutai. Its rulers claimed descent from the shamkhals of the [[s:kazikumukh-shamkhalate|Kazikumukh Shamkhalate]]. Its early history is poorly documented.
mekhtuli-khanate.r: The khans ruled Kumyk and [[e:avars|Avar]] villages through nobles and customary law, and their position between the plains and the highlands gave them a role in regional alliances. Akhmed Khan led resistance to [[e:russia|Russia]] in 1818 before submitting, and later khans held Russian military rank and pensions.
mekhtuli-khanate.e: The khanate came under Russian protection in the 1820s and supported [[e:russia|Russia]] during the wars of the [[s:caucasian-imamate|Caucasian Imamate]]. In 1867 the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] abolished it and incorporated its lands into the [[e:dagestan-oblast|Dagestan Oblast]].

march-of-montferrat.t: Marquisate in Piedmont whose Aleramici and Palaiologos rulers were crusaders and kings in the East, raised to a duchy in 1574.
march-of-montferrat.o: In 967 [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] confirmed Aleramo, a nobleman of Frankish descent, as margrave of lands in the hills south of the Po between Turin and [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]], later called Montferrat. His descendants, the Aleramici, ruled it for more than three centuries.
march-of-montferrat.r: The Aleramici were famed crusaders: [[e:conrad-of-montferrat|Conrad of Montferrat]] defended [[s:tyre|Tyre]] and was elected King of [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]] in 1192, and Boniface I led the [[e:fourth-crusade|Fourth Crusade]] and became King of Thessalonica. In 1306 the march passed to Theodore I Palaiologos, son of the Byzantine emperor [[e:andronikos-ii-palaiologos|Andronikos II]], whose family ruled until 1533. Casale [[s:duchy-of-montferrat|Monferrato]] became the capital in the 15th century. The territory produced grain and wine.
march-of-montferrat.e: After the last Palaiologos died in 1533, [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] awarded Montferrat to Federico II Gonzaga of [[s:duchy-of-mantua|Mantua]] in 1536. In 1574 [[e:maximilian-ii-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Maximilian II]] raised it to a duchy. The Gonzaga held it until 1708, when it passed to [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]].

megalopolis.t: 'Great City' of Arcadia, founded as a bulwark against Sparta, home of the statesman Philopoemen and the historian Polybius.
megalopolis.o: Megalopolis was founded between 371 and 368 BCE as the capital of the new [[s:arcadian-league|Arcadian League]], by moving the people of around forty villages of south-western Arcadia into a single city on the Helisson river. Its purpose was to block Spartan routes north and to give the Arcadians a shared centre.
megalopolis.r: The city was laid out on a grand scale with walls of more than 8 kilometres, the largest [[e:theatre|theatre]] in [[e:greece|Greece]] and the Thersilion, a hall for the federal assembly. Its population never filled the walls. Megalopolis was consistently hostile to [[s:sparta|Sparta]] and pro-Macedonian. Its tyrant Lydiadas voluntarily laid down power and took it into the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]] in 235 BCE.
megalopolis.e: [[e:cleomenes-iii|Cleomenes III of Sparta]] sacked it in 223 BCE, but it was rebuilt and produced the Achaean leader Philopoemen and the historian Polybius. It lost independence after the [[e:achaean-war|Achaean War]] of 146 BCE and declined under Roman rule; Strabo called it a great desert.

ma-i.t: A Philippine trading polity known from Chinese records of the 10th to 14th centuries, among the earliest named states of the archipelago.
ma-i.o: The [[e:song-dynasty|Song dynasty]] history records merchants from Ma-i bringing goods to [[e:guangzhou|Guangzhou]] in 971 and again in 982. Its location is debated: most scholars favour Mindoro, others Bay on [[e:laguna-de-bay|Laguna de Bay]] in Luzon.
ma-i.r: Zhao Rugua's Zhufan zhi of 1225 describes a settlement of over a thousand families on a river, whose chief used a white umbrella. Chinese traders anchored offshore and handed goods to local merchants, who carried them to other islands and returned to pay in beeswax, [[e:cotton|cotton]], pearls and tortoiseshell. [[e:bronze|Bronze]] Buddhist images were said to stand in the countryside.
ma-i.e: Ma-i appears in Chinese texts until the 14th century and then drops from the record. Later Chinese and Spanish sources do not mention it, and its trade passed to ports such as [[s:kingdom-of-tondo|Tondo]] and [[s:kingdom-of-maynila|Maynila]].

musabbaat-sultanate.t: A Fur-linked sultanate in Kordofan, rival of the Funj and Darfur, that briefly dominated the plains between the Nile and Darfur.
musabbaat-sultanate.o: The Musabba'at were a branch of the ruling [[e:keira-dynasty|Keira]] family of [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] who moved east into [[e:kordofan|Kordofan]] in the 17th century after a dynastic dispute. They founded a sultanate in the plains of northern and central Kordofan, around Bara.
musabbaat-sultanate.r: [[e:kordofan|Kordofan]] was a contested frontier rich in gum, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and slaves, crossed by routes between the [[e:nile|Nile]] and [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]]. Under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Hashim in the later 18th century, the Musabba'at expanded their rule over much of Kordofan, competing with the [[s:funj-sultanate|Funj Sultanate]] and the [[s:darfur-sultanate|Darfur Sultanate]]. Little is known of their institutions.
musabbaat-sultanate.e: In 1785 Muhammad Tayrab of [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] invaded [[e:kordofan|Kordofan]] and drove Hashim out, ending the Musabba'at state. Kordofan stayed under Darfur until the [[s:turco-egyptian-sudan|Turco-Egyptian Sudan]] conquered it in 1821.

maihar-state.t: A Kachhwaha Rajput state of Baghelkhand, home of the Sharda Devi hill temple and of the Maihar school of Hindustani music.
maihar-state.o: The ruling family of Maihar were Kachhwaha [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]] who had served the Bundela rulers of [[s:panna-state|Panna]] and received lands in the area. Around 1778 they established Maihar as their own principality, and the British confirmed it by sanad in the early 19th century.
maihar-state.r: Maihar was a 9-gun salute state of the [[e:baghelkhand-agency|Baghelkhand Agency]], ruled by a Raja. The goddess Sharda's temple on Trikuta hill drew pilgrims from across north [[e:india|India]]. Raja Brijnath Singh made the sarod master Allauddin Khan his court musician, and pupils such as [[e:ravi|Ravi]] Shankar and Ali [[e:akbar|Akbar]] Khan trained there, creating the Maihar gharana.
maihar-state.e: After independence Maihar was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] in 1948 and joined Madhya Pradesh in 1956.

madras-presidency.t: The British province of southern India governed from Fort St George at Madras, the East India Company's oldest presidency.
madras-presidency.o: In 1639 the [[e:east-india-company|English East India Company]] obtained land at Madraspatnam from a local Nayaka and began building Fort St George there the following year. In 1652 the settlement was raised to the status of a presidency, independent of [[s:banten-sultanate|Bantam]]. Victories over the French in the [[e:carnatic-wars|Carnatic Wars]] and over the [[s:kingdom-of-mysore-1399-1799|Kingdom of Mysore]] in 1799 extended it across most of southern [[e:india|India]].
madras-presidency.r: A governor and council ruled from Madras, under the Governor-General of [[e:bengal|Bengal]] from 1773. [[e:thomas-munro|Thomas Munro]] introduced the ryotwari system, assessing land revenue directly on peasant cultivators. The presidency covered Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada areas. Railways, irrigation such as the Kaveri anicuts, universities and newspapers spread, while famines, notably in 1876 to 1878, caused great loss of life.
madras-presidency.e: Madras became a province of [[s:british-raj|British India]] under the [[e:british-raj|British Raj]], gained elected ministries from 1920 and joined the [[s:dominion-of-india|Dominion of India]] in 1947 as [[e:madras-state|Madras State]]. It was divided on linguistic lines from 1953 to 1956, and the remainder was renamed Tamil Nadu in 1969.

maharam-state.t: A Khasi chiefdom of the south-western Khasi Hills, one of the 25 Khasi states that acceded to India in 1948.
maharam-state.o: Hima Maharam was one of the Khasi chiefdoms of the Meghalaya plateau; its origins are known only from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
maharam-state.r: Maharam was headed by a Syiem chosen from a royal clan, with succession through the female line and decisions taken with clan elders. Little written record of its history exists.
maharam-state.e: Maharam came under British supervision in the 19th century and acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1948, joining Assam. It is now part of Meghalaya.

mytilene.t: Chief city of Lesbos, home of the poets Sappho and Alcaeus, whose revolt against Athens in 428 BCE prompted the famous Mytilenean Debate.
mytilene.o: [[e:aeolians|Aeolian Greeks]] settled Lesbos around 1000 BCE, and Mytilene grew on the south-east coast of the island, with harbours facing [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]]. By the 7th century BCE it was the leading city of Lesbos, founding settlements in the Troad and fighting [[s:athens|Athens]] for Sigeion.
mytilene.r: Aristocratic feuds and tyrants such as Myrsilus marked the 7th century BCE, ended when Pittacus, one of the [[e:seven-sages-of-greece|Seven Sages]], ruled as elected aesymnetes c. 590 to 580 BCE. Sappho and Alcaeus wrote lyric poetry there. Mytilene shared in the Greek trading post at Naucratis, and later belonged to the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]] as a ship-providing ally.
mytilene.e: After its revolt of 428 BCE [[s:athens|Athens]] first voted to kill all its men, then relented. Mytilene sided with Mithridates of the [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Kingdom of Pontus]], and its capture by [[e:rome|Rome]] in 79 BCE, where the young [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar]] won the civic crown, ended its independence, though [[e:pompey|Pompey]] later granted it freedom.

mosquito-kingdom.t: A Miskito kingdom on the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and Honduras, allied with Britain, which kept Spain out of the coast for two centuries.
mosquito-kingdom.o: The Miskito people of the [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]] coast, who absorbed Africans from shipwrecks and runaways in the 17th century, formed close ties with English traders and buccaneers. By the mid-17th century their leaders were recognised by the English as kings, a title confirmed through the governors of [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]].
mosquito-kingdom.r: Miskito kings were often crowned under British auspices in [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]] or [[s:belize|Belize]] and relied on British arms and trade. Real power was shared with regional governors, generals and admirals. Miskito warriors raided Spanish settlements and other indigenous groups, taking captives for sale. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] maintained the [[s:mosquito-shore|Mosquito Shore]] settlement from 1749 to 1787 and later declared a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]], with Bluefields as the centre.
mosquito-kingdom.e: Under the Treaty of Managua of 1860 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] recognised Nicaraguan [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], and the kingdom became the self-governing [[s:mosquito-reserve|Mosquito Reserve]]. The Miskito remain the main people of the coast.

mihrabanid-dynasty.t: A Persian dynasty of maliks that ruled Sistan for three centuries under Mongol, Timurid and Safavid overlords.
mihrabanid-dynasty.o: [[e:shams-al-din-ali-ibn-masud|Shams al-Din Ali ibn Mas'ud]] established the dynasty in Sistan in 1236, after the Mongol devastation ended the [[s:nasrid-maliks-of-sistan|Nasrid Maliks of Sistan]]. The family claimed descent from the [[s:saffarid-dynasty|Saffarids]] and ruled from Zaranj and later other centres of the Helmand delta.
mihrabanid-dynasty.r: The Mihrabanid maliks governed an irrigated land of canals and dams on the Helmand, repeatedly damaged by war. They accepted the overlordship of the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]] and the [[s:kart-dynasty|Kart dynasty]] of [[e:herat|Herat]], and suffered heavily when [[e:timur|Timur]] invaded Sistan in 1383, destroying dams and towns. Under the [[s:timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]] they continued as local rulers, keeping the old title malik and Sistan's distinct identity. The Ihya al-Muluk, a later local chronicle, records their history.
mihrabanid-dynasty.e: In the early 16th century Sistan was absorbed into the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]]; by 1537 the maliks had lost independence, although members of the family served as Safavid governors.

margraviate-of-meissen.t: The Wettin march on the middle Elbe whose silver mines and rulers laid the foundations of the later Electorate and Kingdom of Saxony.
margraviate-of-meissen.o: After the death of Margrave Gero in 965, [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] created a march around the stronghold of Meissen, founded by [[e:henry-the-fowler|Henry the Fowler]] in 929 among the [[s:sorbs|Sorbs]]. A bishopric followed in 968. From 1089 the march was held by the Wettin family, who kept it for more than eight centuries in its successor states.
margraviate-of-meissen.r: The Wettins promoted German settlement among the [[s:sorbs|Sorbs]] and founded towns such as Leipzig and Dresden. The discovery of [[e:silver|silver]] at Freiberg around 1168 made the margraves wealthy; [[e:otto-the-rich|Otto the Rich]] used it to fortify his lands. [[e:henry-iii-margrave-of-meissen|Henry the Illustrious]] added the [[s:landgraviate-of-thuringia|Landgraviate of Thuringia]] in 1264, making the Wettins a leading princely house.
margraviate-of-meissen.e: In 1423 [[e:sigismund-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Sigismund]] granted Frederick the Warlike the [[s:duchy-of-saxe-wittenberg|Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg]] with its electoral dignity, after the Ascanian line died out. The margraviate merged into the [[s:electorate-of-saxony|Electorate of Saxony]], and the name Saxony moved up the Elbe to the old lands of Meissen.

media-atropatene.t: A Hellenistic Iranian kingdom in north-western Iran founded by the Persian satrap Atropates, whose name survives in 'Azerbaijan'.
media-atropatene.o: Atropates had served as [[e:satrapy|satrap]] of [[e:median-empire|Media]] under [[e:darius-iii|Darius III]] and under [[e:alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great]]. After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, while the rest of Media passed to his successors, Atropates kept the northern part and ruled it as an independent kingdom, which the [[e:greeks|Greeks]] called Media Atropatene.
media-atropatene.r: Its kings ruled from Ganzak, near the later [[e:fire-temple|fire temple]] of Takht-e Soleyman, over a land of horse pastures and mountains. [[e:zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]] was strong, and the region later held one of the great fire temples of [[e:iran|Iran]], Adur Gushnasp. The kingdom stood between the [[s:seleucid-empire|Seleucid Empire]], the [[s:parthian-empire|Parthian Empire]], [[s:armenia|Armenia]] and [[e:rome|Rome]]: in 36 BCE Artavasdes I helped repulse [[e:mark-antony|Mark Antony's]] siege of Phraaspa, then allied with him, and from the 1st century CE members of the Arsacid house often held the throne.
media-atropatene.e: Atropatene came under the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] around 226 CE, when [[e:ardashir-i|Ardashir I]] conquered it and made it a province. Its name became [[e:middle-persian|Middle Persian]] Aturpatakan and later [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]].

menapii.t: Belgic people of the Scheldt and lower Rhine who held off Caesar for years by retreating into their marshes and forests.
menapii.o: The Menapii lived in the low, marshy lands of [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]] and the southern [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]], from the Scheldt to the [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. They joined the Belgic league in 57 BCE.
menapii.r: They lived in scattered farmsteads and avoided pitched battle, withdrawing into woods and swamps. In 55 BCE the Germanic Usipetes and [[s:tencteri|Tencteri]] crossed the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and seized part of their land.
menapii.e: Caesar campaigned against them in 56 and 55 BCE and finally subdued them in 53 BCE by burning their settlements. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their capital was Castellum Menapiorum (Cassel). The usurper Carausius, who ruled [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] from 286 CE, was a Menapian.

makuria.t: The Christian Nubian kingdom of Dongola that halted the Arab advance up the Nile and flourished for some seven centuries.
makuria.o: Makuria arose around the 5th century in the [[e:nile|Nile]] valley between the Third and Fifth Cataracts, one of three kingdoms that succeeded the [[s:kushite-empire|Kushite Empire]]. Its capital was Old Dongola. The court accepted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] in the mid-6th century, and by around 700 Makuria had absorbed [[s:nobadia|Nobadia]] to the north.
makuria.r: Makurian [[e:archery|archers]] defeated Arab armies in 642 and 652, leading to the Baqt, a treaty with [[e:egypt|Egypt]] that exchanged slaves for grain, cloth and wine and kept the peace for centuries. Under kings such as Merkurios and Georgios I, who visited [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] around 835, Makuria flourished. The kingdom followed the [[e:coptic-orthodox-church|Coptic Church]], wrote in [[e:old-nubian|Old Nubian]], Greek and Coptic, and decorated churches such as Faras cathedral with fine paintings.
makuria.e: From the 1270s the [[s:mamluk-sultanate|Mamluk Sultanate]] intervened in royal succession, and in 1317 the throne hall at Dongola became a mosque. Arab migration, plague and the [[s:banu-kanz-emirate|Banu Kanz]] weakened the state, and by the late 14th century the court had left Dongola. A rump kingdom survived briefly further north.

mastieni.t: An Iberian people of the Cartagena region, whose town Mastia marked the limit set on Roman shipping in a 4th-century BCE treaty with Carthage.
mastieni.o: The Mastieni lived in south-eastern [[e:iberia|Iberia]], around modern [[e:carthago-nova|Cartagena]] and [[e:murcia|Murcia]]. Greek writers knew them from the 6th century BCE, and they belonged to the Iberian culture of the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] coast.
mastieni.r: Almost nothing is known of their institutions. Their chief town, Mastia, is named in the second treaty between [[e:rome|Rome]] and [[e:carthage|Carthage]], of 348 BCE, as the point beyond which [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] could not trade or found cities. The region was rich in [[e:silver|silver]] and lead, later intensively mined.
mastieni.e: Around 227 BCE the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal founded [[e:carthago-nova|Qart Hadasht]], later Carthago Nova, probably on or near the site of Mastia, making it the capital of [[s:barcid-iberia|Barcid Iberia]]. The Mastieni name then disappears.

mong-mao.t: A Tai Mao kingdom on the Shweli river along today's China-Myanmar border, a regional power in the 14th century that the Ming crushed in the 1440s.
mong-mao.o: Mong Mao arose among the [[e:tai-mao|Tai Mao]] people of the Shweli valley in the early 14th century, after the [[e:mongol-conquest-of-dali|Mongol conquest of Dali]] opened space for local powers. Under Si Kefa, in Shan tradition Hso Hkan Hpa, it expanded in the 1340s and 1350s, resisting Yuan armies and raiding into upper [[s:myanmar|Burma]].
mong-mao.r: Mong Mao's rulers dominated neighbouring Tai principalities, including [[s:hsenwi-state|Hsenwi]], [[s:mohnyin|Mohnyin]] and [[s:mogaung|Mogaung]], which later Shan chronicles present as its offshoots. The Ming called it Luchuan and named its ruler a pacification commissioner. Its power rested on [[e:rice|rice]] valleys and cavalry, and its rulers fought both the Chinese and the [[s:ava-kingdom|Ava Kingdom]].
mong-mao.e: [[e:si-renfa|Si Renfa]] defied the Ming, who launched the Luchuan-Pingmian campaigns of 1436 to 1449; he fled to Ava, which handed him over. The kingdom fragmented, and its remnants lingered as small border chiefdoms under Chinese and Burmese pressure. Its memory remains central to Shan and Dai identity.

midrarid-emirate.t: The emirate of Sijilmasa, a Saharan oasis city that grew rich as the northern terminus of the gold trade from Ghana.
midrarid-emirate.o: [[e:sijilmasa|Sijilmasa]] was founded in the Tafilalt oasis of south-eastern [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]] in 757 by Sufri Kharijite [[e:berbers|Berbers]] of the Miknasa tribe. Their first leader, Isa ibn Yazid, was deposed in 772, and his successor [[e:abu-al-qasim-samgu|Abu al-Qasim Samgu]] founded the line of the Banu Midrar, who gave the dynasty its name and ruled the city as [[e:emir|emirs]] for two centuries.
midrarid-emirate.r: [[e:sijilmasa|Sijilmasa]] was the chief northern market of trans-Saharan trade, where caravans brought gold from the [[s:ghana-empire|Ghana Empire]] to be exchanged for salt, [[e:copper|copper]] and textiles; its mint struck gold coins. The [[e:emir|emirs]] kept ties with the [[s:rustamid-imamate|Rustamid imamate]]. Between about 905 and 909 the future Fatimid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] Ubayd Allah was held captive there until rescued by [[e:abu-abdallah-al-shii|Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i]], who executed the emir al-[[e:yasa|Yasa]].
midrarid-emirate.e: The Midrarids returned as Fatimid [[e:vassal|vassals]], but Muhammad ibn al-Fath adopted [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni Islam]] and a caliphal title, provoking the Fatimid general [[s:jawhar-state|Jawhar]] to take the city in 958. In 976 the [[s:maghrawa-emirate-of-fez|Maghrawa emirate of Fez]] seized [[e:sijilmasa|Sijilmasa]], ending the dynasty.

marshall-islands-protectorate.t: A German protectorate over the Marshall Islands and later Nauru, run largely by a Hamburg trading company for the copra trade.
marshall-islands-protectorate.o: German traders dominated copra buying in the [[e:marshall-islands|Marshall Islands]] from the 1870s, and in 1878 a German naval officer secured a treaty with chiefs on Jaluit. In 1885, as [[e:germany|Germany]] and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] were dividing the western Pacific into spheres of influence, Germany declared a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]], with an imperial commissioner at Jaluit.
marshall-islands-protectorate.r: From 1888 the Jaluit Gesellschaft, a merger of the [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] trading houses, paid the costs of administration in return for a trade monopoly, so the colony was in effect run by a company. Marshallese paramount chiefs, the iroij, kept authority over land and people and collected copra as tribute. [[s:territory-of-nauru|Nauru]] was annexed in 1888 and attached to the [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]. Protestant missionaries from the American Board were active.
marshall-islands-protectorate.e: The Reich took over administration from the company, and in 1906 the [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] was merged into [[s:german-new-guinea|German New Guinea]]. [[e:japan|Japan]] occupied the islands in 1914, ruling them under the [[s:south-seas-mandate|South Seas Mandate]], while [[s:territory-of-nauru|Nauru]] became the Territory of Nauru.

mangkunegaran.t: Javanese princely house founded by the rebel Raden Mas Said, a small but innovative court at Surakarta.
mangkunegaran.o: Raden Mas Said, a [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram]] prince known as Pangeran Sambernyawa, fought both the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] and the royal courts for years. By the Treaty of Salatiga in 1757 he received an apanage carved out of the [[s:surakarta-sunanate|Surakarta Sunanate]] and the title Mangkunegara I, founding a princely house subordinate in rank but autonomous in practice.
mangkunegaran.r: The princes ruled from the Puro Mangkunegaran palace in [[s:surakarta-sunanate|Surakarta]]. They maintained the Mangkunegaran [[e:legion|Legion]], a European-style force formed in 1808. [[e:mangkunegara-iv|Mangkunegara IV]] built [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] mills and [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] estates that made the house wealthy, and [[e:mangkunegara-vii|Mangkunegara VII]] was a celebrated patron of dance, music and early radio broadcasting.
mangkunegaran.e: Like the [[s:surakarta-sunanate|Surakarta]] court, Mangkunegaran lost its autonomy in 1946 amid revolutionary opposition to the Javanese nobility, and its lands were absorbed into the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]]. The Puro Mangkunegaran remains a living cultural centre headed by the Mangkunegara.

mahafaly-kingdoms.t: Small cattle-herding kingdoms of arid south-west Madagascar, best known for their elaborate tombs with carved aloalo posts.
mahafaly-kingdoms.o: The Mahafaly kingdoms emerged in the 17th century in the dry plateau between the Onilahy and Menarandra rivers, under dynasties related to the Maroserana who founded the Sakalava kingdoms. Several separate kingdoms coexisted rather than a single state.
mahafaly-kingdoms.r: Royal authority rested on [[e:sacred-kingship|sacred kingship]], ancestral cults and control of [[e:cattle|cattle]], the main measure of wealth in a region where farming was difficult. Mahafaly tombs, large stone rectangles decorated with cattle horns and carved wooden aloalo posts showing scenes from the dead person's life, became the region's best-known art form. Few written records exist before the 19th century.
mahafaly-kingdoms.e: The Mahafaly were never conquered by the [[s:merina-kingdom|Merina Kingdom]], but French forces brought the region under colonial rule around 1900. The Mahafaly remain a distinct people, and their tomb-building tradition continues.

middle-kingdom-of-egypt.t: Reunited Egypt of the Eleventh to Thirteenth Dynasties, famed for its literature, its Nubian fortresses and the reclamation of the Faiyum.
middle-kingdom-of-egypt.o: [[e:mentuhotep-ii|Mentuhotep II]] of the [[s:theban-eleventh-dynasty|Theban Eleventh Dynasty]], who came to the throne around 2055 BCE, reunited [[e:egypt|Egypt]] during his long reign. Around 1985 BCE the [[e:vizier|vizier]] Amenemhat I took the throne, founded the Twelfth Dynasty and moved the capital to a new city, Itjtawy, near Lisht at the entrance to the Faiyum.
middle-kingdom-of-egypt.r: The Twelfth Dynasty kings ruled through co-regencies and a growing bureaucracy. [[e:senusret-iii|Senusret III]] curbed the provincial nomarchs and extended the chain of mud-brick fortresses in [[e:nubia|Nubia]] around the Second Cataract, as at Semna. [[e:amenemhat-iii|Amenemhat III]] developed the Faiyum and built the pyramid at Hawara. This was the classical age of Egyptian literature, with the Tale of Sinuhe and wisdom texts, and of fine jewellery and portrait sculpture.
middle-kingdom-of-egypt.e: The Thirteenth Dynasty kept Itjtawy but saw dozens of short reigns, while the [[s:fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Fourteenth Dynasty of Egypt]] ruled the eastern Delta. Around 1650 BCE the [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Hyksos]] of the Fifteenth Dynasty of [[e:egypt|Egypt]] took Memphis, opening the [[e:second-intermediate-period|Second Intermediate Period]].

moche.t: A coastal civilisation of northern Peru that built huge adobe pyramids and produced the most lifelike portrait pottery and metalwork of the ancient Andes.
moche.o: The Moche, or Mochica, culture developed around 100 CE in the river valleys of [[e:peru|Peru's]] north coast, especially the Moche and Chicama valleys near modern Trujillo. Local elites drew on earlier coastal traditions such as Cupisnique and Salinar and extended irrigation canals across the desert.
moche.r: Moche society was ruled by warrior-priest lords. Its capital at Huacas de Moche had the Huaca del Sol, one of the largest adobe structures in the [[e:americas|Americas]], and the painted Huaca de la Luna. The tombs of the [[e:lord-of-sipan|Lord of Sipán]], found in 1987, and the [[e:lady-of-cao|Lady of Cao]] show the wealth of gold, [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:copper|copper]] regalia. Moche pottery includes realistic portrait vessels and painted scenes of warfare, sacrifice and daily life.
moche.e: Heavy El Niño floods and droughts in the 6th century disrupted Moche society, and its centres shifted north to Pampa Grande and Galindo before collapsing around 800 CE. Its traditions passed to the [[s:sican|Sicán]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-chimor|Kingdom of Chimor]].

marcomanni.t: A Suebian Germanic people who settled Bohemia and fought Rome in the Marcomannic Wars, the hardest frontier struggle of Marcus Aurelius' reign.
marcomanni.o: The Marcomanni ('border men') first appear among Ariovistus' followers in 58 BCE, probably living near the upper [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and Main. Around 9 BCE, under pressure from Roman campaigns led by Drusus, their leader [[e:maroboduus|Maroboduus]] led them east into [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]], the former land of the [[s:boii|Boii]], where they formed the core of a powerful kingdom.
marcomanni.r: After [[e:maroboduus|Maroboduus]] fell, the Marcomanni were usually ruled by kings who acted as Roman clients, receiving [[e:subsidy|subsidies]] and trading through Carnuntum on the [[e:danube|Danube]]. Roman goods are common in their graves. From 166/167 they and the [[s:quadi|Quadi]] broke through the frontier, sparking the [[e:marcomannic-wars|Marcomannic Wars]]; around 170 they besieged Aquileia in [[e:italy|Italy]], and [[e:marcus-aurelius|Marcus Aurelius]] fought them until his death in 180.
marcomanni.e: Commodus made peace in 180, and the Marcomanni remained a frontier people for two more centuries, with a queen, Fritigil, converting to [[e:christianity|Christianity]] around 396. They faded from the record in the 5th century, many joining the [[e:huns|Huns]] or merging into the people later called Bavarians.

marhashi.t: A wealthy kingdom of the Iranian plateau, east of Elam, that traded luxury stone vessels and exotic animals with Mesopotamia and fought the kings of Akkad.
marhashi.o: Marhashi (Parahshum in Akkadian) lay beyond [[e:elam|Elam]], probably in the [[e:kerman|Kerman]] and Jiroft region of south-eastern [[e:iran|Iran]], where the [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] Jiroft culture produced carved chlorite vessels found as far afield as [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]]. It is first mentioned in the mid-third millennium BCE as a powerful eastern land.
marhashi.r: Mesopotamian texts present Marhashi as a large kingdom with its own kings and wide trade links across the plateau to the [[e:indus|Indus]], supplying semi-precious stones, chlorite bowls and animals such as the 'dogs of Marhashi'. Its kings allied with [[e:elam|Elam]] against [[e:sargon-of-akkad|Sargon]] and [[e:rimush|Rimush]] of the [[s:akkadian-empire|Akkadian Empire]], and Rimush records defeating Abalgamash, king of Marhashi. Under the [[s:neo-sumerian-empire|Neo-Sumerian Empire]] relations were peaceful: [[e:shulgi|Shulgi]] married a daughter to Libanukshabash of Marhashi.
marhashi.e: Marhashi is last mentioned in the early second millennium BCE, and its decline mirrors the collapse of the trading towns of south-eastern [[e:iran|Iran]] around 1900 BCE. Its identification with the Jiroft finds remains a hypothesis.

metapontum.t: Achaean Greek city on the Gulf of Taranto, rich in grain, where Pythagoras spent his last years.
metapontum.o: Achaean settlers founded Metapontum in the 7th century BCE on the coastal plain between the Bradano and Basento rivers. Ancient sources say [[s:sybaris|Sybaris]] encouraged the colony to block the expansion of Spartan [[s:taras|Taras]]. Earlier native and Greek settlement existed nearby, and the city grew quickly on the plain.
metapontum.r: Metapontum's wealth came from grain, celebrated on its coins with an ear of barley and by a 'golden harvest' it dedicated at [[s:delphi|Delphi]]. Archaeologists have traced the division of its countryside into regular plots and many farmhouses. The Tavole Palatine, fifteen standing columns of a temple of Hera, survive outside the town. Pythagoras moved there after being driven from [[s:croton|Croton]], and his school stayed influential in the city.
metapontum.e: Metapontum joined the Athenian side in 413 BCE and later suffered from Lucanian pressure. It came under Roman control after the war with Pyrrhus around 272 BCE, sided with [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] and was abandoned by many of its people when he left [[e:italy|Italy]] in 207 BCE. It survived as a small Roman town.

mthethwa-paramountcy.t: The northern Nguni paramountcy of Dingiswayo, whose military reorganisation and patronage of the young Shaka paved the way for the Zulu Kingdom.
mthethwa-paramountcy.o: The Mthethwa were settled near the coast between the Mfolozi and Mhlathuze rivers. Under Jobe in the late 18th century they were already a significant chiefdom, and after a succession dispute his son Dingiswayo returned from exile around 1795 to take power and expand it into a paramountcy over many neighbours.
mthethwa-paramountcy.r: Dingiswayo organised young men into age-based regiments and brought neighbouring chiefdoms under his authority, often leaving their ruling families in place. He encouraged trade in [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] with [[e:delagoa-bay|Delagoa Bay]]. Shaka served in his army and, with Dingiswayo's backing, became ruler of the [[e:zulu-kingdom|Zulu]], a Mthethwa dependent.
mthethwa-paramountcy.e: Around 1818 Dingiswayo was captured and killed by Zwide of the [[s:ndwandwe-kingdom|Ndwandwe Kingdom]]. The Mthethwa paramountcy collapsed, and its people were absorbed into Shaka's expanding [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zulu Kingdom]].

maguindanao-sultanate.t: The Muslim sultanate of the Cotabato basin in Mindanao, which under Sultan Kudarat held off Spanish conquest in the 17th century.
maguindanao-sultanate.o: Tradition holds that Sharif Muhammad Kabungsuan, a preacher from [[s:johor-sultanate|Johor]], landed at the mouth of the Pulangi River around 1520, married into the local ruling family and brought [[e:islam|Islam]]. His descendants founded the sultanate based at Cotabato, while a related line ruled upstream as the [[s:buayan-sultanate|Buayan Sultanate]].
maguindanao-sultanate.r: Maguindanao's sultans ruled through datus and controlled the river trade in [[e:rice|rice]], wax and slaves. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Kudarat, reigning from about 1619 to 1671, united much of Mindanao, fought Governor Sebastian Hurtado de Corcuera in 1637 and made peace with [[e:spain|Spain]] on his own terms. [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English traders also visited.
maguindanao-sultanate.e: Maguindanao weakened in the 19th century as [[s:buayan-sultanate|Buayan]] rose and [[e:spain|Spain]] advanced. The Spanish occupied Cotabato in 1861, and after 1899 American rule ended the sultanate's independence by 1905. Its heritage is central to the Bangsamoro identity of the southern [[s:philippines|Philippines]].

mzab-confederation.t: A self-governing league of Ibadi oasis towns in the Algerian Sahara, ruled by religious councils for nearly nine centuries.
mzab-confederation.o: After the fall of the [[s:rustamid-imamate|Rustamid imamate]] in 909, Ibadi refugees settled at [[s:sultanate-of-ouargla|Ouargla]] and Sedrata, then moved into the barren Mzab valley of the northern [[e:sahara|Sahara]]. The first town, El Atteuf, was founded around 1012, followed by Bou Noura, Ghardaïa, Melika and Beni Isguen, the Pentapolis of the Mzab.
mzab-confederation.r: Each walled hilltop town was governed by a council of clerics, the halqa of the azzaba, together with assemblies of lay notables, under strict Ibadi religious law. The Mozabites dug deep [[e:well|wells]] and ingenious dams to water their palm groves, and their merchants formed trading communities in the cities of the north. Their compact architecture later inspired modern architects such as Le Corbusier.
mzab-confederation.e: From the 16th century the Mzab paid tribute to the [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]]. It accepted a French [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1853 and was annexed to [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]] in 1882, keeping its religious institutions. The valley is now a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage]] site.

maitraka-dynasty.t: The kings of Valabhi in Saurashtra, whose capital was a great centre of Buddhist and Jain learning compared by Chinese pilgrims to Nalanda.
maitraka-dynasty.o: The dynasty was founded around 475 by Bhatarka, a general of the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]], who made himself ruler in Saurashtra as Gupta power declined. His successors made Valabhi, on the [[e:gulf-of-khambhat|Gulf of Khambhat]], their capital and gradually assumed full royal titles.
maitraka-dynasty.r: The Maitrakas issued well over a hundred [[e:copper|copper]]-plate land grants that document their administration and [[e:gujarat|Gujarat's]] villages. They were mostly Shaivas but generously endowed Buddhist monasteries; the Chinese pilgrims Xuanzang and [[e:yijing|Yijing]] described Valabhi as a wealthy port and a university rivalling Nalanda. [[e:dhruvasena-ii|Dhruvasena II]] married a daughter of [[e:harsha|Harsha]] of the [[s:pushyabhuti-dynasty|Pushyabhuti dynasty]]. Jain tradition holds that its scriptures were written down at a council in Valabhi.
maitraka-dynasty.e: The Maitrakas weakened in the 8th century and Valabhi was sacked, apparently by an Arab expedition from Sindh, around 776. The dynasty disappeared and [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] later passed to the [[s:chavda-dynasty|Chavda dynasty]] and the [[s:gurjara-pratihara|Gurjara-Pratihara]].

massagetae.t: A powerful nomadic confederation east of the Caspian, best known for Queen Tomyris, whose warriors defeated and killed Cyrus the Great in 530 BCE.
massagetae.o: Greek historians, above all [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]], describe the Massagetae living beyond the Araxes, usually identified with the [[e:oxus|Amu Darya]] or [[e:syr-darya|Syr Darya]], on the plains east of the [[e:caspian-sea|Caspian Sea]] from the 6th century BCE. They were related to the [[s:saka|Saka]] and are often treated as one of the major Saka groupings.
massagetae.r: [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] describes a people fighting both on horseback and on foot with bows, lances and bronze-headed battle-axes, using gold and bronze but no iron or [[e:silver|silver]]. They worshipped the sun, to which they sacrificed horses, and lived on herds and fish. Some groups occupied the deltas of the [[e:oxus|Amu Darya]], near the farming towns of the [[s:kingdom-of-khwarazm|Kingdom of Khwarazm]].
massagetae.e: After their victory over Cyrus, the Massagetae fade from detailed record. They are mentioned in [[e:alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great's]] campaigns in [[s:principality-of-samarkand|Sogdiana]], then dissolve into later steppe groupings, among them the peoples displaced by the [[s:yuezhi|Yuezhi]]. Their name was later revived by Byzantine writers as a learned label for [[e:huns|Huns]].

muisca-confederation.t: A union of chiefdoms in Colombia's eastern highlands whose gold offerings in Lake Guatavita gave rise to the legend of El Dorado.
muisca-confederation.o: The Muisca settled the high plateau of [[s:free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamarca|Cundinamarca]] and Boyacá, in the Eastern Ranges of the Colombian [[s:andecavi|Andes]], and by around 800 their chiefdoms had taken shape. Over the following centuries they grouped into larger confederations led by the zipa in the south and the zaque in the north.
muisca-confederation.r: Muisca society was divided between the [[s:zipazgo-of-bacata|Zipazgo of Bacatá]] in the south, the [[s:zacazgo-of-hunza|Zacazgo of Hunza]] in the north, and independent territories such as [[s:iraca|Iraca]] and [[s:tundama|Tundama]]. Rulers inherited power through the maternal line, from uncle to nephew. The Muisca traded salt from Zipaquirá and Nemocón, emeralds and [[e:cotton|cotton]] cloth for gold, which they cast into tunjos, votive figures. The installation of a new ruler at [[e:lake-guatavita|Lake Guatavita]], covered in gold dust, became the legend of [[e:el-dorado|El Dorado]].
muisca-confederation.e: [[e:gonzalo-jimenez-de-quesada|Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada]] led a Spanish expedition into Muisca lands in 1537, defeating the zipa and zaque within two years. [[e:bogota|Santa Fe de Bogotá]] was founded in 1538 as the centre of the [[s:new-kingdom-of-granada|New Kingdom of Granada]]. The Muisca language died out in the 18th century.

miguelist-portugal.t: The absolutist regime of King Miguel I, whose seizure of the throne in 1828 sparked Portugal's Liberal Wars.
miguelist-portugal.o: On John VI's death in 1826 his heir Pedro, emperor of [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]], granted Portugal a constitutional Charter and abdicated for his daughter [[e:maria-ii-of-portugal|Maria II]], naming his brother Miguel regent. In 1828 Miguel, backed by absolutists and the Church, had the Cortes proclaim him king.
miguelist-portugal.r: Miguel abolished the Charter and ruled as an absolute monarch, persecuting liberals, many of whom fled abroad or to the Azores. He enjoyed popular support in the countryside and among the clergy, but most European powers refused to recognise him. The liberals held Terceira and formed a government in exile.
miguelist-portugal.e: Pedro returned from [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]], landed near Porto in 1832 and endured a long siege before liberal forces took [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]] in 1833. Miguel surrendered by the Concession of Evoramonte in May 1834 and went into permanent exile, and [[e:maria-ii-of-portugal|Maria II]] was restored to the [[s:kingdom-of-portugal|Kingdom of Portugal]].

mani.t: The Maya province of the Tutul Xiu lineage in western Yucatán, which allied with the Spanish in 1542 and preserved some of the richest Maya records.
mani.o: The Xiu, who claimed origins outside Yucatán and links with [[s:uxmal|Uxmal]], led the revolt that destroyed the [[s:league-of-mayapan|League of Mayapan]] around 1441. They then founded a province centred on Maní, south of the Puuc hills, which became one of the most powerful in the peninsula.
mani.r: Maní was ruled by a halach uinic of the Xiu lineage, the Tutul Xiu, who governed many towns through local batabs. Its feud with the Cocom of [[s:sotuta|Sotuta]] flared in 1536, when the Xiu lord [[e:ah-dzun-xiu|Ah Dzun Xiu]] was murdered at Otzmal. Xiu scribes kept genealogies and later compiled the Book of Chilam Balam of Maní.
mani.e: In 1542 [[e:ah-kukum-xiu|Ah Kukum Xiu]] came to T'ho and submitted to Montejo the Younger, giving the Spanish a vital ally. In 1562 [[e:diego-de-landa|Diego de Landa]] held his notorious auto-da-fé at Maní, burning Maya books. The Xiu family retained noble status in colonial times.

ming-xia.t: A rebel 'Great Xia' empire in Sichuan, founded by a Red Turban general and remembered for mild rule before its conquest by the Ming in 1371.
ming-xia.o: [[e:ming-yuzhen|Ming Yuzhen]], a commander of [[e:xu-shouhui|Xu Shouhui's]] Red Turban regime, led an army up the [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] into [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] in 1357 and took Chongqing. After [[e:chen-youliang|Chen Youliang]] murdered Xu in 1360, Ming Yuzhen refused to accept him, and in 1362 proclaimed himself emperor of [[s:western-xia|Great Xia]] at Chongqing.
ming-xia.r: [[e:ming-yuzhen|Ming Yuzhen]] governed [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] with comparatively light taxes, held civil service examinations on the Chinese model and promoted the Maitreya [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] of the Red Turbans while restraining other cults. Protected by the [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] gorges, the state stayed out of the great wars in the lower valley, though an invasion of Yunnan failed.
ming-xia.e: [[e:ming-yuzhen|Ming Yuzhen]] died in 1366, leaving his ten-year-old son [[e:ming-sheng|Ming Sheng]] under regents. In 1371 [[s:ming-empire|Ming Empire]] armies under [[s:later-tang|Tang]] He and Fu Youde advanced by river and over the mountains; Chongqing surrendered, and Ming Sheng was sent into exile in [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]].

mengujekids.t: A Turkish dynasty of the upper Euphrates whose masterpiece, the Great Mosque and Hospital of Divrigi, is a World Heritage Site.
mengujekids.o: After the battle of [[e:battle-of-manzikert|Manzikert]] in 1071, the [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] commander [[e:mengujek-gazi|Mengujek Gazi]] took Erzincan, Kemah, Divrigi and Sebinkarahisar on the upper [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]], establishing a small principality between the [[s:danishmendids|Danishmendids]], the [[s:saltukids|Saltukids]] and the Byzantine and Georgian frontiers.
mengujekids.r: The Mengujekids were patrons of Persian culture and architecture. Fakhr al-Din Bahramshah of Erzincan, who ruled for some sixty years, received the dedication of [[e:nizami-ganjavi|Nizami's]] poem Makhzan al-Asrar. In 1228-1229 Ahmad Shah of Divrigi and his wife Turan Malik built the [[e:divrigi-great-mosque-and-hospital|Great Mosque and Hospital of Divrigi]], whose carved stone portals are among the most extraordinary in medieval Islamic art. Their towns had large Armenian and Greek populations.
mengujekids.e: The [[s:sultanate-of-rum|Sultanate of Rum]] absorbed the Erzincan branch around 1228 under Kayqubad I. The Divrigi branch survived as Seljuk and then Mongol [[e:vassal|vassals]] until it disappears from the record in 1277.

momeik-state.t: A northern Shan state in Myanmar's Shan hills, near the ruby mines of Mogok, that kept its hereditary rulers until 1959.
momeik-state.o: Momeik, Shan Mong Mit, traces its ruling house to the 13th century in Shan tradition, and for much of its early history it was closely linked to [[s:hsenwi-state|Hsenwi]]. It lay north-east of Mandalay, between the Irrawaddy valley and the Shan plateau.
momeik-state.r: Its saopha ruled valleys of [[e:rice|rice]] and [[e:tea|tea]] worked by Shan, Palaung and Kachin peoples, under the overlordship first of Ava and later of the Toungoo and Konbaung kings. The state's territory at times included Mogok, whose rubies made the region famous, though the mines were usually under direct royal control.
momeik-state.e: After the British annexation of [[e:upper-burma|Upper Burma]] in 1885, Momeik became one of the Shan states under British protection and later part of the [[s:federated-shan-states|Federated Shan States]]. Like other saophas, its ruler surrendered his powers to the [[e:shan-state|Shan State]] government in 1959.

mataram-sultanate.t: The great inland Javanese sultanate of Sultan Agung, which ruled most of Java before dividing into Surakarta and Yogyakarta in 1755.
mataram-sultanate.o: [[e:panembahan-senapati|Sutawijaya]], son of [[e:ki-ageng-pemanahan|Ki Ageng Pemanahan]], built a court at Kotagede on land given by [[s:pajang-sultanate|Pajang]]. He threw off Pajang's authority and from around 1587 ruled as Panembahan Senapati, conquering much of Central and East [[e:java|Java]].
mataram-sultanate.r: [[e:sultan-agung|Sultan Agung]], ruling from 1613 to 1645, conquered the coastal states including [[s:duchy-of-surabaya|Surabaya]] in 1625, but twice failed to take [[e:batavia|Dutch Batavia]] in 1628 and 1629. He created the Javanese calendar of 1633, fusing Islamic and Hindu-Javanese traditions. Royal power rested on control of [[e:rice|rice]] lands and [[e:appanage|appanages]]. His son Amangkurat I ruled harshly and provoked the Trunajaya rebellion, which sacked his capital Plered in 1677.
mataram-sultanate.e: Mataram survived only with help from the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]], which gained land and trade rights in return. After a series of succession wars the Treaty of Giyanti of 1755 split the realm into [[s:surakarta-sunanate|Surakarta]] and [[s:yogyakarta-sultanate|Yogyakarta]], whose courts still exist.

mogaung.t: A powerful Shan state in Kachin country of northern Myanmar, a centre of the jade trade that fought Ava and China before Konbaung absorbed it.
mogaung.o: Mogaung, Shan Mong Kawng, on the Mogaung river in present-day Kachin State, was one of the northern Shan states; Shan chronicles date the founding of its ruling house to the early 13th century. It belonged to the wider world of the [[e:tai-mao|Tai Mao]], often linked to [[s:mong-mao|Mong Mao]].
mogaung.r: Its saopha ruled over Shan, Kachin and other upland peoples, drawing wealth from [[e:rice|rice]] valleys and from the jade mines of Hpakant, which supplied Chinese markets. Mogaung frequently raided the [[s:ava-kingdom|Ava Kingdom]], joining other Shan states, and at times also paid tribute to [[e:ming-empire|Ming China]].
mogaung.e: Bayinnaung of the [[s:first-toungoo-empire|First Toungoo Empire]] subdued Mogaung in the 1550s, and its rebellions were crushed later. The [[s:konbaung-dynasty|Konbaung dynasty]] abolished its saopha line in the late 18th century, placing the area under direct royal governors. The town of Mogaung remains in Kachin State.

margraviate-of-upper-lusatia.t: The land of Bautzen and Görlitz, a Sorb homeland ruled for centuries by Bohemia, famed for its Six Towns League and Herrnhut.
margraviate-of-upper-lusatia.o: The area around Bautzen, the land of the Slavic Milceni, belonged to the [[s:margraviate-of-meissen|Margraviate of Meissen]]. In 1158 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] granted the land of Bautzen to [[e:vladislaus-ii-of-bohemia|Vladislaus II of Bohemia]], starting a long Bohemian connection. From the 15th century the region came to be called [[e:upper-lusatia|Upper Lusatia]], in contrast to [[e:lower-lusatia|Lower Lusatia]].
margraviate-of-upper-lusatia.r: [[e:upper-lusatia|Upper Lusatia]] was ruled by distant Bohemian kings but largely governed by its estates and towns. In 1346 Bautzen, Görlitz, Zittau, Lauban, Kamenz and Löbau formed the [[s:lusatian-league|Six Towns League]], protecting trade routes. The mystic Jakob Böhme lived in Görlitz, and in 1722 Moravian refugees founded Herrnhut under Count Zinzendorf.
margraviate-of-upper-lusatia.e: The Peace of [[e:prague|Prague]] of 1635 transferred [[e:upper-lusatia|Upper Lusatia]] to the [[s:electorate-of-saxony|Electorate of Saxony]]. In 1815 the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] gave the north-eastern half, including Görlitz, to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. Today it is split between Saxony and [[e:poland|Poland]], with a Sorbian minority around Bautzen.

maroneia.t: Chian colony on the coast of Thrace, famed since Homer for its strong wine.
maroneia.o: Maroneia was founded by settlers from [[s:chios|Chios]] c. 650 BCE on the Thracian coast east of [[s:abdera|Abdera]], near the land of the Cicones. Its name recalled Maron, the priest of Apollo who gave Odysseus the potent wine he used to intoxicate the Cyclops.
maroneia.r: Maroneia's wealth came from wine and trade with Thracians, and its coins showed a prancing horse and vines. It paid tribute in the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]] and later joined the [[s:second-athenian-league|Second Athenian League]]. The city's Dionysus sanctuary and [[e:theatre|theatre]] reflected its wine economy, and it built a strong harbour.
maroneia.e: Maroneia passed under [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II]], then the [[s:ptolemaic-empire|Ptolemaic Empire]] and the [[s:antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia|Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia]]. [[e:philip-v-of-macedon|Philip V]]'s troops massacred many citizens in 184 BCE. [[e:rome|Rome]] made it a free city, and it came under Roman control by 146 BCE.

margraviate-of-burgau.t: Swabian margraviate between Ulm and Augsburg that the Habsburgs held for five centuries as part of Further Austria, ruled from Günzburg.
margraviate-of-burgau.o: The margraves of Burgau, a branch of the counts of Berg, held lands on the [[e:danube|Danube]] and the lower Mindel and Günz rivers from the early 13th century, using the margravial title from about 1212. When their line died out in 1301, the margraviate passed to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]], who added it to their scattered Swabian possessions.
margraviate-of-burgau.r: Burgau was a weak territory: the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] often pledged it, and many monasteries, imperial cities and nobles inside its borders claimed their own rights, leaving the margrave chiefly with high justice and taxation. From 1609 Günzburg was the residence of Margrave Charles of Burgau, son of Archduke Ferdinand II and Philippine Welser. In the 18th century Günzburg housed an important Austrian mint.
margraviate-of-burgau.e: After [[e:austria|Austria's]] defeat by [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], the [[e:peace-of-pressburg-1805|Peace of Pressburg]] of 1805 transferred Burgau to the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]], soon the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. Its lands now lie in the Bavarian district of Swabia.

mari.t: Mari, a city-kingdom on the middle Euphrates whose royal archives give the most detailed picture of diplomacy and daily politics in the age of Hammurabi.
mari.o: Mari was founded c. 2900 BCE at Tell Hariri as a planned circular city controlling river traffic between [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and southern [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]]. Rebuilt after a destruction, it flourished c. 2500 to 2300 BCE as a rival of [[s:ebla|Ebla]], then was governed by military governors, the shakkanakku, under the [[s:akkadian-empire|Akkadian Empire]] and its successors.
mari.r: Around 1800 BCE the Amorite Lim dynasty ruled from a vast palace of some 260 rooms. Mari lived from river tolls, trade in [[e:tin|tin]] and textiles, and irrigated farming, while its kings negotiated constantly with tribal groups. The archive of over 20,000 tablets, written in Akkadian, records letters, prophecies, treaties and court life under [[e:zimri-lim|Zimri-Lim]].
mari.e: Shamshi-Adad's [[s:kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia|Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia]] briefly absorbed Mari before [[e:zimri-lim|Zimri-Lim]] regained the throne. His former ally [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi]] of the [[s:babylonian-empire|Babylonian Empire]] conquered the city c. 1761 BCE and destroyed it c. 1759 BCE. It never recovered as a capital, but French excavations from 1933 made its palace and archive famous.

mori-clan-domain.t: The domain of the Mori of Aki, who rose under Mori Motonari to rule most of western Honshu and later led the losing side at Sekigahara.
mori-clan-domain.o: [[e:mori-motonari|Mori Motonari]], a minor lord of Aki based at Yoshida-Koriyama castle, built up power between the Ouchi and Amago. After defeating [[e:sue-harukata|Sue Harukata]] at Itsukushima in 1555 he destroyed the Ouchi in 1557 and took their lands, and in 1566 he conquered the Amago.
mori-clan-domain.r: Motonari placed his sons at the head of the Kikkawa and Kobayakawa families, the two rivers supporting the Mori, and legend tells of his lesson of three arrows on family unity. The domain covered some ten provinces in the Chugoku region and had a powerful navy. His grandson Terumoto fought [[e:oda-nobunaga|Oda Nobunaga]], then made peace with [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] in 1582 and founded [[e:hiroshima|Hiroshima]] in 1589.
mori-clan-domain.e: Terumoto was nominal commander of the western army at [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]] in 1600. [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] reduced Mori lands to Suo and Nagato, which became the [[s:choshu-domain|Choshu Domain]].

mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate.t: A failed division of Mount Lebanon into Christian and Druze districts, which ended in the civil war of 1860.
mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate.o: After the end of the [[s:mount-lebanon-emirate|Mount Lebanon Emirate]] in 1842 and fighting between Druze and Maronites, the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] and the European powers agreed to divide the mountain along the Beirut-[[e:damascus|Damascus]] road. A Maronite qaimaqam governed the north and a Druze qaimaqam the south, both under the Ottoman governor in [[s:beirut|Beirut]].
mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate.r: The division ignored the many mixed villages, and the 1845 rules of Shakib Efendi added councils representing each community, which did not end the tensions. In 1858 Maronite peasants of Kisrawan led by Tanyus Shahin rose against their Khazin overlords and expelled them, a social revolt that alarmed Druze lords in the south.
mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate.e: In 1860 a civil war broke out in which Druze fighters killed thousands of Christians, followed by a massacre in [[e:damascus|Damascus]]. [[e:france|France]] sent troops, and an international commission created the [[s:mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate|Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate]] in 1861.

mira.t: Mira, the strongest of the vassal kingdoms carved out of Arzawa, whose king's name was read on the Karabel rock relief near Izmir.
mira.o: After [[e:mursili-ii|Mursili II]] of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] defeated [[s:arzawa|Arzawa]] c. 1320 BCE, he made Mashuiluwa, a prince who had sought refuge at the Hittite court, king of Mira, the land around the upper Maeander valley and its neighbour Kuwaliya.
mira.r: Mira's kings ruled by treaty with the Hittite great king, and their line included Kupanta-Kurunta. A reading of the Karabel relief near [[s:smyrna|Izmir]], published in 1998, names Tarkasnawa, king of Mira, showing his realm reached towards the [[e:aegean|Aegean]]. Its people spoke Luwian.
mira.e: Mashuiluwa rebelled and was deposed, but Mira stayed a Hittite [[e:vassal|vassal]] until the empire collapsed c. 1180 BCE. The western Anatolian kingdoms then disappear from records; the region later became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-lydia|Kingdom of Lydia]].

madurai-sultanate.t: A short-lived Muslim sultanate in Tamil country, founded by a rebel Delhi governor and visited by Ibn Battuta.
madurai-sultanate.o: After [[e:malik-kafur|Malik Kafur's]] campaigns, the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] governed the [[e:madurai|Madurai]] region, known as Ma'bar, through officials. In 1335 the governor [[e:jalal-al-din-ahsan-shah|Jalal al-Din Ahsan Shah]] rebelled against [[e:muhammad-bin-tughluq|Muhammad bin Tughluq]] and declared independence, founding a sultanate based at Madurai.
madurai-sultanate.r: The sultanate ruled a largely [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] population with a small Muslim military elite and was marked by instability and violence; several sultans were murdered or died after short reigns. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]], who married Ahsan Shah's daughter, visited Ghiyath al-Din Damghani's court around 1344 and described its cruelty and an epidemic that struck the army. Coins are a major source.
madurai-sultanate.e: The rising [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara Empire]] attacked from the north; Kumara Kampana, son of Bukka I, defeated the sultan around 1370, and the sultanate's last remnants disappeared by 1378. The campaign is celebrated in the [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] poem Madhura Vijayam by his wife Gangadevi.
