miyoshi-clan-domain.t: The regime of Miyoshi Nagayoshi, who controlled Kyoto and the home provinces in the 1550s, ruling central Japan before Oda Nobunaga.
miyoshi-clan-domain.o: The Miyoshi were retainers of the Hosokawa deputy [[e:shogun|shoguns]], with a base in Awa on Shikoku. In 1549 [[e:miyoshi-nagayoshi|Miyoshi Nagayoshi]] turned against his master Hosokawa Harumoto, defeated his forces at Eguchi and took control of [[e:kyoto|Kyoto]], driving the shogun into exile.
miyoshi-clan-domain.r: Nagayoshi and his brothers controlled the Kinai and much of Shikoku, ruling through the [[e:shogun|shogun]] when it suited them. From 1560 he made Iimoriyama castle his seat. Some historians regard his regime as the first true central power of the [[e:sengoku-period|Sengoku period]], with direct control of the capital, its merchants and trade through [[s:sakai|Sakai]], and with close links to linked-verse poets and [[e:tea|tea]] masters.
miyoshi-clan-domain.e: After Nagayoshi died in 1564, his heir Yoshitsugu, the three Miyoshi elders and Matsunaga Hisahide's son Hisamichi killed the [[e:shogun|shogun]] Ashikaga Yoshiteru in 1565 but then fought each other. [[e:oda-nobunaga|Oda Nobunaga]] drove them from [[e:kyoto|Kyoto]] in 1568; Yoshitsugu was killed in 1573, and the last resistance ended in 1575.

mylliem-state.t: One of the largest Khasi states of the Meghalaya plateau, within whose territory the British built Shillong, capital of Assam and later of Meghalaya.
mylliem-state.o: Hima Mylliem was one of the Khasi chiefdoms that emerged on the Shillong plateau; their origins are known from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
mylliem-state.r: Like other Khasi states it was headed by a Syiem chosen from a royal clan by the heads of the leading clans, with succession passing through the female line, typically to a sister's son. Local markets and village councils (dorbar) were central to its life. Shillong, founded as a British station in the 1860s, lay inside Mylliem's lands.
mylliem-state.e: Mylliem signed agreements with the British in the 19th century and acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1948, joining Assam. Since 1972 it has been part of Meghalaya, where its Syiem keeps a customary role.

madurai-nayak-dynasty.t: Telugu Nayaka rulers of Madurai who built the great Meenakshi temple complex and ruled most of Tamil country for two centuries.
madurai-nayak-dynasty.o: Around 1529 the [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara Empire]] appointed [[e:vishwanatha-nayak|Vishwanatha Nayak]], son of a Vijayanagara general, as governor of [[e:madurai|Madurai]] after a rebellion there. He organised the region into some seventy-two palayams held by military chiefs, the Palaiyakkarars, and his successors ruled the southern Tamil country, becoming independent after Vijayanagara's decline.
madurai-nayak-dynasty.r: [[e:tirumala-nayak|Tirumala Nayak]], in the 17th century, rebuilt much of the Meenakshi Amman temple and built the Tirumalai Nayak palace in [[e:madurai|Madurai]]. The Nayaks controlled the pearl fishery coast, and [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] missionaries worked in their realm, among them Roberto de Nobili at Madurai. Queen Mangammal, regent around 1700, built roads, rest houses and tanks. The court used Telugu while Tamil culture flourished.
madurai-nayak-dynasty.e: After Vijaya Ranga Chokkanatha died in 1731, his widow Meenakshi became regent amid disputes. [[e:chanda-sahib|Chanda Sahib]] of the [[s:carnatic-sultanate|Carnatic Sultanate]] seized [[e:madurai|Madurai]] in 1736, ending the dynasty. The region passed to the Nawabs and then the British.

mito-domain.t: The Tokugawa branch domain whose scholars compiled the Great History of Japan and whose ideas inspired the movement to restore the emperor.
mito-domain.o: [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] gave Mito in Hitachi to his eleventh son [[e:tokugawa-yorifusa|Tokugawa Yorifusa]] in 1609. The domain, of about 350,000 koku, became one of the three Gosanke branch houses of the Tokugawa.
mito-domain.r: [[e:tokugawa-mitsukuni|Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] began the Dai Nihonshi, a history of [[e:japan|Japan]], in 1657; work on it continued until 1906 and gave rise to the Mito school, stressing loyalty to the emperor. In the 1840s [[e:tokugawa-nariaki|Tokugawa Nariaki]] pushed military reform and coastal defence and founded the Kodokan school. Mito men killed the great elder [[e:ii-naosuke|Ii Naosuke]] in 1860.
mito-domain.e: Violent feuds between factions, including the Tengu party rising of 1864, shattered the domain. Nariaki's son became [[e:tokugawa-yoshinobu|Tokugawa Yoshinobu]], the last [[e:shogun|shogun]]. After abolition in 1871 the domain became part of Ibaraki Prefecture.

manapii.t: People of south-east Ireland named by Ptolemy, with a town called Manapia, sharing their name with the Menapii of the Low Countries.
manapii.o: [[e:geography-ptolemy|Ptolemy's Geography]] of about 150 places the Manapii on the east coast of Ireland, south of the [[s:cauci|Cauci]], usually located around Wicklow or north Wexford, with a settlement named Manapia. Their name matches the [[s:menapii|Menapii]] of Belgic Gaul, which has led to suggestions of migration or trading links across the sea.
manapii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Some scholars connect them with later Irish population names such as the Monaig, recorded in [[s:kingdom-of-leinster|Leinster]] and [[s:northern-ireland|Ulster]], and with the [[s:kingdom-of-fermanagh|Fir Manach]] who gave their name to Fermanagh, but these links rest only on the similarity of names.
manapii.e: The Manapii do not appear in later records. Their part of the coast later lay within the [[s:kingdom-of-leinster|Kingdom of Leinster]], and especially the lands of the [[s:ui-chennselaig|Ui Chennselaig]].

mankot-state.t: A small Rajput hill state between Jammu and Basohli, remembered for the Mankot school of Pahari painting.
mankot-state.o: Mankot, also called Ramkot, was ruled by the Mankotia [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]]; tradition dates the state to around 1400, but its early history is poorly recorded.
mankot-state.r: The Mankot court produced a distinctive school of Pahari [[e:persian-miniature|miniature painting]] in the late 17th and 18th centuries, related to the [[s:basohli-state|Basohli]] style and known for bold portraits of local rulers. Politically it was a minor state in the shadow of Jammu.
mankot-state.e: Mankot was absorbed by the [[e:dogras|Dogra]] rulers of Jammu around 1820 and became part of [[s:jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state|Jammu and Kashmir (princely state)]] in 1846. The area, around Ramkot, is now in Jammu and [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]].

makran-state.t: A coastal Baloch principality under the Khanate of Kalat, ruled by Gichki Nawabs from Turbat, which joined Pakistan in 1948.
makran-state.o: Makran, the arid coastal region of southern Balochistan, was under the overlordship of the [[s:khanate-of-kalat|Khanate of Kalat]], while local power lay with the Gichki family. By the end of the 19th century the Gichki Nawabs ruled Kech-Makran as a dependency of Kalat.
makran-state.r: The state was thinly populated, with date palms in the Kech valley, fishing on the coast and trade through ports such as Pasni. The Nawabs ruled with [[s:khanate-of-kalat|Kalat]] and British political officers looking on. The port of Gwadar on its coast belonged to [[e:muscat|Muscat]] until 1958.
makran-state.e: In March 1948 Makran acceded to [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] independently of [[s:khanate-of-kalat|Kalat]]. It joined the [[s:baluchistan-states-union|Baluchistan States Union]] in 1952 and was merged into [[e:west-pakistan|West Pakistan]] in 1955; it is now a division of Balochistan.

mushasha.t: A messianic Shia Arab dynasty of Khuzestan, founded by a self-proclaimed Mahdi, that later ruled 'Arabistan' as Safavid vassals for two centuries.
mushasha.o: [[e:muhammad-ibn-falah|Muhammad ibn Falah]], a scholar from Wasit trained in [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] theology at Hilla, proclaimed himself the representative of the [[e:imamate|Hidden Imam]], or the [[e:mahdi|Mahdi]] himself, in the 1430s. Gathering Arab tribes of the marshes, he founded a state in Khuzestan around 1436 with its capital at Hoveyzeh.
mushasha.r: The early Musha'sha held extreme (ghulat) [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] beliefs: Muhammad's son [[e:mawla-ali|Mawla Ali]] claimed that [[e:ali-ibn-abi-talib|Ali ibn Abi Talib]] was divine and sacked Najaf in 1453. The state rested on Arab tribal warriors and the date and [[e:rice|rice]] lands of the Karun and Karkheh rivers. After Shah [[e:ismail-i|Ismail I]] conquered Khuzestan in 1508, the Musha'sha became walis (governors) of [[s:sheikhdom-of-mohammerah|Arabistan]] under the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]] and moved towards conventional [[e:twelver-shiism|Twelver Shi'ism]].
mushasha.e: The Musha'sha declined in the 18th century amid Afghan and Ottoman invasions after the Safavid collapse. By 1729 real power had passed to other tribes, notably the [[s:banu-kab-sheikhdom|Banu Ka'b sheikhdom]], though Musha'sha sayyids kept a local role at Hoveyzeh.

mawiang-state.t: A small Khasi chiefdom of the West Khasi Hills, one of the 25 Khasi states that acceded to India in 1948.
mawiang-state.o: Hima Mawiang was one of the Khasi chiefdoms of the Meghalaya plateau; its origins are known only from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
mawiang-state.r: Mawiang was headed by a Syiem chosen from a royal clan, with succession through the female line and decisions taken with clan elders in a dorbar. Little written record of its history exists.
mawiang-state.e: Mawiang came under British supervision in the 19th century and acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1948, joining Assam. It is now part of Meghalaya.

mount-lebanon-emirate.t: The autonomous emirate of the Druze and Maronite mountain, ruled by the Ma'n and Shihab families and the forerunner of modern Lebanon.
mount-lebanon-emirate.o: After the Ottoman conquest of 1516, the Druze chiefs of the Shuf mountains were left to govern themselves as tax farmers. The Ma'n family rose to dominate them, and under [[e:fakhr-al-din-ii|Fakhr al-Din II]] (1591-1633) their [[e:emirate|emirate]] extended over much of [[s:lebanese-republic|Lebanon]], [[e:galilee|Galilee]] and the coast.
mount-lebanon-emirate.r: The [[e:emir|emirs]] ruled a feudal society of Druze and Maronite lords and peasants from Deir al-Qamar. [[e:fakhr-al-din-ii|Fakhr al-Din II]] allied with [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]], lived in exile in [[e:italy|Italy]] in 1613-1618 and promoted [[e:silk|silk]] production, but was executed by the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1635. In 1697 the Shihab family succeeded the Ma'ns. [[e:bashir-shihab-ii|Bashir II]] (1789-1840), who became Christian, built the palace of Beiteddine and sided with [[e:muhammad-ali-of-egypt|Muhammad Ali of Egypt]].
mount-lebanon-emirate.e: When the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] expelled the [[e:egyptians|Egyptians]] in 1840, [[e:bashir-shihab-ii|Bashir II]] went into exile. His successor Bashir III was deposed in 1842 amid Druze-Maronite fighting, and the Ottomans replaced the [[e:emirate|emirate]] with the [[s:mount-lebanon-double-qaimaqamate|Mount Lebanon Double Qaimaqamate]].

maseko-ngoni-kingdom.t: The Ngoni kingdom of the Maseko in the Dedza highlands of Malawi, whose king Gomani was executed by the British in 1896.
maseko-ngoni-kingdom.o: The Maseko [[e:ngoni|Ngoni]] left the [[e:zulu-kingdom|Zulu]] region in the 1820s and crossed the [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]] under their leader [[e:ngwana|Ngwana]]. They moved as far north as the Songea area of southern [[s:tanzania|Tanzania]] under Mputa before being driven south again, settling around 1870 in the highlands southwest of [[e:lake-malawi|Lake Malawi]] under Chidiaonga.
maseko-ngoni-kingdom.r: The Maseko kept the [[e:nguni|Nguni]] regimental system and ruled over many [[e:chewa|Chewa]] and Nyanja villages, whose men were drawn into their regiments. Raiding for [[e:cattle|cattle]] and captives, and tribute from subject peoples, supported the royal villages. A long civil war in the 1870s and 1880s divided the kingdom.
maseko-ngoni-kingdom.e: Gomani I resisted British demands for labour and stopped his people from working for planters. He was defeated and executed in 1896, and the kingdom was absorbed into the [[s:british-central-africa-protectorate|British Central Africa Protectorate]].

massangano.t: The Da Cruz family's fortified state on the Zambezi, which repeatedly defeated Portuguese armies in the 19th century.
massangano.o: The Da Cruz family, Afro-Portuguese prazo holders, built their stronghold at Massangano where the Luenha joins the [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]], above Tete. Under António Vicente da Cruz, known as Bonga, it became an independent power controlling the river route in the mid-19th century.
massangano.r: From a large aringa, a stockaded fort, the Da Cruz rulers commanded Chikunda soldiers, taxed river traffic and raided for slaves and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]]. They mixed Portuguese and African forms of authority and relied on [[e:spirit-medium|spirit mediums]] as well as firearms. Bonga destroyed four Portuguese expeditions between 1867 and 1869, an embarrassment to [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]].
massangano.e: After Bonga's death in 1879 his successors continued to resist, but a Portuguese force supported by rival warlords such as those of [[s:makanga|Makanga]] captured Massangano in 1888, and the region came under [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Portuguese Mozambique]].

massachusetts-bay-colony.t: The Puritan colony centred on Boston, founded to be a godly 'city upon a hill', which became the dominant power of early New England.
massachusetts-bay-colony.o: After an advance party under [[e:john-endecott|John Endecott]] settled at Salem in 1628, the Massachusetts Bay Company won a royal charter in 1629 and carried it to America. [[e:john-winthrop|John Winthrop]] led a fleet of about 1,000 settlers in 1630, founding [[e:boston|Boston]]. In the Great Migration of the 1630s some 20,000 English Puritans followed.
massachusetts-bay-colony.r: The colony governed itself under its charter through a governor and a General Court elected by freemen, who for decades had to be church members. Congregational churches shaped law and daily life, and Harvard College was founded in 1636. Dissenters were expelled: [[e:roger-williams|Roger Williams]] and Anne Hutchinson went to what became the [[s:colony-of-rhode-island-and-providence-plantations|Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations]]. Farming, fishing, shipbuilding and [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic trade]] made [[e:boston|Boston]] prosperous.
massachusetts-bay-colony.e: [[s:province-of-massachusetts-bay|Massachusetts]] absorbed [[e:new-hampshire|New Hampshire]] for a time and the [[s:province-of-maine|Province of Maine]]. Its charter was revoked in 1684 and it was merged into the [[s:dominion-of-new-england|Dominion of New England]] in 1686. After that regime fell, the charter of 1691 created the Province of Massachusetts Bay.

mansa-state.t: A small Chavda Rajput state in northern Gujarat whose rulers claimed descent from the founders of medieval Anhilwad Patan.
mansa-state.o: [[e:mansa|Mansa]] was held by Chavda [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]], who traced their line to the [[s:chavda-dynasty|Chavda dynasty]] that founded Anhilwad Patan in the 8th century. The family established its holding around Mansa by about 1600.
mansa-state.r: The ruler governed a small agricultural territory in the [[e:mahi-kantha-agency|Mahi Kantha]] region, paying tribute through the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads of Baroda]] and supervised by the British Mahi Kantha Agency. Few further details of its rulers are widely recorded.
mansa-state.e: [[e:mansa|Mansa]] merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960. The town now lies in Gandhinagar district.

miraj-junior.t: The junior of two Patwardhan Brahmin states formed from Miraj in 1820, ruled from Budhgaon in the southern Maratha country.
miraj-junior.o: Miraj Junior was created in 1820 when the Patwardhan holding of Miraj, itself one of the shares from the family partition of 1811, was divided between two branches. The junior branch took scattered villages and made Budhgaon its seat.
miraj-junior.r: It was a small state of the [[e:southern-maratha-country|Southern Maratha Country]], later the [[e:deccan-states-agency|Deccan States Agency]], with lands interspersed among those of [[s:miraj-senior|Miraj Senior]] and [[s:sangli-state|Sangli State]]. Little else is recorded of its internal history.
miraj-junior.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Miraj Junior was merged into [[e:bombay-state|Bombay State]] in 1948 and has been part of Maharashtra since 1960; Budhgaon lies in [[s:sangli-state|Sangli]] district.

mughan-soviet-republic.t: A Soviet republic proclaimed for a few weeks in 1919 by Bolsheviks among the Russian settlers of the Mughan steppe in south-eastern Azerbaijan.
mughan-soviet-republic.o: In spring 1919 the [[s:provisional-military-dictatorship-of-mughan|Provisional Military Dictatorship of Mughan]] was overthrown when a congress of local settlers, influenced by Bolsheviks, turned against the White officers who ran it. In May 1919 the congress at Lankaran proclaimed the Mughan Soviet Republic. Its leaders hoped for help from [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]] across the Caspian.
mughan-soviet-republic.r: The republic was based on councils of Russian settler villages, including Molokans, and sought to join [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]]. It tried to extend its control to Talysh and Azerbaijani villages, provoking fighting with local forces. Isolated and with little outside support, it never developed a stable administration.
mughan-soviet-republic.e: In July 1919 troops of the [[s:azerbaijan-democratic-republic|Azerbaijan Democratic Republic]] and local Talysh forces captured Lankaran and ended the republic. The region came under Soviet rule with the rest of [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] in 1920.

minyue.t: The kingdom of the Min Yue people in Fujian, ruled by descendants of Goujian of Yue, which Han armies destroyed in 110 BCE.
minyue.o: The Min Yue were a Baiyue people of Fujian. Their leader Wuzhu, who claimed descent from [[e:goujian|King Goujian]] of the [[s:state-of-yue|State of Yue]], had been demoted under the [[s:qin-dynasty|Qin dynasty]] but supported [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]] against [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]]. In 202 BCE the [[s:han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] recognised him as King of Minyue, with his capital at [[s:dongye|Dongye]] (Fuzhou).
minyue.r: Minyue was a coastal and mountain kingdom of [[e:rice|rice]] farmers, fishermen and seafarers. The walled Han-period city at Chengcun near Wuyishan shows a mixture of Han and Yue building styles. Its kings expanded aggressively, attacking [[s:dongou|Dong'ou]] in 138 BCE and [[s:nanyue|Nanyue]] in 135 BCE, when King Zou Ying was killed by his own brother Yushan to avert a Han invasion.
minyue.e: In 111 BCE Zou Yushan declared himself emperor and attacked Han forces. Han armies invaded by land and sea, his followers killed him, and in 110 BCE the Han moved much of the population north to the Yangtze-Huai region and abolished the kingdom.

mazyadid-dynasty.t: An Arab Shia dynasty of the Banu Asad that ruled central Iraq along the Euphrates and founded the city of Hilla.
mazyadid-dynasty.o: The Mazyadids, leaders of the Bedouin tribe of Banu Asad, held lands along the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] south of [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]]. Their founder, [[e:ali-ibn-mazyad|Ali ibn Mazyad]], was recognised by the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyid dynasty]] in the later 10th century. The family controlled the farming districts and the routes to the [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] shrine cities of Najaf and [[e:battle-of-karbala|Karbala]].
mazyadid-dynasty.r: The Mazyadids were [[e:twelver-shiism|Twelver Shia]] and patrons of [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] scholarship. [[e:sadaqa-ibn-mansur|Sadaqa ibn Mansur]], the greatest of the line, founded al-Hilla around 1101 on the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] near ancient [[e:babylon|Babylon]], which became a major centre of Shia learning. The dynasty balanced between the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] and the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]]; Sadaqa sheltered rebels and was killed fighting [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Muhammad Tapar in 1108. His son Dubays allied with Zengi and other enemies of the [[e:caliphate|caliphs]].
mazyadid-dynasty.e: Weakened by wars with the [[e:caliphate|caliphs]], the Mazyadids lost Hilla, and by the mid-12th century the revived Abbasid caliphate had ended their rule. Hilla remained an important [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] city.

methone-pieria.t: Eretrian colony on the Macedonian coast whose siege in 354 BCE cost Philip II an eye, and whose pottery bears some of the oldest Greek writing.
methone-pieria.o: Methone was founded on the coast of Pieria, on the Thermaic Gulf, by settlers from [[s:eretria|Eretria]] c. 733 BCE; Plutarch says they were Eretrians driven out of [[s:corcyra|Corcyra]]. The site, on a low hill by the sea, had been inhabited since the Neolithic.
methone-pieria.r: Methone was a trading port linking the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] with Macedonian [[e:timber|timber]] and metals. Excavations since 2003 have found a deposit of pottery from c. 700 BCE inscribed with some of the earliest Greek alphabetic writing, as well as metalworking debris. In the Classical period it was an ally of [[s:athens|Athens]] and a base for Athenian interference in [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]].
methone-pieria.e: [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-macedon|Kingdom of Macedon]] besieged Methone in 354 BCE, losing an eye to an arrow. After its surrender he razed the city and divided its land among [[e:macedonian-empire|Macedonians]]. The site later became a small village.

mohawk-nation.t: The People of the Flint, Keepers of the Eastern Door of the Iroquois Confederacy, key partners of the Dutch and British and today spread across New York, Quebec and Ontario.
mohawk-nation.o: The Mohawk lived in the Mohawk River valley of eastern [[e:new-york|New York]], the easternmost of the five [[s:iroquois-confederacy|Haudenosaunee]] nations. Haudenosaunee tradition holds that they were the first nation to accept the Peacemaker's [[e:great-law-of-peace|Great Law of Peace]], around the mid-15th century, and so hold an elder place in the Iroquois [[s:confederate-states-of-america|Confederacy]].
mohawk-nation.r: Nine Mohawk chiefs sat in the [[e:grand-council-qing|Grand Council]]. Trade with [[s:new-netherland|New Netherland]] at [[e:fort-orange|Fort Orange]] from the 1610s gave the Mohawk firearms and made them leading players in the [[e:fur-trade|fur trade]] and the [[e:beaver-wars|Beaver Wars]]. [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] missions drew Catholic converts north, among them Kateri Tekakwitha, to Kahnawake near Montreal. In the 18th century [[e:hendrick-theyanoguin|Hendrick Theyanoguin]], Molly Brant and [[e:joseph-brant|Joseph Brant]] built close ties with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and the Indian superintendent William Johnson.
mohawk-nation.e: After fighting for [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in the Revolution, most Mohawk left [[e:new-york|New York]] for [[e:grand-river-ontario|Grand River]] and Tyendinaga in Ontario. Mohawk communities today include Akwesasne, Kahnawake and Kanesatake, scene of the 1990 Oka crisis, along with [[s:iroquois-confederacy|Six Nations]] and Tyendinaga in Ontario.

march-of-friuli.t: Carolingian frontier march in north-eastern Italy whose margrave Berengar became King of Italy and emperor.
march-of-friuli.o: After Duke Hrodgaud's revolt in 776, [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] replaced the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] dukes of Friuli with Frankish officials. The territory was expanded into a march facing the [[e:avars|Avars]] and the [[e:slavs|Slavs]], and its margraves commanded forces that, under [[e:eric-of-friuli|Eric of Friuli]], captured the Avar Ring and its treasure in 796.
march-of-friuli.r: The march was a military command reaching from the [[e:alps|Alps]] to [[s:histria|Istria]] and into [[e:pannonia|Pannonia]], with Cividale as its centre. After 828 it was reorganised, and from about 846 it was held by the Unruoching family, beginning with Eberhard, a cultured noble who married [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious's]] daughter Gisela and owned a notable library. His son Berengar became margrave in 874.
march-of-friuli.e: [[e:berengar-i-of-italy|Berengar of Friuli]] was elected King of [[e:italy|Italy]] in 888 and crowned emperor in 915, while Hungarian raids devastated the region. In 952 [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] took Friuli from Italian control and attached it, with [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]], to the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria|Duchy of Bavaria]] as the [[s:march-of-verona|March of Verona]].

moghulistan.t: The eastern Chagatai khanate of the Tian Shan and Ili valley, where the Mongol nomads converted to Islam and resisted Timur.
moghulistan.o: When the [[e:chagatai-khanate|Chagatai Khanate]] split in the 1340s, the [[e:dughlat|Dughlat]] amir Puladchi enthroned [[e:tughlugh-timur|Tughlugh Timur]], a claimed descendant of Chagatai, as khan of the eastern part in 1347. The western [[e:persians|Persians]] called this nomadic region and its people Moghulistan, 'land of the [[e:mongols|Mongols]]'.
moghulistan.r: [[e:tughlugh-timur|Tughlugh Timur]] converted to [[e:islam|Islam]] with many of his followers around 1354, and invaded [[e:transoxiana|Transoxiana]] in 1360 and 1361. The khanate was nomadic, with powerful [[e:dughlat|Dughlat]] [[e:amir|amirs]] controlling the Tarim cities of [[s:kingdom-of-shule|Kashgar]] and Aksu. [[e:timur|Timur]] campaigned against it repeatedly but never conquered it. Khans such as [[e:yunus-khan|Yunus Khan]], grandfather of the Mughal emperor [[e:babur|Babur]], maintained links with Timurid Transoxiana.
moghulistan.e: Divided by civil war, Moghulistan split in the 1460s between [[e:yunus-khan|Yunus Khan]] in the west and his brother Esen Buqa's line in the east. Yunus later reunited it, but after his death in 1487 his sons divided it again, and the eastern part under [[e:ahmad-alaq|Ahmad Alaq]] became the [[s:turpan-khanate|Turpan Khanate]]. Its western pastures were taken by the [[s:kazakh-khanate|Kazakh Khanate]] and the Kyrgyz, and the [[s:yarkent-khanate|Yarkent Khanate]] arose in the Tarim.

masaesyli.t: The Berber kingdom of western Numidia under Syphax, a power courted by both Rome and Carthage in the Second Punic War.
masaesyli.o: The Masaesyli were a [[e:berbers|Berber]] people of western and central [[e:algeria|Algeria]]. By the late 3rd century BCE they formed a kingdom ruled from Siga, near the mouth of the Tafna river, with a second capital at Cirta after Syphax conquered eastern lands. Their rise came amid the struggle of [[e:rome|Rome]] and the [[s:punic-empire|Punic Empire]].
masaesyli.r: Syphax ruled a large realm of pastoral and farming tribes, minted coins with his portrait in Hellenistic style and kept a strong cavalry. He first made contact with [[e:rome|Rome]] and received envoys from Scipio, but in 205 BCE married Sophonisba, daughter of the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal, and sided with [[e:carthage|Carthage]]. A royal mausoleum at Beni Rhenane near Siga is attributed to his dynasty.
masaesyli.e: In 203 BCE Roman and [[s:massylii|Massylii]] forces defeated Syphax and captured him. His son Vermina ruled a reduced western kingdom for a time, but after Zama in 202 BCE most Masaesylian land fell to [[e:masinissa|Masinissa's]] kingdom of [[s:numidia|Numidia]].

meldi.t: Small Gallic people of the Marne valley whose town Iatinum became Meaux.
meldi.o: The Meldi lived on the Marne east of the [[s:parisii|Parisii]]. Caesar mentions that in 54 BCE some of the ships for his second expedition to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] were built in their territory.
meldi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions.
meldi.e: Under [[e:rome|Rome]] they formed a small civitas with Iatinum as its chief town, later called Meldi after the people, the origin of Meaux, which became a bishopric.

mamertine-messana.t: Messana under the Mamertines, Campanian mercenaries whose appeals to both Carthage and Rome set off the First Punic War in 264 BCE.
mamertine-messana.o: The Mamertines were Campanian [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] who had served [[e:agathocles-of-syracuse|Agathocles of Syracuse]]. After his death they seized Messana by treachery around 288 BCE, killing or expelling many of the men and taking their property. They called themselves Mamertini, 'sons of Mamers', the Oscan war god.
mamertine-messana.r: From Messana the Mamertines raided and taxed much of north-eastern [[e:sicily|Sicily]], ruling as a military community with Oscan magistrates; their coins name them in Greek. Their power was broken by [[e:hiero-ii-of-syracuse|Hieron II of Syracuse]], who defeated them at the Longanus river in the 260s BCE. Facing capture, one faction called in a Carthaginian garrison while another appealed to [[e:rome|Rome]].
mamertine-messana.e: [[e:rome|Rome's]] decision to send an army to Messana in 264 BCE began the [[e:first-punic-war|First Punic War]]. Messana became an ally of Rome, and after the war in 241 BCE it was a privileged allied city in Roman [[e:sicily|Sicily]], today Messina.

matsya-union.t: A union of four princely states of eastern Rajputana, named after the ancient Matsya kingdom, which lasted from 1948 to 1949.
matsya-union.o: In March 1948 [[s:alwar-state|Alwar State]], [[s:bharatpur-state|Bharatpur State]], [[s:dholpur-state|Dholpur State]] and [[s:karauli-state|Karauli]] were merged into the United State of [[s:matsya|Matsya]], named after the Matsya kingdom of the Mahabharata, which had lain in the same region. Alwar was the capital.
matsya-union.r: Maharaj Rana [[e:udaybhan-singh|Udaybhan Singh]] of [[s:dholpur-state|Dholpur]] was Rajpramukh, and [[e:shobha-ram|Shobha Ram]] led the government. The union was formed shortly after Alwar's ruler had been suspected of links to the extremists behind [[e:mahatma-gandhi|Gandhi's]] assassination, which hastened central intervention.
matsya-union.e: After a short existence the Matsya Union was merged into the [[s:united-state-of-rajasthan|United State of Rajasthan]] in May 1949.

muzaffarid-dynasty.t: A Persian dynasty that ruled Fars, Kerman and central Iran after the Ilkhanate collapsed, remembered as the patrons, and sometimes the critics, of the poet Hafez.
muzaffarid-dynasty.o: The Muzaffarids were a family of Arab descent who served the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]] as local officials. In 1319 [[e:mubariz-al-din-muhammad|Mubariz al-Din Muhammad]] defeated the [[s:atabegs-of-yazd|Atabegs of Yazd]] and took the city. After the death of the [[e:ilkhan|Ilkhan]] Abu Sa'id in 1335 he expanded rapidly, taking [[e:kerman|Kerman]] in 1340 and [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]] from the [[s:injuid-dynasty|Injuid dynasty]] in 1353.
muzaffarid-dynasty.r: Mubariz al-Din was a stern ruler who closed taverns in [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]], a mood Hafez mocked in his verse; in 1358 his sons blinded and deposed him. [[e:shah-shuja-muzaffarid|Shah Shuja]] (1358 to 1384) presided over a brilliant court in Shiraz where Hafez wrote much of his poetry, though the family was torn by fratricidal wars. The dynasty ruled Yazd, [[e:kerman|Kerman]], [[e:fars|Fars]] and [[e:isfahan|Isfahan]] through princes of the house.
muzaffarid-dynasty.e: [[e:timur|Timur's]] invasions overwhelmed the divided family. [[e:shah-mansur|Shah Mansur]] defied him and was killed near [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]] in 1393, and Timur executed the remaining princes, incorporating their lands into the [[s:timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]].

messene.t: City founded by Epaminondas in 369 BCE to free the Messenians from centuries of Spartan helotry, with some of the finest surviving Greek fortifications.
messene.o: For centuries the Messenians had been helots, forced to work their land for [[s:sparta|Sparta]]. After defeating [[e:sparta|Sparta]] at Leuctra, the Theban general [[e:epaminondas|Epaminondas]] invaded the Peloponnese and in 369 BCE founded [[s:zancle|Messene]] on the slopes of Mount Ithome, calling back Messenians scattered across the Greek world. Sparta refused for decades to recognise the new state.
messene.r: [[s:zancle|Messene]] was built from scratch with a ring of stone walls some 9 kilometres long, towers and the great Arcadian Gate. It had a council and assembly and celebrated its restored identity in cults of Zeus Ithomatas and the hero Aristomenes. Fearing [[s:sparta|Sparta]], it sought protection from [[s:thebes|Thebes]], then [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II]] and later the Hellenistic kings.
messene.e: [[s:zancle|Messene]] joined the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]] in 191 BCE, revolted, and in 182 BCE executed the captured Achaean general Philopoemen before being forced back. After the [[e:achaean-war|Achaean War]] in 146 BCE it passed under Roman rule. Excavations have uncovered its [[e:theatre|theatre]], stadium and [[e:agora|agora]], among the best-preserved in [[e:greece|Greece]].

mrauk-u-kingdom.t: The coastal kingdom of Arakan that ruled from the temple city of Mrauk U, mixed Buddhist kingship with Bengal Sultanate styles and dominated the Bay of Bengal.
mrauk-u-kingdom.o: [[e:min-saw-mon|Min Saw Mon]], the exiled last king of the Lemro period of the Kingdom of Arakan, regained his throne in 1429 with an army from the [[s:bengal-sultanate|Bengal Sultanate]] and in 1430 founded a new capital at Mrauk U. For a time Arakan paid tribute to [[e:bengal|Bengal]], and its Buddhist kings took Persian-style Muslim titles and issued coins with Persian inscriptions.
mrauk-u-kingdom.r: Under Min Bin in the 16th century Mrauk U became independent and powerful, controlling Chittagong and raiding [[e:bengal|Bengal]] with fleets that included Portuguese [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]]. Slaves captured in Bengal worked its [[e:rice|rice]] lands. The capital's stone temples, such as Shitthaung and Koe-thaung, survive. Its court hosted the Bengali poets Alaol and Daulat [[e:qazi|Qazi]], and Muslim and Buddhist officials served together.
mrauk-u-kingdom.e: The [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]] took Chittagong in 1666, and internal instability followed. In 1784 to 1785 the [[s:konbaung-dynasty|Konbaung dynasty]] under Bodawpaya conquered Arakan and carried off the [[e:mahamuni-buddha|Mahamuni Buddha]]. Refugee flows into British [[e:bengal|Bengal]] helped trigger the [[e:first-anglo-burmese-war|First Anglo-Burmese War]].

musulamii.t: A Berber tribal confederation of the Algerian-Tunisian highlands whose leader Tacfarinas fought Rome for seven years.
musulamii.o: The Musulamii were a large [[e:berbers|Berber]] people living on the high plains around Theveste (Tébessa) and Ammaedara, on the border between [[s:numidia|Numidia]] and the Roman province of [[e:africa|Africa]]. They appear in Roman sources from the 1st century BCE as semi-nomadic herders whose seasonal routes ran across land [[e:rome|Rome]] wanted for farming.
musulamii.r: Their society was tribal, under chiefs. In 17 CE Tacfarinas, a Musulamian who had served in the Roman auxiliary army, led a revolt that drew in the [[s:gaetuli|Gaetuli]] and Moorish groups, using [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] tactics against the Third Augustan legion. [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] describes the war in detail.
musulamii.e: Tacfarinas was killed in 24 CE, and the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]] confined the Musulamii to defined lands, later marked by boundary stones under [[e:trajan|Trajan]]. Roman colonies and veteran settlements spread over their territory, and they were gradually absorbed into provincial society.

margraviate-of-brandenburg.t: The electorate of the Hohenzollerns around Berlin, a sandy frontier march that grew into the Kingdom of Prussia.
margraviate-of-brandenburg.o: [[e:albert-the-bear|Albert the Bear]] secured [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] an der Havel in 1157, after inheriting it from the [[s:principality-of-the-hevelli|Hevelli]] prince Pribislav-Henry, and called himself [[e:margrave-of-brandenburg|Margrave of Brandenburg]]. His Ascanian successors pushed east to the Oder, encouraging German settlement and founding towns, including the twin towns of Berlin and Cölln in the 13th century.
margraviate-of-brandenburg.r: The [[e:golden-bull-of-1356|Golden Bull of 1356]] confirmed the margrave as an elector. In 1415 [[e:sigismund-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Sigismund]] gave [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] to the Hohenzollern [[e:frederick-i-elector-of-brandenburg|Frederick VI of Nuremberg]]. [[e:joachim-ii-hector|Joachim II]] introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1539. [[e:frederick-william-elector-of-brandenburg|The Great Elector]], Frederick William, rebuilt after the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]], welcoming Huguenot refugees in 1685 and creating a standing army.
margraviate-of-brandenburg.e: In 1701 [[e:frederick-i-of-prussia|Elector Frederick III]] crowned himself King in [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], and [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] became the heartland of the Prussian state. The margraviate ended formally with the Empire in 1806; it later became a Prussian province and is today the German state of Brandenburg around Berlin.
margraviate-of-brandenburg.re: Catholic Christianity, then Lutheranism and Calvinism

mandatory-iraq.t: The British-run League of Nations mandate that created the modern state of Iraq from three Ottoman provinces and installed a Hashemite king.
mandatory-iraq.o: British and Indian troops landed at [[e:basra|Basra]] in November 1914, took [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] in 1917 and occupied [[e:mosul|Mosul]] after the [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|armistice]] of 1918. The San Remo conference of April 1920 assigned the former Ottoman provinces of Basra, Baghdad and Mosul to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] as a [[e:league-of-nations-mandate|League of Nations mandate]]. The great revolt of 1920 against British rule was suppressed at heavy cost.
mandatory-iraq.r: At the [[e:cairo|Cairo]] Conference of 1921, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] chose the Hashemite prince Faisal, recently expelled from [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]], as king; after a staged referendum he was crowned in [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] in August 1921. British High Commissioners such as Sir Percy Cox advised the monarchy, while the Anglo-Iraqi treaties kept British control of foreign policy, finance and air bases. The League awarded the [[e:mosul|Mosul]] region to [[e:iraq|Iraq]] in 1925, confirmed by treaty with [[e:turkey|Turkey]] in 1926, and oil was struck at Baba Gurgur near Kirkuk in 1927.
mandatory-iraq.e: After the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of 1930, [[e:iraq|Iraq]] joined the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] as an independent state in October 1932, ending the mandate; the [[s:kingdom-of-iraq|Kingdom of Iraq]] continued with strong British ties.

musunuri-nayaks.t: Telugu warrior chiefs who drove the Delhi Sultanate out of Warangal a decade after the fall of the Kakatiyas.
musunuri-nayaks.o: After the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] captured Warangal in 1323, former Kakatiya Nayaka commanders organised resistance. [[e:prolaya-nayaka|Prolaya Nayaka]] of the Musunuri family led a confederacy of chiefs in coastal Andhra, and his cousin [[e:kapaya-nayaka|Kapaya Nayaka]], allied with the founders of the [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara Empire]], recaptured Warangal from the Tughluq governor around 1336.
musunuri-nayaks.r: Kapaya ruled Telangana from Warangal as the leader of a confederacy of Nayaka chiefs rather than as an absolute king. The Vilasa [[e:copper|copper]]-plate grant of [[e:prolaya-nayaka|Prolaya Nayaka]] describes the suffering under [[e:delhi|Delhi]] rule and the restoration of temples and [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] land grants. Kapaya also supported the revolt that created the [[s:bahmani-sultanate|Bahmani Sultanate]], hoping to weaken Delhi.
musunuri-nayaks.e: The alliance with the Bahmanis soon turned to rivalry. Bahmani armies forced Kapaya to cede Golconda, and around 1368 he was killed in battle against the [[s:recherla-nayakas|Recherla Nayakas]], who with Bahmani backing took over Telangana. Warangal later passed to the [[s:bahmani-sultanate|Bahmani Sultanate]].

melid.t: Melid, a Neo-Hittite kingdom at Malatya on the upper Euphrates, ruled by heirs of the Hittite royal house until Assyria annexed it.
melid.o: Melid, at Arslantepe near [[e:malatya|Malatya]], had been an important town since the 4th millennium BCE. After the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] fell c. 1180 BCE, a dynasty descended from Kuzi-Teshub of the [[s:kingdom-of-carchemish|Kingdom of Carchemish]] ruled the region, also called Kammanu, as an independent kingdom.
melid.r: Its kings wrote Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions and adorned the gate of their citadel with reliefs of lions and of the king pouring offerings to the storm god, now in Ankara. Melid lived from the farmland of the [[e:malatya|Malatya]] plain and the river crossing, paying tribute to the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] or the [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Kingdom of Urartu]].
melid.e: [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] deposed King Tarhunazi in 712 BCE, made Melid an Assyrian province and gave part of it to [[s:kummuh|Kummuh]]. The Neo-Hittite citadel at Arslantepe was later abandoned.

malla-republic.t: A clan republic of the Ganges plain in whose town of Kushinagar the Buddha died.
malla-republic.o: The Mallas were a warrior clan whose land lay east of [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kosala]], in modern eastern Uttar Pradesh. By the 6th century BCE they formed a gana-sangha, a republic of leading families, and were counted among the sixteen mahajanapadas. They were divided into two branches, centred on Kushinagar and Pava.
malla-republic.r: Affairs were decided by assemblies of clan heads meeting in a hall called the santhagara. Buddhist texts describe how the Mallas of Kushinagar received the dying Buddha, cremated him and shared his relics, while Jain tradition places Mahavira's death at Pava. Mallas were famed as wrestlers and soldiers, and Bandhula, a Malla, served as general to Prasenajit of the [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kingdom of Kosala]].
malla-republic.e: Weakened by internal division and pressed by stronger neighbours, the Mallas were absorbed by the [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Kingdom of Magadha]] in the 5th or 4th century BCE. Kushinagar became one of the four main places of Buddhist pilgrimage.

mac-dynasty.t: A Vietnamese dynasty founded by the general Mac Dang Dung, who usurped the Le throne in 1527 and fought a long civil war against Le loyalists.
mac-dynasty.o: [[e:mac-dang-dung|Mac Dang Dung]], a fisherman's son who rose to command the Le court guard, took advantage of the weak late [[s:later-le-dynasty|Later Le dynasty]] and in 1527 forced the emperor to abdicate, founding his own dynasty at [[e:thang-long|Thang Long]]. In 1540 he avoided a threatened Ming invasion by ceding border districts and accepting the lower rank of commissioner.
mac-dynasty.r: The Mac kept Le institutions, holding examinations regularly and promoting trade and crafts in the [[e:red-river-asia|Red River]] delta. Their opponents, led by [[e:nguyen-kim|Nguyen Kim]] and then [[e:trinh-kiem|Trinh Kiem]], restored a Le emperor in 1533 in [[e:thanh-hoa|Thanh Hoa]], beginning the war between the Northern Mac and Southern Le courts.
mac-dynasty.e: The war lasted until 1592, when [[e:trinh-tung|Trinh Tung]] captured [[e:thang-long|Thang Long]] and executed the Mac emperor [[e:mac-mau-hop|Mac Mau Hop]]. Mac survivors, with Ming protection, kept a rump state in [[e:cao-bang|Cao Bang]] until 1677, known as the [[s:mac-rule-in-cao-bang|Mac rule in Cao Bang]].

mycenaean-kingdom-of-iolkos.t: Mycenaean palace centre on the Gulf of Pagasae in Thessaly, the legendary home of Jason and the Argonauts.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-iolkos.o: Iolkos lies at modern Volos, on the Pagasetic Gulf, the best harbour of Thessaly. Settlement there goes back to the [[e:early-bronze-age|Early Bronze Age]], and by c. 1600 BCE a Mycenaean elite had appeared. Excavations at Kastro and especially Dimini, where a 14th to 13th century BCE palatial complex was uncovered, suggest a palace centre in the area.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-iolkos.r: Little is known of its government. The Dimini complex had large buildings with storerooms and workshops, and its finds show contact with the southern palace centres. Tholos tombs at Kapakli and Dimini show a wealthy elite. Greek myth made Iolkos the city of Pelias and the starting point of Jason's voyage on the Argo.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-iolkos.e: The Dimini complex was abandoned c. 1200 BCE, during the general collapse of palace societies, though Iolkos itself stayed inhabited. In 293 BCE [[e:demetrius-i-of-macedon|Demetrius Poliorcetes]] moved its population into his new city of Demetrias nearby.

maeatae.t: Confederation just north of the Antonine Wall whose raids drew Septimius Severus to Scotland, and whose name survives in Dumyat near Stirling.
maeatae.o: The Maeatae are first named by [[e:cassius-dio|Cassius Dio]], who describes them as living close to the wall that divided the island, with the [[s:caledonii|Caledonians]] beyond them. They seem to have been a grouping of peoples in the Forth valley and Stirling area that emerged in the later 2nd century, perhaps including the earlier [[s:venicones|Venicones]].
maeatae.r: Dio portrays them, like the [[s:caledonii|Caledonians]], as living in tents, holding wives in common and fighting from [[e:chariot|chariots]], a stereotype of barbarians rather than a reliable description. Around 197 the governor Virius Lupus had to buy peace from them with large sums of money. The hill names Dumyat and Myot Hill near Stirling are thought to preserve their name.
maeatae.e: Renewed raids brought [[e:septimius-severus|Septimius Severus]] to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], and from 208 to 211 he campaigned against the Maeatae and [[s:caledonii|Caledonii]]. The Maeatae revolted again in 210. After Severus died at York, [[e:rome|Rome]] withdrew, and by about 300 the northern peoples were known as Picts, later forming the [[s:kingdom-of-the-picts|Kingdom of the Picts]].

musasir.t: A small mountain city-state, sacred centre of the Urartian god Haldi, whose temple was plundered by Sargon II of Assyria in 714 BCE.
musasir.o: Musasir, called Ardini by the Urartians, lay in the mountains between [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] and [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Urartu]], probably near modern Mudjesir in the [[e:kurdistan|Kurdistan]] Region of [[e:iraq|Iraq]]. It appears in Assyrian texts by the 9th century BCE and was ruled by its own kings while being bound to the Kingdom of Urartu by religion.
musasir.r: The city's great temple of Haldi, the chief god of [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Urartu]], made it a pilgrimage and coronation site for Urartian kings, who dedicated weapons, shields and statues there. Its rulers balanced between [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] and Urartu; the best known, Urzana, wrote to [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II]] while honouring Urartian rites. The kingdom was small, its wealth coming mostly from the temple treasury.
musasir.e: In 714 BCE, on his eighth campaign, [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II]] marched on Musasir, Urzana fled, and the [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyrians]] carried off a vast treasure listed in his account; a relief at [[e:khorsabad|Khorsabad]] depicts the temple. The city later recovered as a cult centre but lost its independence.

matsya.t: A small early kingdom in eastern Rajasthan, remembered in the Mahabharata as the land where the Pandavas spent their year in hiding.
matsya.o: The Matsyas appear in the Rigveda and later Vedic texts as a people west of the Yamuna and south of the Kurus. By the 6th century BCE they formed one of the sixteen mahajanapadas in Buddhist lists, with their capital at Viratanagara, modern Bairat near Jaipur.
matsya.r: Little is known about its government or society. In the Mahabharata King Virata of Matsya shelters the Pandava brothers in disguise during their thirteenth year of exile, and tradition derived the capital's name from him. The country lay between the Aravalli hills and the Yamuna and seems to have been politically weak, at times dominated by its neighbours.
matsya.e: Matsya was absorbed by [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] in the 4th century BCE. Under the [[e:maurya-empire|Mauryas]] Bairat had a Buddhist monastery, and [[e:ashoka|Ashoka's]] Bhabru edict, addressed to the Buddhist community, was found nearby. The area later passed through many hands before becoming part of Rajasthan.

muflihi-sheikhdom.t: A small tribal sheikhdom of the Aden hinterland, among the last to join the Federation of South Arabia.
muflihi-sheikhdom.o: The Muflihi sheikhdom, with its seat at Al Jurba, lay in the highlands near the Yafa sultanates north-east of Aden. It emerged as a distinct tribal polity around 1800. Its history before British contact is almost unrecorded.
muflihi-sheikhdom.r: The sheikhs ruled a small farming and herding population by tribal custom. The territory became part of the [[s:aden-protectorate|Aden Protectorate]] through treaties with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and joined the [[s:federation-of-south-arabia|Federation of South Arabia]] in the mid-1960s.
muflihi-sheikhdom.e: After the National Liberation Front took power in 1967, the sheikhdom was abolished and incorporated into [[s:south-yemen|South Yemen]].

mandatory-palestine.t: The British-ruled mandate territory of Palestine, where the conflict between Jewish and Arab national movements took shape.
mandatory-palestine.o: After the [[s:occupied-enemy-territory-administration|Occupied Enemy Territory Administration]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] set up a civil government under [[e:herbert-samuel|Herbert Samuel]] in July 1920. The [[e:league-of-nations-mandate|League of Nations mandate]], approved in 1922, incorporated the 1917 Balfour Declaration's promise of a Jewish national home, while [[s:emirate-of-transjordan|Transjordan]] was administered separately.
mandatory-palestine.r: A high commissioner ruled without an elected legislature. Jewish immigration, land purchase and institutions such as the Jewish Agency and the Histadrut built the Yishuv, while Arab leaders opposed the national home. Violence erupted in 1920, 1921 and 1929, and the Arab revolt of 1936-1939 led the Peel Commission to propose partition. The 1939 White Paper limited Jewish immigration, and after 1944 Jewish groups fought the British.
mandatory-palestine.e: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] referred the question to the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]], which approved partition in November 1947. The mandate ended on 14-15 May 1948, when the State of [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]] was declared and war with Arab states followed.

maghrawa-emirate-of-fez.t: A Zenata Berber emirate that ruled Fez and northern Morocco as allies of Córdoba, between the Idrisids and the Almoravids.
maghrawa-emirate-of-fez.o: The Maghrawa, a [[e:zanata-berbers|Zenata Berber]] tribe, became allies of the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]] in its struggle with the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]]. Around 987 their chief [[e:ziri-ibn-atiyya|Ziri ibn Atiyya]] took control of [[e:fez|Fez]] as [[e:cordoba|Córdoba's]] governor, while another branch of the tribe had seized [[e:sijilmasa|Sijilmasa]] from the [[s:midrarid-emirate|Midrarid emirate]] in 976.
maghrawa-emirate-of-fez.r: [[e:ziri-ibn-atiyya|Ziri ibn Atiyya]] founded the city of Oujda in 994. He rebelled against the Córdoban regent al-Mansur, was defeated in 998, and his son al-Mu'izz was restored as a [[e:vassal|vassal]]. The [[e:emir|emirs]] ruled through tribal alliances and the urban notables of [[e:fez|Fez]], which grew as a centre of trade and learning. After [[e:cordoba|Córdoba's]] collapse in 1031 they ruled independently, though weakened by wars with the [[s:banu-ifran-emirate|Banu Ifran emirate]].
maghrawa-emirate-of-fez.e: In the 1060s the [[s:almoravid-empire|Almoravid Empire]] advanced from the south. [[e:yusuf-ibn-tashfin|Yusuf ibn Tashfin]] took [[e:fez|Fez]] around 1069 to 1070, ending Maghrawa rule in [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]]. Fez went on to become a leading city of the Almoravid and later Moroccan states.

methymna.t: Second city of Lesbos, rival of Mytilene, birthplace of the legendary singer Arion and a loyal ally of Athens.
methymna.o: Methymna was founded by Aeolian settlers on the north coast of Lesbos c. 1000 BCE, on a headland facing the Troad. It grew into the second city of the island and a long-standing rival of [[s:mytilene|Mytilene]] for control of Lesbos.
methymna.r: Methymna was governed mostly by aristocracies and oligarchies. [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] tells how the singer Arion of Methymna was saved by a dolphin. In 428 BCE it refused to join Mytilene's revolt and remained an autonomous ship-providing ally in the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]], later joining the [[s:second-athenian-league|Second Athenian League]]. The city was famed for its wine.
methymna.e: Methymna came under Hellenistic kings and in the 2nd century BCE became an ally of [[e:rome|Rome]]. It was included in the Roman province of [[e:asia|Asia]] from 129 BCE. The town survives as modern Mithymna, also called Molyvos.

mangrol-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled port state on the coast of Saurashtra whose wavering accession in 1947 became part of the Junagadh crisis.
mangrol-state.o: Mangrol, an old port on the south-west coast of Kathiawar, came under a line of Muslim Sheikhs in the mid-18th century as Mughal authority collapsed. The rulers were long tributary to the Nawabs of [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh State]], who claimed suzerainty over them.
mangrol-state.r: The Sheikh governed the port and nearby villages, with fishing and coastal trade as the main occupations. Under the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]] Mangrol was a minor state with a mixed [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Muslim population.
mangrol-state.e: In 1947 the Sheikh of Mangrol acceded to [[e:india|India]], then withdrew his accession under pressure from [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]], which had joined [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]]. India used the dispute as one ground for taking control of the area, and Mangrol was merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948.

moab.t: Moab, a kingdom east of the Dead Sea whose king Mesha recorded his revolt against Israel on the famous Mesha Stele.
moab.o: Moab took shape in the [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] on the plateau east of the [[e:dead-sea|Dead Sea]], between the Arnon and Zered gorges. Egyptian texts mention the land in the 13th century BCE, and by the 9th century BCE it was a kingdom with its capital at Dibon.
moab.r: Moabite kings ruled a land of wheat fields and sheep pastures under the protection of the god Chemosh. The Mesha Stele, found at Dhiban in 1868, tells how Mesha freed Moab from the [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Kingdom of Israel]] after Ahab's dynasty had held it, building towns and [[e:reservoir|reservoirs]]. Its language was close to [[e:hebrew|Hebrew]].
moab.e: Moab became a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] in the 8th century BCE and later of the [[s:chaldean-empire|Chaldean Empire]]. A Babylonian campaign in 582 BCE ended its independence, and Arab tribes and later the [[s:nabataean-kingdom|Nabataean Kingdom]] took over the region.

marquisate-of-finale.t: A small Ligurian marquisate of the Del Carretto family whose port became Spain's private gateway to the Duchy of Milan.
marquisate-of-finale.o: In 1162 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] confirmed the rights of Enrico il Guercio, a member of the Aleramici family, over lands in western Liguria, including Finale. His descendants, the [[e:del-carretto|Del Carretto]], made Finalborgo their seat.
marquisate-of-finale.r: The marquises ruled a small coastal and hill territory from the walled town of Finalborgo and the castle of Govone. They were repeatedly at war with the [[s:republic-of-genoa|Republic of Genoa]], which wanted to control the whole Ligurian coast; [[e:genoa|Genoa]] occupied Finale during a war in the mid-15th century and again in the 16th century. The [[e:del-carretto|Del Carretto]] relied on imperial and Spanish protection, as Finale offered a landing place outside Genoese control.
marquisate-of-finale.e: The last marquis sold his rights to [[e:spain|Spain]], which took possession in 1602, and Finale served [[s:habsburg-spain|Habsburg Spain]] as a port for troops bound for [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]]. In 1713 [[e:charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Charles VI]] sold it to [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]].

margraviate-of-brandenburg-kustrin.t: A short-lived Hohenzollern margraviate in the Neumark, whose margrave John fortified Küstrin and ran a notably thrifty Lutheran government.
margraviate-of-brandenburg-kustrin.o: Elector Joachim I of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]], against Hohenzollern house law, divided his lands in his will. On his death in 1535 his elder son [[e:joachim-ii-hector|Joachim II]] became elector of the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Margraviate of Brandenburg]], while the younger, John, received the Neumark east of the Oder, with Crossen and other districts, ruling from Küstrin.
margraviate-of-brandenburg-kustrin.r: Margrave John, known as Hans of Küstrin, introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1538, ahead of his brother. He turned Küstrin into a powerful fortress where the Warta meets the Oder, reorganised finances and ran a frugal, efficient government that filled his treasury. In the Schmalkaldic War he eventually sided with [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]].
margraviate-of-brandenburg-kustrin.e: John died in 1571, ten days after his brother, without male heirs, and the Neumark reverted to [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] under [[e:john-george-elector-of-brandenburg|Elector John George]]. Küstrin remained a major fortress, where the young [[e:frederick-the-great|Frederick the Great]] was imprisoned in 1730.

march-of-tuscany.t: The great march of Tuscany, ruled from Lucca and later by the house of Canossa, whose Countess Matilda backed the papacy against the emperor.
march-of-tuscany.o: The [[e:carolingian-empire|Carolingians]] governed [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]] through counts at [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]]. In 846 Adalbert I, of the Bonifacian family, succeeded his father and gathered the counties of Tuscany into a march, with the duty of defending the coast against Arab raids. His son [[e:adalbert-ii-of-tuscany|Adalbert II]], called the Rich, made the margraves among the most powerful lords in [[e:italy|Italy]].
march-of-tuscany.r: The margraves ruled a vast territory from [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]], with influence in [[e:rome|Rome]] and over the Italian crown. [[e:hugh-of-tuscany|Hugh the Great]], who died in 1001, endowed the Badia of [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]] founded by his mother Willa. From 1027 the house of Canossa held the march; [[e:matilda-of-tuscany|Countess Matilda]] (ruled 1076–1115) hosted the meeting at Canossa in 1077 where [[e:henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Henry IV]] sought [[e:pope-gregory-vii|Pope Gregory VII's]] forgiveness, and fought for the [[e:papacy|papacy]] for decades.
march-of-tuscany.e: After Matilda died in 1115, her will, leaving her lands to the Church, set pope against emperor. Imperial [[e:legatus|legates]] governed the march while the cities of [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]], Pisa, [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]] and [[s:republic-of-siena|Siena]] grew into self-governing communes. After Emperor Henry VI died in 1197 the Tuscan cities formed the League of San Genesio, ending the march.

manchukuo.t: The puppet state that Japan created in north-east China in 1932, with the last Qing emperor Puyi as its figurehead ruler.
manchukuo.o: In September 1931 officers of the [[e:kwantung-army|Kwantung Army]], based in the [[s:kwantung-leased-territory|Kwantung Leased Territory]], staged an explosion on the South [[e:manchuria|Manchuria]] Railway near Mukden and used it as a pretext to occupy all of Manchuria. In March 1932 they proclaimed the state of Manchukuo, with [[e:puyi|Puyi]] as chief executive and Hsinking (Changchun) as capital; he was enthroned as emperor in 1934.
manchukuo.r: Chinese ministers such as [[s:zheng-wang-shichong|Zheng]] Xiaoxu and Zhang Jinghui held office, but Japanese vice-ministers and the [[e:kwantung-army|Kwantung Army]] held real power. The [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] refused recognition, and [[e:japan|Japan]] left the League in 1933. Manchukuo became a laboratory for state-planned heavy industry, mining and railways, and received Japanese and Korean settlers. Resistance was suppressed brutally, and Unit 731 conducted lethal human experiments near Harbin.
manchukuo.e: The [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] invaded in August 1945, and the state collapsed within days; [[e:puyi|Puyi]] was captured. [[e:manchuria|Manchuria]] passed back to [[e:china|China]], and its industries became a prize in the civil war.
manchukuo.re: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism, State Shinto

miletus.t: The greatest Ionian city, mother of some ninety colonies around the Black Sea and birthplace of Greek natural philosophy with Thales and Anaximander.
miletus.o: After the [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] town of [[s:millawanda|Millawanda]] was destroyed, [[e:ionia|Ionian Greeks]] settled Miletus near the mouth of the Maeander c. 1000 BCE; tradition named Neleus, son of [[e:codrus|Codrus of Athens]], as founder. By the 7th century BCE it was a wealthy trading city and a leading member of the [[s:ionian-league|Ionian League]].
miletus.r: Miletus founded colonies such as [[s:sinope|Sinope]], [[s:cyzicus|Cyzicus]], [[s:histria|Histria]] and [[s:apollonia-pontica|Apollonia Pontica]], and traded at Naucratis in [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes worked there in the 6th century BCE. Tyrants such as Thrasybulus alternated with oligarchic factions. Miletus came under the [[s:kingdom-of-lydia|Kingdom of Lydia]] and then the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]], and its tyrants Histiaeus and [[e:aristagoras-of-miletus|Aristagoras]] launched the [[e:ionian-revolt|Ionian Revolt]] in 499 BCE.
miletus.e: [[e:persia|Persia]] sacked the city in 494 BCE after the [[e:battle-of-lade|Battle of Lade]]. Rebuilt on a grid plan associated with Hippodamus, it joined the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]] and was taken by Alexander in 334 BCE. After Hellenistic rule it passed to [[e:rome|Rome]] in 133 BCE as part of the province of [[e:asia|Asia]].
miletus.re: Greek religion; oracle of Apollo at Didyma

mamluk-iraq.t: The rule of Georgian mamluk pashas over Baghdad and Basra, who governed Iraq almost independently of the Ottoman sultan for over a century.
mamluk-iraq.o: In 1704 the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] appointed [[e:hasan-pasha-of-baghdad|Hasan Pasha]] governor of [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]]. He and his son [[e:ahmad-pasha-of-baghdad|Ahmad Pasha]] built a household of slave soldiers, mostly from [[s:georgia|Georgia]], trained for war and administration. In 1749 one of these mamluks, Sulayman Abu Layla, became pasha, and mamluk officers then ruled Baghdad, [[e:basra|Basra]] and Shahrizor in succession.
mamluk-iraq.r: The pashas paid tribute and recognised the sultan but chose their successors from their own households. They fought Persian invasions, Arab tribes such as the [[s:muntafiq-confederation|Muntafiq confederation]], Kurdish [[e:emir|emirs]] and Wahhabi raiders. [[e:buyuk-suleyman-pasha|Büyük Süleyman Pasha]] (1780 to 1802) restored order, and [[e:dawud-pasha|Dawud Pasha]] (1817 to 1831) introduced reforms, factories and a modern-style army, and dealt with the British [[e:east-india-company|East India Company's]] residents.
mamluk-iraq.e: In 1831 plague and floods devastated [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]], and the Ottoman envoy Ali Rıza Pasha deposed [[e:dawud-pasha|Dawud Pasha]], restoring direct Ottoman rule over [[e:iraq|Iraq]].

miraj-senior.t: The senior of two Patwardhan Brahmin states at Miraj in the southern Maratha country, a town famed for Hindustani music and instrument makers.
miraj-senior.o: Miraj had been the seat of the Patwardhan family, [[e:chitpavan-brahmins|Chitpavan Brahmin]] generals of the [[e:peshwa|Peshwas]]. After the family's lands were divided in 1811, the Miraj share was split again in 1820 into a Senior branch at Miraj and a Junior branch at Budhgaon.
miraj-senior.r: Miraj Senior was a small state of the [[e:southern-maratha-country|Southern Maratha Country]], later the [[e:deccan-states-agency|Deccan States Agency]]. Its town became a centre of Hindustani classical music, where Abdul [[e:karim-khan-zand|Karim Khan]] of the Kirana gharana settled, and was famed for its sitar and tanpura makers.
miraj-senior.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Miraj Senior was merged into [[e:bombay-state|Bombay State]] in 1948 and has been part of Maharashtra since 1960; it lies in [[s:sangli-state|Sangli]] district.

mac-william-iochtar.t: The Gaelicised Burke lordship of Mayo, ruled by the Lower Mac William, whose title survived until the late Tudor conquest of Connacht.
mac-william-iochtar.o: After the murder of the last [[e:william-donn-de-burgh-3rd-earl-of-ulster|Earl of Ulster]] in 1333, [[e:edmund-albanach-de-burgh|Edmund Albanach de Burgh]] took control of the de Burgh lands in north [[s:kingdom-of-connacht|Connacht]] and adopted the Gaelic title Mac William Iochtar, the Lower Mac William. His descendants ruled much of modern Mayo.
mac-william-iochtar.r: The Mayo Burkes lived as Gaelic lords, electing their chief by tanistry, employing gallowglasses and poets, and allying with or fighting the O'Donnells, O'Malleys and the [[s:clanricarde|Clanricarde]] Burkes. Richard an Iarainn Burke, 'Iron Dick', married [[e:grace-omalley|Grace O'Malley]].
mac-william-iochtar.e: Under the Composition of [[s:kingdom-of-connacht|Connacht]] in 1585 the title was abolished, and Mayo was shired. After Burke rebellions, Theobald Burke, 'Tibbot na Long', son of [[e:grace-omalley|Grace O'Malley]], sided with the crown and was made Viscount Mayo in 1627.

menteshe.t: A Turkish beylik on the Carian coast of south-western Anatolia, known for its naval raids into the Aegean.
menteshe.o: In the 1260s and 1270s [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] raiders led by [[e:menteshe-bey|Menteshe Bey]] occupied the Byzantine coastlands of [[s:hecatomnid-caria|Caria]] around Milas, Pecin and [[s:miletus|Miletus]] (Balat), founding one of the first maritime [[e:beylik|beyliks]].
menteshe.r: The Menteshe rulers raided the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] islands, clashing with the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Knights Hospitaller]] of [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] and [[e:venice|Venice]], but also traded with Italian merchants in Balat. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] visited Milas in the 1330s and praised its ruler [[e:orhan-bey-of-menteshe|Orhan Bey]]. [[e:ilyas-bey-of-menteshe|Ilyas Bey]] built the mosque of Balat in 1404 next to the ruins of [[s:miletus|Miletus]]. Treaties with Venice and [[e:crete|Crete]] regulated trade in grain, horses and slaves, and Turkish sailors from Menteshe ports joined the [[s:aydinids|Aydinids]] in raids on the islands.
menteshe.e: [[e:bayezid-i|Bayezid I]] annexed the [[e:beylik|beylik]] in 1390. [[e:timur|Timur]] restored it after defeating Bayezid in 1402, but the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] took it back for good in 1424.

mongolia.t: The democratic Mongolian state created by the 1992 constitution after the peaceful end of communist rule.
mongolia.o: Peaceful demonstrations in Ulaanbaatar in the winter of 1989 to 1990 forced the ruling party of the [[s:mongolian-peoples-republic|Mongolian People's Republic]] to give up its monopoly of power. Multi-party elections followed in 1990, and a new constitution adopted in 1992 renamed the country simply Mongolia, with a parliament, the State Great Khural, and a directly elected president.
mongolia.r: The loss of Soviet aid caused severe hardship in the early 1990s as Mongolia moved to a market economy and privatised its herds. Mining, especially [[e:copper|copper]] at Oyu Tolgoi and [[e:coal|coal]], later drove rapid growth and made the economy dependent on [[e:china|China]]. [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] revived, [[e:genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]] became a national symbol, and a 'third neighbour' foreign policy sought partners beyond [[e:russia|Russia]] and China.
mongolia.e: Power has changed hands repeatedly through elections, though politics has been marked by corruption scandals and protests, notably in 2008. Mongolia remains a parliamentary democracy with its capital at Ulaanbaatar, where nearly half the population now lives.

magan.t: The copper land of south-eastern Arabia, known to Mesopotamian kings as the source of metal and hard stone shipped up the Gulf.
magan.o: Magan appears in [[e:cuneiform|cuneiform]] texts from the 23rd century BCE, when [[e:sargon-of-akkad|Sargon of Akkad]] recorded that ships from Magan, [[e:meluhha|Meluhha]] and [[s:dilmun|Dilmun]] moored at his capital. The name covered the [[e:copper|copper]]-bearing Hajar Mountains of modern [[e:oman|Oman]] and the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]], home of the Umm an-Nar culture with its round stone tombs and towers such as those at Hili and Bat.
magan.r: Little is known of its politics. [[e:naram-sin|Naram-Sin]] of the [[s:akkadian-empire|Akkadian Empire]] claimed to have defeated Manium, lord of Magan, and brought back diorite for statues. Magan exported [[e:copper|copper]], diorite and [[e:timber|timber]] in Magan-boats, and later [[e:third-dynasty-of-ur|Ur III]] texts record merchants trading wool, textiles and oil for its copper. Whether it was ever a single kingdom or a federation of oasis communities is unclear.
magan.e: References fade after the early 2nd millennium BCE as [[s:dilmun|Dilmun]] took over the [[e:copper|copper]] trade. The name revived in Assyrian records and as Maka, a land listed among the subjects of the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] in the 6th century BCE. Its copper mines and tombs remain the main witnesses to the [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] of [[e:oman|Oman]].

marajoara.t: Mound-building chiefdoms on Marajó Island at the mouth of the Amazon, whose elaborate painted funerary urns show that complex societies flourished in Amazonia.
marajoara.o: From around 400 CE people on the eastern part of Marajó Island, in the [[e:amazon|Amazon]] delta of [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]], began raising large earthen mounds called tesos above the seasonally flooded savannas. The Marajoara phase grew from earlier local pottery traditions and lasted roughly a thousand years.
marajoara.r: The largest mounds, such as Camutins and Pacoval, held houses, cemeteries and ceremonial spaces, and some supported thousands of people. Society was probably organised in ranked chiefdoms. The economy relied on fish managed in ponds and channels, palm fruits and root crops rather than intensive [[e:maize|maize]] farming. Marajoara potters made polychrome burial urns, figurines and ceramic tangas, small triangular pubic covers, decorated with incised and painted designs, many with female imagery.
marajoara.e: Mound building ceased around 1400, before European arrival, possibly because of social change or new groups entering the island. Marajoara urns are prized museum pieces and inspired modern Brazilian decorative styles. The culture is central to debates over how many people lived in pre-Columbian Amazonia.

mahameghavahana-dynasty.t: The Kalinga dynasty of the warrior king Kharavela, whose Hathigumpha inscription is one of ancient India's great royal records.
mahameghavahana-dynasty.o: After the decline of the [[s:maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]], [[s:kingdom-of-kalinga|Kalinga]] on the Odisha coast regained its independence under kings who claimed descent from the ancient [[s:chedi|Chedi]] line. The dynasty is known almost entirely from the Hathigumpha inscription carved in a cave on Udayagiri hill near Bhubaneswar, probably in the 1st century BCE.
mahameghavahana-dynasty.r: The inscription records year by year the deeds of Kharavela, a devout Jain: he repaired the capital Kalinganagari after a cyclone, dug canals, staged festivals and led campaigns against the [[s:satavahana-dynasty|Satavahana dynasty]] to the west, against [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]], from which he recovered a Jain image carried off by a Nanda king, and against the [[s:later-pandyan-empire|Pandyas]] in the far south. He and his queen excavated rock-cut monastic cells for Jain monks at Udayagiri and Khandagiri.
mahameghavahana-dynasty.e: Kharavela's successors, Kudepasiri and Vadukha, are known only from short inscriptions, and the dynasty fades from the record by the 1st century. Its rock-cut caves remain an important Jain site.
