mawsynram-state.t: A small Khasi state on the southern edge of the Meghalaya plateau, around the village now often called the wettest inhabited place on Earth.
mawsynram-state.o: Hima Mawsynram was one of the Khasi chiefdoms of the plateau; its origins are known from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
mawsynram-state.r: Like other Khasi states it was headed by a Syiem from a royal clan, chosen with clan elders, with succession through the female line. Little written record of its history exists.
mawsynram-state.e: Mawsynram came under British supervision in the 19th century and acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1948, joining Assam. It is now part of East Khasi Hills district, Meghalaya.

marquisate-of-saluzzo.t: An Alpine marquisate in south-western Piedmont that balanced between Savoy, France and the Dauphiné for four centuries.
marquisate-of-saluzzo.o: The marquisate was formed in 1142 when the lands of Boniface del Vasto were divided among his sons, and Manfred I received Saluzzo and the upper valleys of the Po, Varaita and Maira.
marquisate-of-saluzzo.r: The marquises ruled from their castle at Saluzzo over a small state of mountain valleys and plain. Squeezed between the [[s:county-of-savoy|County of Savoy]] and the [[s:dauphine-of-viennois|Dauphiné]], they often sought French protection. Marquis Thomas III wrote the allegorical romance Le Chevalier errant around 1400. Ludovico II opened the Buco di Viso tunnel under the [[e:alps|Alps]] around 1480 to trade salt and goods with [[s:county-of-provence|Provence]], and the town flourished as a small [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] court.
marquisate-of-saluzzo.e: After quarrels in the ruling family, King [[e:henry-ii-of-france|Henry II of France]] annexed the marquisate in 1548. It was occupied by Charles Emmanuel I of the [[s:duchy-of-savoy|Duchy of Savoy]] in 1588 and formally ceded to [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] by the Treaty of Lyon in 1601.

mombasa.t: A Swahili island city-state on the Kenyan coast that resisted the Portuguese for nearly a century before they made it their East African stronghold.
mombasa.o: Mombasa grew from about the 12th century as a Muslim trading town on an island with a deep natural harbour. Arab geographers mention it, and [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]], who visited in 1331, described its wooden mosques and pious, peaceable inhabitants. Its people called the town Mvita, and it competed with [[s:malindi|Malindi]] and [[s:kilwa-sultanate|Kilwa]] for the coastal trade.
mombasa.r: The city was ruled by a sultan or shaykh supported by its merchant clans, who traded [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], gold, slaves and grain with [[e:arabia|Arabia]], [[e:persia|Persia]] and [[e:india|India]]. In the 15th century it became the strongest town on the northern [[e:swahili|Swahili]] coast. When the Portuguese arrived it was their most stubborn enemy, sacked in 1505 by [[e:francisco-de-almeida|Francisco de Almeida]], in 1528 and again in 1589.
mombasa.e: In 1593 the Portuguese took the island, built [[e:fort-jesus|Fort Jesus]] and installed the ruler of [[s:malindi|Malindi]] as sultan, beginning [[s:portuguese-mombasa|Portuguese Mombasa]]. Later fought over by [[e:oman|Oman]] and the [[s:mazrui-sultanate|Mazrui Sultanate]], Mombasa remains Kenya's main port.

mataka-chiefdom.t: The most powerful Yao chiefdom, which grew rich on the ivory and slave trade between Lake Malawi and the Indian Ocean coast.
mataka-chiefdom.o: The Yao chief Mataka I Nyambi built up a following on the highlands east of [[e:lake-malawi|Lake Malawi]] in the early 19th century, gathering dependants and captives around his town of Mwembe in what is now Niassa province of [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]]. [[e:david-livingstone|David Livingstone]] visited Mwembe in 1866 and described a large, prosperous settlement.
mataka-chiefdom.r: The chiefdom lived from long-distance trade: caravans carried [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and enslaved people to [[s:kilwa-sultanate|Kilwa]] and other [[e:swahili|Swahili]] ports and brought back cloth, [[e:bead|beads]] and guns. Successive chiefs took the title Mataka. Coastal contact brought [[e:islam|Islam]], which later Matakas adopted along with Swahili dress and literacy, making the Yao one of the most Muslim peoples of the interior.
mataka-chiefdom.e: Mataka's people resisted the Portuguese [[s:niassa-company|Niassa Company]] for two decades until its forces took Mwembe in 1912. Mataka's domain then became part of [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Portuguese Mozambique]]. Yao communities remain in northern [[e:mozambique|Mozambique]] and southern Malawi, still largely Muslim.

margraviate-of-hachberg.t: Breisgau branch of the margraves of Baden, named after the Hachberg castle and later holding Rötteln, Sausenberg and Neuchâtel before reuniting with Baden in 1503.
margraviate-of-hachberg.o: Around 1190 the lands of Margrave Hermann IV of Baden were divided, and his son Henry received the castle of Hachberg, the Hochburg near Emmendingen, with lands in the Breisgau. Henry and his heirs styled themselves margraves of Hachberg, founding a separate branch of the house of Zähringen-Baden.
margraviate-of-hachberg.r: The margraves held scattered lordships in the Breisgau and Markgräflerland. In 1306 the house split into Hachberg proper and Hachberg-Sausenberg, which gained Rötteln in 1315 and, through marriage, the [[s:principality-of-neuchatel|County of Neuchâtel]] in the 15th century. Hachberg proper was sold back to Baden in 1415. [[e:philip-of-hachberg-sausenberg|Philip of Hachberg-Sausenberg]] served the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] and the French crown.
margraviate-of-hachberg.e: Philip died in 1503 without a son, and under an inheritance treaty his lands returned to the margraves of Baden, while Neuchâtel passed through his daughter to the Orléans-Longueville family. The Markgräflerland name recalls their rule.

malerkotla-state.t: An Afghan-ruled Muslim state in the Punjab whose Nawab protested the execution of Guru Gobind Singh's young sons, an act Sikhs remembered for centuries.
malerkotla-state.o: Tradition holds that the [[e:sufism|Sufi]] Shaikh Sadruddin [[e:sadr|Sadr]]-i-Jahan, of Sherwani Afghan descent, settled in the area in 1454 and married a daughter of [[e:bahlul-lodi|Bahlul Lodi]], receiving land grants. His descendants became hereditary Nawabs of Malerkotla.
malerkotla-state.r: In 1705 Nawab Sher Muhammad Khan, then serving the Mughal governor of [[e:sirhind|Sirhind]], protested against the execution of the young sons of [[e:guru-gobind-singh|Guru Gobind Singh]]. [[e:sikhism|Sikhs]] later honoured this, and Malerkotla survived among Sikh states. The town was the scene of the killing of Kuka (Namdhari) rebels by blowing from guns in 1872.
malerkotla-state.e: Malerkotla was largely spared the violence of Partition in 1947. In 1948 it joined the [[s:patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union|Patiala and East Punjab States Union]], which merged into [[e:punjab|Punjab]] in 1956. Malerkotla became a district of Punjab in 2021.

matsumae-domain.t: The northernmost domain of Tokugawa Japan, which held a monopoly on trade with the Ainu and controlled southern Hokkaido.
matsumae-domain.o: The Kakizaki family had established themselves on the southern tip of Hokkaido in the 15th century. Kakizaki Yoshihiro, who took the name Matsumae, received a charter from [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] in 1604 granting his family the exclusive right to trade with the Ainu.
matsumae-domain.r: Matsumae grew no [[e:rice|rice]] and lived on trade. Retainers received trading posts instead of land, later contracted out to merchants who exploited Ainu labour in fisheries. Ainu resentment fuelled the revolt of Shakushain in 1669 and the Kunashir-Menashi uprising of 1789. Fearing Russian expansion, the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] took direct control of Ezo from 1799 to 1821 and again from 1855.
matsumae-domain.e: In 1868 forces of the [[s:republic-of-ezo|Republic of Ezo]] captured Fukuyama castle, completed in 1854 as the last traditional castle in [[e:japan|Japan]]. Restored in 1869 and renamed Tate, the domain was abolished in 1871 and absorbed into Hokkaido.

mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate.t: An autonomous Ottoman district of Mount Lebanon under a Christian governor and European guarantee, the core of the later Lebanese state.
mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate.o: After the 1860 civil war, the Ottoman government and five European powers agreed in 1861 a Reglement Organique that united [[e:mount-lebanon|Mount Lebanon]] as a single autonomous district. It was governed by a non-Lebanese Ottoman Catholic mutasarrif appointed with the powers' consent.
mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate.r: The first mutasarrif was [[e:garabet-artin-davoud-pasha|Daud Pasha]], an Armenian Catholic. An administrative council represented the religious communities in proportion, an early form of [[e:lebanon|Lebanon's]] confessional system. Feudal privileges were abolished and the mountain enjoyed decades of peace. [[e:silk|Silk]] production for French mills flourished, schools multiplied and emigration to the [[e:americas|Americas]] grew. The district lacked [[s:beirut|Beirut]] and the Beqaa, which remained in Ottoman provinces.
mount-lebanon-mutasarrifate.e: In 1915 Jamal Pasha ended the autonomy; wartime [[e:naval-blockade|blockade]] and famine killed a large part of the population. French troops arrived in 1918, and in 1920 the mountain became the heart of [[s:greater-lebanon|Greater Lebanon]].

mpondomise-kingdom.t: A southern Nguni kingdom of the eastern Cape whose last independent king, Mhlontlo, led a revolt against Cape rule in 1880.
mpondomise-kingdom.o: The Mpondomise share their earliest royal genealogy with the Mpondo, from whom they separated many generations before written records. By the 17th century they occupied the upper Mzimvubu and Tsitsa valleys, around modern Tsolo and Qumbu in the eastern Cape.
mpondomise-kingdom.r: Kings ruled through royal kin and councillors over chiefdoms of [[e:cattle|cattle]]-herding and cereal-farming homesteads. The Mpondomise were renowned as rainmakers and were respected by neighbouring peoples for their ritual standing. In the 19th century they were caught between the Mpondo, the Thembu and incoming Mfengu and Sotho groups, and the kingdom was often divided between rival branches.
mpondomise-kingdom.e: Mhlontlo accepted a Cape magistrate in 1873, but in 1880 his followers killed the magistrate Hamilton Hope and rose in revolt. The rising was crushed, Mhlontlo fled to [[s:basutoland|Basutoland]], and the Mpondomise lands were absorbed into the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]].

marinid-sultanate.t: The Zenata Berber dynasty that replaced the Almohads in Morocco and made Fez a great centre of learning, adorned with celebrated madrasas.
marinid-sultanate.o: The Banu Marin were Zenata nomads from the steppes of the eastern Moroccan frontier. As the [[s:almohad-caliphate|Almohad Caliphate]] weakened they raided [[e:morocco|Morocco's]] plains, took Meknes and then [[e:fez|Fez]] in 1248, and in 1269 [[e:abu-yusuf-yaqub-ibn-abd-al-haqq|Abu Yusuf Yaqub]] captured [[e:marrakesh|Marrakesh]], ending [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] rule. Their emergence as a regional power is often dated to the 1240s.
marinid-sultanate.r: The [[e:marinid-dynasty|Marinids]] governed from [[e:fez|Fez]], founding the royal city of Fes el-Jdid in 1276 and building [[e:madrasa|madrasas]] such as the Bou Inania and al-Attarine to train [[e:maliki-school|Maliki]] scholars. They intervened in [[e:iberia|Iberia]] to support the [[s:emirate-of-granada|Emirate of Granada]]. Abu al-Hasan conquered the [[s:zayyanid-kingdom-of-tlemcen|Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen]] and briefly [[e:tunis|Tunis]], but lost at the Rio Salado in 1340. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] wrote his travels for Abu Inan.
marinid-sultanate.e: After Abu Inan's death in 1358 real power passed to [[e:vizier|viziers]], notably the [[s:wattasid-sultanate|Wattasids]]. Portugal took [[e:ceuta|Ceuta]] in 1415. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Abd al-Haqq II was killed in a [[e:fez|Fez]] uprising in 1465, and the Wattasid Sultanate eventually succeeded.

megara-hyblaea.t: Greek colony on Sicily's east coast whose excavated remains are a key source for early Greek town planning, destroyed by Gelon of Syracuse in 483 BCE.
megara-hyblaea.o: Settlers from [[s:megara|Megara]] in [[e:greece|Greece]], after failed attempts elsewhere, were offered land by the Sicel king Hyblon and founded Megara Hyblaea around 728 BCE, on the coast north of [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]]. The name honoured both their mother city and their native host.
megara-hyblaea.r: Excavations by French archaeologists have shown that the town was laid out with regular streets and house plots soon after its foundation, among the earliest planned Greek settlements known. An [[e:agora|agora]] with temples and stoas developed in the 7th century BCE. Its territory was limited by [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] and [[s:leontini|Leontini]], so around 628 BCE it founded the more distant colony of [[s:selinous|Selinous]] in western [[e:sicily|Sicily]].
megara-hyblaea.e: [[e:gelon|Gelon of Syracuse]] captured Megara Hyblaea in 483 BCE, moved its wealthy citizens to [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] and sold the common people into [[e:slavery|slavery]]. A smaller town was refounded in the time of Timoleon in the 340s BCE and destroyed again by the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] in 214 BCE.

melikdoms-of-karabakh.t: Five Armenian principalities in the highlands of Karabakh whose meliks kept local self-rule under Persian overlords until the rise of the Karabakh Khanate.
melikdoms-of-karabakh.o: In the early 17th century the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]] recognised local Armenian lords, called meliks, in the mountains of Karabakh, many descended from the [[s:principality-of-khachen|Principality of Khachen]]. Five melikdoms, Gulistan, Jraberd, Khachen, Varanda and Dizak, became known as the Khamsa, the Five.
melikdoms-of-karabakh.r: Each melik ruled his district from fortresses with his own troops, collecting taxes for the Persian governor at [[s:ganja-khanate|Ganja]]. The meliks maintained churches and the Gandzasar catholicosate. In the 1720s, as Safavid power collapsed, [[e:avan-yuzbashi|Avan Yuzbashi]] led Armenian resistance to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in alliance with Davit [[e:bek|Bek]] of [[s:kingdom-of-syunik|Syunik]], and [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]] later granted the meliks wide autonomy.
melikdoms-of-karabakh.e: From the 1750s [[e:panah-ali-khan|Panah Ali Khan]], aided by Melik Shahnazar of Varanda, built Shusha and subordinated the meliks to the [[s:karabakh-khanate|Karabakh Khanate]]. Many meliks emigrated to [[s:georgia|Georgia]] and [[e:russia|Russia]], and the last melikdoms disappeared with the [[e:russian-empire|Russian Empire's]] annexation of Karabakh by 1822.

monarchy-of-the-north.t: A royalist counter-revolution that restored the monarchy in northern Portugal for less than a month in 1919.
monarchy-of-the-north.o: After the assassination of the dictator [[e:sidonio-pais|Sidónio Pais]] in December 1918, royalists saw an opportunity to overthrow the [[s:first-portuguese-republic|First Portuguese Republic]]. On 19 January 1919 [[e:henrique-paiva-couceiro|Henrique Paiva Couceiro]] proclaimed the monarchy in Porto in the name of the exiled [[e:manuel-ii-of-portugal|Manuel II]].
monarchy-of-the-north.r: A royal governing junta ruled Porto and much of the north, restored the blue-and-white monarchist flag and the Charter of 1826. [[e:manuel-ii-of-portugal|Manuel II]], in exile in [[e:england|England]], did not endorse the rising. A parallel royalist rising near [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]], at Monsanto, was quickly defeated.
monarchy-of-the-north.e: Republican forces, supported by armed civilians, advanced north, and a republican revolt in Porto on 13 February 1919 ended the royalist regime. Paiva Couceiro fled to [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria|Galicia]]. It was the last serious attempt to restore the Portuguese monarchy.

malayan-union.t: Short-lived British union of the Malay states, Penang and Malacca whose plan for equal citizenship provoked the birth of Malay nationalism.
malayan-union.o: Planned during the war, the Malayan Union was inaugurated on 1 April 1946. It joined the [[s:federated-malay-states|Federated Malay States]], the [[s:unfederated-malay-states|Unfederated Malay States]] and the former [[s:straits-settlements|Straits Settlements]] of [[s:prince-of-wales-island|Penang]] and [[e:malacca|Malacca]], leaving out [[s:singapore|Singapore]]. Sir Harold MacMichael had secured the sultans' signatures to new treaties transferring their [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] to the British crown.
malayan-union.r: The union was ruled by a British governor, Sir Edward Gent, from [[e:kuala-lumpur|Kuala Lumpur]]. It offered citizenship on equal terms to Chinese and Indian residents and reduced the sultans to religious figureheads. Malays protested in mass rallies, boycotted the inauguration and founded the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) under Onn Jaafar in May 1946.
malayan-union.e: Facing united Malay opposition, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] negotiated a new settlement with the rulers and UMNO. The union was replaced by the [[s:federation-of-malaya|Federation of Malaya]] on 1 February 1948, restoring the sultans and tightening citizenship rules.

mudhol-state.t: The Deccan state of the Ghorpade family, Maratha chiefs who served the Bijapur Sultanate, and the source of the Mudhol hound.
mudhol-state.o: The Ghorpades of Mudhol were [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] military chiefs who held Mudhol as a fief of the [[s:bijapur-sultanate|Bijapur Sultanate]]; family tradition places the grant in the 15th century. The register's start date follows that tradition.
mudhol-state.r: In the 17th century the Mudhol Ghorpades remained loyal to Bijapur and opposed [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]], who killed Baji Ghorpade of Mudhol in 1664. Later the family held its lands under the [[e:peshwa|Peshwas]] and, from 1818, under British protection in the [[e:southern-maratha-country|Southern Maratha Country]]. Its rulers promoted the lean Mudhol hound, a sight-hound now used by the [[e:indian-army|Indian Army]].
mudhol-state.e: Mudhol merged into [[e:bombay-state|Bombay State]] in 1948 and was transferred to Mysore, now Karnataka, in 1956. It is in Bagalkot district.

mangbetu-kingdom.t: A kingdom of the Uele region in northeastern Congo, famous through European visitors for its court art, ironwork and royal splendour.
mangbetu-kingdom.o: In the early 19th century the Mangbetu ruler Nabiembali conquered neighbouring peoples in the Uele basin and forged a kingdom out of a cluster of clans. His heirs extended it, though it was always challenged by rival branches of the royal family and by the expanding Zande kingdoms.
mangbetu-kingdom.r: Kings ruled from large courts with spacious audience halls, supported by tribute in food, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and labour from subject peoples. Mangbetu craftsmen were renowned for ironwork, pottery and carved figures, and the elite shaped infants' skulls into an elongated form. The botanist Georg Schweinfurth described the court of King Munza in 1870 in vivid detail.
mangbetu-kingdom.e: Munza was killed in 1873 by northern traders allied with his rivals, and the kingdom fragmented under pressure from slave and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] traders and the Zande. The [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]] occupied the region in the 1890s.

margraviate-of-moravia.t: Land of the Bohemian Crown with Brno and Olomouc as its centres, a margraviate for over seven centuries until the end of Austria-Hungary.
margraviate-of-moravia.o: [[s:great-moravia|Moravia]] had been the core of Great [[e:moravia|Moravia]] and was later ruled by Přemyslid princes as [[e:appanage|appanages]] of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]]. In 1182 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Emperor Frederick Barbarossa]] named [[e:conrad-iii-otto|Conrad III Otto]] margrave, briefly making Moravia a direct imperial fief. It soon returned under Bohemian kings, remaining a distinct land with its own estates, diet and law.
margraviate-of-moravia.r: Margraves were usually members or appointees of the Bohemian royal house, among them the future [[e:charles-iv|Charles IV]] and [[e:jobst-of-moravia|Jobst of Moravia]], who was elected King of the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] in 1410. Brno and Olomouc competed as capitals. Czech and German were spoken, and [[s:great-moravia|Moravia]] sheltered the Unity of the Brethren, whose Kralice Bible shaped written Czech. After 1620 [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] rule enforced [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]], and Brno later became a textile centre.
margraviate-of-moravia.e: [[s:great-moravia|Moravia]] remained a crown land of the [[s:habsburg-monarchy|Habsburg Monarchy]], [[s:austrian-empire|Austrian Empire]] and [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] until 1918, when it joined [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]]. It was merged with Czech [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]] in 1928 and abolished as a unit in 1949; it now forms the eastern Czech Republic.

malindi.t: A Swahili city-state on the Kenyan coast, famous as the place that welcomed Vasco da Gama and became Portugal's first ally in East Africa.
malindi.o: Malindi grew as a Muslim trading town on the Kenyan coast from about the 12th century, part of the network of [[e:swahili|Swahili]] ports between [[s:sultanate-of-mogadishu|Mogadishu]] and [[s:kilwa-sultanate|Kilwa]]. In the mid-1410s envoys from Malindi brought a giraffe to the [[e:yongle-emperor|Yongle Emperor]] of [[e:china|China]], and [[e:zheng-he|Zheng He's]] fleet later carried them home.
malindi.r: Malindi was ruled by a sultan and merchant elite who traded [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], gold and slaves with [[e:arabia|Arabia]] and [[e:india|India]]. Its long rivalry with [[s:mombasa|Mombasa]] shaped its politics. In 1498 its ruler welcomed [[e:vasco-da-gama|Vasco da Gama]] and provided a pilot to guide him to India, and da Gama's stone pillar still stands. Thereafter it was a loyal ally and [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:portuguese-empire|Portuguese Empire]].
malindi.e: In 1593 the Portuguese moved their base to [[s:mombasa|Mombasa]] and installed the Malindi dynasty there, after which Malindi declined. The dynasty's rule ended after its sultan Yusuf ibn al-Hasan revolted against the Portuguese at Mombasa in 1631. The town was largely abandoned until revived in the 19th century under [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]].

mesembria.t: Dorian Greek city on a rocky peninsula of the Bulgarian Black Sea coast, whose long life as a trading port survives in the old town of Nesebar.
mesembria.o: Mesembria took its name from an earlier Thracian settlement called Menebria. Greek colonists from [[s:megara|Megara]] and its colonies [[s:chalcedon|Chalcedon]] and [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] settled there around the end of the 6th century BCE; [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] says refugees from [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantium]] and Chalcedon came after the Persian suppression of the [[e:ionian-revolt|Ionian Revolt]]. The narrow isthmus made it easy to defend.
mesembria.r: A Doric-speaking polis with council and assembly, Mesembria lived from sea trade, fishing and exchange with the Thracians of the interior, and struck coins in [[e:silver|silver]] and later gold. It competed with its northern neighbour Apollonia and sometimes fought it. Hellenistic Mesembria built strong walls and temples to Apollo and Zeus.
mesembria.e: Roman forces under [[e:marcus-terentius-varro-lucullus|Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus]] subdued the West Pontic cities in 72-71 BCE. Mesembria became part of the province of Thrace and later an important Byzantine fortress and bishopric, contested with the Bulgarians. Its Byzantine churches and ancient walls make Nesebar a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

maona-of-chios.t: Genoese chartered company that ruled Chios for over two centuries and grew rich on the island's unique mastic monopoly.
maona-of-chios.o: In 1346 a Genoese fleet under [[e:simone-vignoso|Simone Vignoso]], financed by private shareholders, seized [[s:chios|Chios]] from the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] and also Old and [[e:new-phocaea|New Phocaea]] on the Anatolian coast. [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]], unable to repay the investors, let them govern and exploit the island through a company, the maona, whose members took the shared surname Giustiniani.
maona-of-chios.r: The maona appointed a podesta and council, collected taxes and controlled the export of mastic, a resin produced only in southern [[s:chios|Chios]] and prized as a chewing gum and medicine, as well as alum and [[e:silk|silk]]. The Greek [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] population kept its church and grew prosperous through trade. From the early 15th century the maona paid tribute to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]].
maona-of-chios.e: In 1566 the Ottoman admiral Piyale Pasha occupied [[s:chios|Chios]] without a fight, ending Genoese rule. Many Giustiniani were deported, while the mastic villages kept special privileges under the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]].

mitla.t: The great Postclassic Zapotec religious centre of the Valley of Oaxaca, famed for the stone fretwork mosaics on its palaces.
mitla.o: Mitla, Lyobaa in Zapotec, was occupied for many centuries, but it grew into a major centre after the decline of [[s:monte-alban|Monte Albán]], from around 900. Spanish sources describe it as the seat of the Zapotec high priest and a place of burial for kings.
mitla.r: Its palace complexes are decorated with intricate geometric step-fret mosaics made of thousands of cut stones fitted without mortar, unlike anything elsewhere in [[e:mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]]. Cruciform tombs lie beneath the courts. Mitla served as a religious centre and was linked politically with the [[s:zaachila|Zapotec kingdom of Zaachila]], while sharing Mixtec artistic influences.
mitla.e: Mitla came under the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] in the late 15th century and was taken by the Spanish around 1521. The Church of San Pablo was built over one of its palaces. It remains a Zapotec town.

macau-portuguese.t: Europe's first and last foothold in China, a Portuguese trading port for over four centuries that returned to Chinese rule in 1999.
macau-portuguese.o: Portuguese merchants, after years of informal trade on the south [[e:china|China]] coast, were allowed by local Ming officials to settle on the [[e:macau|Macau]] peninsula around 1557, paying an annual ground rent. The port grew quickly as the link between [[e:ming-empire|Ming China]] and [[e:japan|Japan]].
macau-portuguese.r: [[e:macau|Macau's]] merchants carried Chinese [[e:silk|silk]] to [[e:nagasaki|Nagasaki]] and Japanese [[e:silver|silver]] back to [[e:china|China]], and the city became a base for [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] missions to China and [[e:japan|Japan]]; the ruined façade of St Paul's dates from this era. A municipal Senate governed with a Portuguese captain, while China kept authority over the Chinese population. The colony repulsed a [[e:dutch|Dutch]] attack in 1622, declined when the Japan trade ended in 1639, and later relied on the [[e:guangzhou|Canton]] trade and gambling.
macau-portuguese.e: Governor Ferreira do Amaral expelled Chinese officials in 1849, and an 1887 treaty recognised perpetual Portuguese occupation. After Portugal's 1974 revolution, the 1987 [[e:sino-portuguese-joint-declaration|Joint Declaration]] arranged its return, and on 20 December 1999 [[e:macau|Macau]] became a [[e:special-administrative-regions-of-china|Special Administrative Region]] of the [[s:peoples-republic-of-china|People's Republic of China]].

marmaridae.t: The Libyan peoples of Marmarica, the arid coastland between Egypt and Cyrenaica, known from Greek and Roman writers.
marmaridae.o: Marmarica, the stretch of coast and desert between the [[e:nile-delta|Nile Delta]] and [[e:cyrenaica|Cyrenaica]], was home to Libyan pastoral groups whom Greek and Roman writers called the Marmaridae from the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]]. They were probably descendants of earlier peoples such as the [[s:libu|Libu]] and lived by herding, small-scale farming and oasis trade.
marmaridae.r: They were organised in clans and tribes rather than a single state. They traded with the coastal towns such as Paraetonium and served as guides and auxiliaries. Under Roman rule they were tributaries of the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]], but they raided settled lands when they could; Roman commanders, including Publius Sulpicius Quirinius under Augustus, campaigned against them.
marmaridae.e: By the late Roman period the name Marmaridae faded as new groups, such as the [[s:austuriani|Austuriani]] and the [[s:laguatan|Laguatan]], dominated the Libyan desert. Their descendants were absorbed into the [[e:berbers|Berber]] and later Arab tribes of the region.

morini.t: Coastal people of the Pas-de-Calais, called by Virgil the farthest of men, from whose harbour Caesar sailed to invade Britain.
morini.o: The Morini, whose name means people of the sea, lived along the Channel coast from the [[e:battle-of-the-somme|Somme]] to the Scheldt, in a land of dunes, marshes and forest. They joined the Belgic coalition of 57 BCE.
morini.r: They lived by farming, herding and salt-making, and took refuge in forests and marshes rather than defending oppida. Their coast was the shortest crossing to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]].
morini.e: Caesar campaigned against them in 56 and 55 BCE and sailed for [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] from Portus Itius in their land, probably [[s:county-of-boulogne|Boulogne]]. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their capital was Tarvenna (Thérouanne), while Gesoriacum (Boulogne) became the base of the Roman Channel fleet.

margraviate-of-baden-baden.t: The Catholic half of the divided margraviate of Baden, ruled from Baden-Baden and Rastatt and made famous by the general 'Türkenlouis'.
margraviate-of-baden-baden.o: The 1535 partition of the [[s:margraviate-of-baden|Margraviate of Baden]] gave [[e:bernhard-iii-margrave-of-baden-baden|Bernhard III]] the territories around Baden-Baden in the middle [[e:rhine|Rhine]] valley, together with a share of the old [[s:county-of-sponheim|County of Sponheim]]. His successors resided in the New Castle above Baden-Baden.
margraviate-of-baden-baden.r: After a Protestant interlude, Baden-Baden was firmly Catholic from the 1620s. Margrave Louis William, an imperial general known as '[[e:louis-william-margrave-of-baden-baden|Türkenlouis]]' for his victories over the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], saw Baden-Baden burned by the French in 1689 and built a new Baroque residence at Rastatt from 1700. His widow [[e:sibylla-augusta-of-saxe-lauenburg|Sibylla Augusta]] completed it and built the Favorite palace nearby.
margraviate-of-baden-baden.e: When Margrave August George died without heirs in 1771, his lands passed to [[e:charles-frederick-grand-duke-of-baden|Charles Frederick]] of the [[s:margraviate-of-baden-durlach|Margraviate of Baden-Durlach]], reuniting Baden, which became the [[s:grand-duchy-of-baden|Grand Duchy of Baden]] in 1806. Baden-Baden later became a fashionable spa town.

mahdid-dynasty.t: A puritanical reformist dynasty that seized Zabid in 1159 and ruled the Yemeni Tihama until the Ayyubid invasion.
mahdid-dynasty.o: [[e:ali-ibn-mahdi|Ali ibn Mahdi]], a preacher from the Tihama, built a following among the tribes of the coastal plain in the 1130s and 1140s, preaching strict morality and condemning the ruling elite. After years of raids he captured Zabid in 1159, ending the [[s:najahid-dynasty|Najahid dynasty]], and died soon after.
mahdid-dynasty.r: His sons, especially [[e:abd-al-nabi-ibn-ali-ibn-mahdi|Abd al-Nabi]], ran a militant state. Contemporary sources, mostly hostile, accuse them of treating other Muslims as unbelievers, punishing minor sins with death and destroying tombs. They raided widely across the Tihama and threatened Aden, ruled by the [[s:zurayid-dynasty|Zurayid dynasty]].
mahdid-dynasty.e: In 1174 the Ayyubid prince Turan-Shah, sent by his brother [[e:saladin|Saladin]], invaded [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]], took Zabid and executed [[e:abd-al-nabi-ibn-ali-ibn-mahdi|Abd al-Nabi]], absorbing the Mahdid lands into [[s:ayyubid-yemen|Ayyubid Yemen]].

mathwar-state.t: A small chiefship in the hills of the Narmada valley in western Malwa, with a largely Bhil population.
mathwar-state.o: Mathwar lay in the Vindhya hills north of the Narmada, on the border of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] and [[e:malwa|Malwa]]. It was held by a local chiefly family from around 1700, though its founding is not well documented.
mathwar-state.r: The chief ruled forested hill country inhabited mainly by Bhils and Bhilalas. In the British period Mathwar was a minor state of the [[e:bhopawar-agency|Bhopawar Agency of Central India]]. Few further details are recorded.
mathwar-state.e: Mathwar joined [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and Madhya Pradesh in 1956. Its lands lie in [[s:alirajpur-state|Alirajpur]] district.

majeerteen-sultanate.t: A Somali sultanate of the Horn's north-eastern tip, rich from the frankincense trade, which held out against Italy until 1927.
majeerteen-sultanate.o: The sultanate took shape in the mid-18th century among the Majeerteen clan of the Darod in the far north-east of [[s:somalia|Somalia]]. Its rulers, with the title boqor (king), were based on the coast at Alula and Bargal, near [[e:cape-guardafui|Cape Guardafui]].
majeerteen-sultanate.r: The boqor ruled through clan elders, collecting revenue from frankincense, livestock and the salvage of ships wrecked on [[e:cape-guardafui|Cape Guardafui]], which brought agreements with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] to protect crews. [[e:boqor-osman-mahamuud|Boqor Osman Mahamuud]] fought a long war with his kinsman [[e:yusuf-ali-kenadid|Yusuf Ali Kenadid]], who left to found the [[s:sultanate-of-hobyo|Sultanate of Hobyo]]. In 1889 Osman signed a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] treaty with [[e:italy|Italy]].
majeerteen-sultanate.e: Italian control remained nominal until 1925 to 1927, when Governor [[e:cesare-maria-de-vecchi|Cesare De Vecchi's]] forces disarmed and conquered the northern sultanates and annexed them to [[s:italian-somaliland|Italian Somaliland]]. The region is now part of Puntland.

millawanda.t: Bronze Age Miletus as named in Hittite texts, a coastal foothold of the Aegean Ahhiyawa on the Anatolian mainland and a flashpoint with the Hittites.
millawanda.o: Excavations at [[s:miletus|Miletus]] show a Minoan-style settlement from c. 1900 BCE, followed after c. 1450 BCE by a town with Mycenaean pottery, tombs and customs. Most scholars identify this town with Millawanda, or Milawata, named in Hittite sources as a place under the influence of [[s:ahhiyawa|Ahhiyawa]], the power of the Mycenaean [[e:greeks|Greeks]].
millawanda.r: The Tawagalawa letter of [[e:hattusili-iii|Hattusili III]], c. 1250 BCE, names Atpa as the local ruler, son-in-law of the rebel Piyamaradu, who used Millawanda as a base for raids on Hittite lands. The town was a port linking the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] with western [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], and the Hittite [[e:mursili-ii|Mursili II]] had sacked it c. 1315 BCE during his wars with [[s:arzawa|Arzawa]].
millawanda.e: The so-called Milawata letter, probably from [[e:tudhaliya-iv|Tudhaliya IV]], shows the town had passed under Hittite control and a new border was being fixed. [[s:miletus|Miletus]] was destroyed c. 1200 BCE, then resettled by [[e:ionia|Ionian Greeks]] as the city-state Miletus.

mac-rule-in-cao-bang.t: A rump Mac state in the northern mountains of Vietnam that survived for eighty years after the Mac lost Thang Long, under Ming and Qing protection.
mac-rule-in-cao-bang.o: After [[e:trinh-tung|Trinh Tung]] took [[e:thang-long|Thang Long]] in 1592 and executed [[e:mac-mau-hop|Mac Mau Hop]], members of the [[s:mac-dynasty|Mac dynasty]] fled to the mountainous province of [[e:cao-bang|Cao Bang]] near the Chinese border. In 1593 [[e:mac-kinh-cung|Mac Kinh Cung]] proclaimed himself emperor, and the Ming court pressured the [[s:later-le-dynasty|Later Le dynasty]] to leave them in possession.
mac-rule-in-cao-bang.r: The Mac ruled a small upland territory of Tay and Nung peoples from [[e:cao-bang|Cao Bang]], relying on diplomatic protection from the Ming and then the Qing. They occasionally raided the lowlands, and in 1623, during a Trinh succession crisis, briefly threatened [[e:thang-long|Thang Long]].
mac-rule-in-cao-bang.e: After the Mac supported the [[e:revolt-of-the-three-feudatories|Revolt of the Three Feudatories]] in [[e:china|China]], the Qing withdrew protection, and in 1677 Trinh forces conquered [[e:cao-bang|Cao Bang]]. The last Mac ruler, [[e:mac-kinh-vu|Mac Kinh Vu]], fled to China, ending the dynasty.

mam-kingdom.t: The highland Maya kingdom of the Mam people, ruled from the fortress city of Zaculeu near modern Huehuetenango until its siege by the Spanish in 1525.
mam-kingdom.o: The Mam are among the oldest established peoples of western [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]], and Zaculeu had been occupied since the [[e:early-classic-period|Early Classic]]. In the Postclassic, from around 1250, it was the capital of a Mam kingdom that controlled much of the western highlands until K'iche' expansion pushed the Mam back.
mam-kingdom.r: Zaculeu stood on a plateau protected by deep ravines, with temples, plazas and a ballcourt. The Mam kingdom was a rival and at times a tributary of the [[s:kiche-kingdom|K'iche' kingdom]]. Its society was led by a hereditary lord and noble lineages, and its economy rested on [[e:maize|maize]] farming and highland trade.
mam-kingdom.e: In 1525 Gonzalo de Alvarado besieged Zaculeu for several months, and the Mam ruler [[e:kaibil-balam|Kaibil Balam]] surrendered when his people were starving. The site was later restored in the 1940s by the [[e:united-fruit-company|United Fruit Company]]. Mam remains a major Maya language.

mayurbhanj-state.t: The largest of the Orissa princely states, ruled by the Bhanja dynasty, whose iron ore fed the Tata steel works at Jamshedpur.
mayurbhanj-state.o: The Bhanja dynasty of Mayurbhanj claimed ancient descent, and tradition places its rule from around 1100, first at [[s:guler-state|Haripur]] and later at Baripada. The state lay in the forested hills of northern Odisha.
mayurbhanj-state.r: Mayurbhanj had a large Santal, Ho and Bhumij population and is the home of the Mayurbhanj Chhau dance. Maharaja Sriram Chandra Bhanj Deo (r. 1882–1912) built schools and hospitals, opened a light railway and allowed Tata to mine the iron ore of Gorumahisani, which supplied the [[e:steel|steel]] works founded at Jamshedpur in 1907.
mayurbhanj-state.e: Maharaja Pratap Chandra Bhanj Deo set up an elected government in 1947 and held out longer than other Orissa states, but Mayurbhanj merged into Orissa on 1 January 1949. It is now a district of Odisha.

metsepole.t: Livonian coastal district north of Riga, known from Henry of Livonia's chronicle and absorbed by the Archbishopric of Riga.
metsepole.o: Metsepole, whose name means 'forest land', was a district of the Finnic-speaking Livonians along the Gulf of Riga north of the Gauja, around modern Limbaži. It appears in the chronicle of the Livonian [[e:crusade|crusade]] in the early 13th century.
metsepole.r: Its people lived from farming, fishing and coastal trade, led by local elders. Little else is recorded beyond their part in the wars and baptisms of the period.
metsepole.e: The Livs of Metsepole submitted to [[e:albert-of-riga|Bishop Albert]] and accepted baptism around 1206, after the failure of a Liv revolt. The area became part of the [[s:archbishopric-of-riga|Archbishopric of Riga]] and [[s:terra-mariana|Terra Mariana]], and the Livonian population merged gradually into the Latvians.

ma-chu.t: The kingdom of the Ma family in Hunan, which grew rich on the tea trade with northern China before collapsing in a family war in 951.
ma-chu.o: [[e:ma-yin|Ma Yin]], a carpenter turned soldier from Xuzhou, came to Hunan with a band of [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] and made himself master of the region from Changsha in 896. In 907 the [[s:later-liang|Later Liang]] recognised him as Prince of Chu, a title he held while accepting the overlordship of the northern courts.
ma-chu.r: [[e:ma-yin|Ma Yin]] encouraged farming and especially [[e:tea|tea]], which was sold in large quantities to the northern dynasties in exchange for [[e:silk|silk]] and war horses. He issued iron and lead coins that could not be spent outside Chu, keeping goods and [[e:silver|silver]] inside the kingdom. The ruling family relied on loyal generals and on alliances with the southern Han regimes.
ma-chu.e: After [[e:ma-yin|Ma Yin]] died in 930, his many sons fought over the throne. During a civil war between Ma Xiguang and Ma Xi'e, [[s:southern-tang|Southern Tang]] invaded and in 951 took Changsha, ending the dynasty. Local commanders soon expelled the Southern [[s:later-tang|Tang]] and held Hunan until the [[s:song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]] took it in 963.

muntafiq-confederation.t: A powerful Arab tribal confederation of the lower Euphrates, led by the Al Sa'dun sheikhs, that dominated southern Iraq for three centuries.
muntafiq-confederation.o: The Muntafiq were a confederation of Arab tribes in the marshes and farmlands between [[e:basra|Basra]] and Samawa. From the 16th century their leadership was held by the Al Shabib, later called Al Sa'dun, a family claiming descent from the [[s:sharifate-of-mecca|Sharifs of Mecca]]. Their power grew as the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire's]] control of southern [[e:iraq|Iraq]] remained weak.
muntafiq-confederation.r: The sheikhs collected tribute from tribal farmers growing dates and [[e:rice|rice]], controlled river traffic and often defied Ottoman governors in [[e:basra|Basra]] and [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]], at times taking Basra itself. Their leaders were [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]], while most tribesmen were [[e:shia-islam|Shia]]. [[e:thuwayni-ibn-abdullah|Thuwayni ibn Abdullah]] was a dominant figure in the late 18th century, and the town of Suq al-Shuyukh served as their market and base.
muntafiq-confederation.e: In the Ottoman reforms of 1871, governor Midhat Pasha made the Muntafiq lands a sanjak, and [[e:nasir-pasha-al-sadun|Nasir Pasha al-Sa'dun]] founded Nasiriyah as its capital. The sheikhs became landlords and officials, losing their independent power.

mannaea.t: An Iron Age kingdom south of Lake Urmia, squeezed between Assyria and Urartu, that eventually merged into the Median state.
mannaea.o: The Mannaeans (Mannai) appear in Assyrian texts from the 840s BCE, inhabiting north-western [[e:iran|Iran]] around the southern shores of [[e:lake-urmia|Lake Urmia]]. By the late 8th century they had become a unified kingdom with its capital at Izirtu (Zirta), perhaps near Saqqez.
mannaea.r: Mannaea was rich in horses and [[e:cattle|cattle]] and controlled routes between [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Urartu]] and the [[e:iranian-plateau|Iranian plateau]]. Its kings usually sided with the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] against the Kingdom of Urartu: Iranzu was [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II's]] ally, and [[e:sargon-of-akkad|Sargon]] confirmed Ullusunu on the throne after he abandoned an alliance with Urartu. Sites such as Ziwiye and Qalaichi, with its stele and glazed bricks, may reflect Mannaean culture. Its language is unknown.
mannaea.e: [[e:ashurbanipal|Ashurbanipal]] defeated King Ahsheri around 660 BCE. In 616 BCE Mannaean troops fought alongside [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] against [[e:nabopolassar|Nabopolassar]], but after Assyria's fall the kingdom was absorbed by the [[s:median-empire|Median Empire]].

mycenaean-kingdom-of-laconia.t: Mycenaean palace state of the Eurotas valley, the Bronze Age Sparta of Homer's Menelaus, recently revealed by the palace and tablets of Ayios Vasileios.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-laconia.o: In the Eurotas valley of Laconia, Mycenaean elites appear from c. 1500 BCE, as shown by the rich tholos tomb of Vapheio with its gold cups. A palace was built at [[e:ayios-vasileios|Ayios Vasileios]], about 12 kilometres south of [[s:sparta|Sparta]], while the Menelaion at Therapne, opposite the later city, held a large mansion.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-laconia.r: Excavations at [[e:ayios-vasileios|Ayios Vasileios]] since 2008 have found a palace with a large court, stoas, wall paintings and the first Linear B tablets from Laconia, recording textiles, personnel and offerings. Laconia also produced the green porphyry stone from Krokeai, exported across the [[e:aegean|Aegean]]. The kingdom presumably ruled the Eurotas plain.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-laconia.e: The [[e:ayios-vasileios|Ayios Vasileios]] palace was destroyed by fire well before the general collapse, and the Menelaion buildings were abandoned c. 1200 BCE. Laconia was largely depopulated afterwards, and Dorian [[s:sparta|Sparta]] later grew nearby. Homer remembered Laconia as the kingdom of Menelaus and Helen.

makrai-state.t: A small Gond principality in the Narmada valley, one of the few princely states inside the Central Provinces.
makrai-state.o: Makrai was held by a [[e:raj-gond|Raj Gond]] family in the hills south of the Narmada, in what became Hoshangabad district. The register dates the state to 1663, though its early history is known mainly from tradition.
makrai-state.r: The Raja ruled a small, heavily forested territory of tribal villages. In the British period Makrai was a feudatory state attached to the [[e:central-provinces|Central Provinces]], and it is recorded as one of the smallest of its kind. Few further details are widely known.
makrai-state.e: Makrai merged into the [[e:central-provinces|Central Provinces and Berar]] in 1948, later Madhya Pradesh. Its lands lie in Harda district.

middle-congo.t: The French colony north of the Congo River whose capital, Brazzaville, governed French Equatorial Africa and briefly hosted Free France.
middle-congo.o: When the [[s:french-congo|French Congo]] was divided in 1903, the lands between [[s:gabon-french-colony|Gabon]] and the Congo and Ubangi rivers became the colony of Middle Congo, with its capital at [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]], the post founded by [[e:pierre-savorgnan-de-brazza|Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza]] on land ceded by the [[s:kingdom-of-tio|Kingdom of Tio]]. From 1910 Brazzaville was also the seat of [[s:french-equatorial-africa|French Equatorial Africa]].
middle-congo.r: Concession companies and forced labour dominated the early economy. The Congo-Ocean railway from [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]] to Pointe-Noire, built between 1921 and 1934, cost the lives of many thousands of conscripted workers. André Matsoua's movement challenged colonial rule from the 1920s. In 1940 Brazzaville became the capital of [[s:free-france|Free France]] in [[e:africa|Africa]], and de Gaulle opened the [[e:brazzaville-conference|Brazzaville Conference]] there in 1944.
middle-congo.e: Middle Congo became the autonomous Republic of the Congo in November 1958 under the priest-politician [[e:fulbert-youlou|Fulbert Youlou]], and gained full independence on 15 August 1960, keeping [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]] as its capital.

malacca-sultanate.t: The great Malay trading sultanate on the Strait of Malacca, whose 15th-century port linked China, India and the spice islands until Portugal took it in 1511.
malacca-sultanate.o: Around 1400 [[e:parameswara|Parameswara]], a prince who had fled the [[s:kingdom-of-singapura|Kingdom of Singapura]], founded a settlement at the mouth of the [[e:malacca|Malacca]] River. He won the protection of [[e:ming-empire|Ming China]], receiving the visits of [[e:zheng-he|Zheng He's]] fleets and travelling to [[e:china|China]] himself in 1411, which shielded the port from Siam and [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]].
malacca-sultanate.r: [[e:malacca|Malacca's]] rulers adopted [[e:islam|Islam]] early in the 15th century, and the port became a centre for the faith's spread. Under Muzaffar Shah and [[e:mansur-shah-of-malacca|Mansur Shah]], and the long-serving bendahara Tun [[s:perak-sultanate|Perak]], it ruled both sides of the Strait. Harbour masters handled merchants from [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]], [[e:china|China]] and [[e:java|Java]], and its legal codes and court etiquette became models for later Malay states.
malacca-sultanate.e: In 1511 [[e:afonso-de-albuquerque|Afonso de Albuquerque]] captured the city, founding [[s:portuguese-malacca|Portuguese Malacca]]. [[e:mahmud-shah-of-malacca|Sultan Mahmud Shah]] fled, and his sons founded the [[s:johor-sultanate|Johor Sultanate]] and the [[s:perak-sultanate|Perak Sultanate]], continuing the dynasty. The [[e:malay-annals|Malay Annals]] record [[e:malacca|Malacca's]] glory.

masmughans-of-damavand.t: Zoroastrian lords of Mount Damavand whose title meant 'great magus', holding out against the Arab conquest until 760.
masmughans-of-damavand.o: The Masmughans ruled the district of Damavand in the central [[e:alborz|Alborz]], east of later Tehran. Their title, from [[e:middle-persian|Middle Persian]] mas-mughan, 'great of the magi', suggests a priestly origin. After the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] fell, they reached terms with Arab commanders around 651 and kept their autonomy.
masmughans-of-damavand.r: Little is known of their rule. They governed a mountain population that remained Zoroastrian, paid tribute to the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] and allied with the neighbouring [[s:dabuyid-dynasty|Dabuyid dynasty]] of Tabaristan. The fortress region around Mount Damavand, the peak of Iranian legend, gave them protection.
masmughans-of-damavand.e: During the Abbasid conquest of Tabaristan in 759 to 760, the last Masmughan was defeated and captured, and Damavand passed under direct caliphal rule.

mahan.t: The largest of the three Samhan confederacies, a group of some fifty-four statelets in western Korea from which the kingdom of Baekje emerged.
mahan.o: Mahan took shape around the 1st century BCE in what are now Gyeonggi, Chungcheong and Jeolla provinces. Its leading statelet, Mokji-guk, supplied a Jin king recognised as head of the confederacy, and [[e:jun-of-gojoseon|King Jun of Gojoseon]] is said to have fled here around 194 BCE.
mahan.r: Chinese records describe fifty-four statelets of varying size living by [[e:rice|rice]] farming in unwalled settlements. Each had sacred precincts called sodo, ruled by priests where fugitives could find refuge, and festivals after sowing in the fifth month and after harvest in the tenth. The Yeongsan river area developed distinctive large jar-coffin burials.
mahan.e: Baekje-guk, one Mahan statelet near the Han river, rose to dominate the rest; [[e:geunchogo-of-baekje|King Geunchogo]] is usually credited with subduing the southern remnants around 369. Jar-coffin elites in the far southwest kept some independence into the 5th century.

malia-state.t: A small Jadeja Rajput principality in northern Kathiawar, on the edge of the Rann of Kutch, ruled by a junior branch of the house of Morvi.
malia-state.o: [[s:palace-state-of-malia|Malia]] was carved out around 1720 by a cadet of the [[e:jadeja|Jadeja Rajput]] family that ruled Morvi, itself an offshoot of the ruling house of Cutch. Like many Kathiawar holdings it began as a family [[e:appanage|appanage]] that became a separate chiefship as the Mughal hold on [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] weakened.
malia-state.r: The Thakor ruled a handful of villages on poor, partly saline land near the Rann. The district was known to British officials for its Miyana community, whose raiding troubled the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]] through the 19th century. Little else about its internal history is recorded.
malia-state.e: [[s:palace-state-of-malia|Malia]] acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1947 and in 1948 was merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Kathiawar]], later Saurashtra State. Its territory, around the town of Maliya-Miyana, is now in [[s:morvi-state|Morbi]] district of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

moro-province.t: Army-governed province of the American Philippines covering Muslim Mindanao and Sulu, marked by harsh campaigns against Moro resistance.
moro-province.o: The [[s:united-states|United States]], which had at first signed the Kiram-Bates Treaty of 1899 recognising the [[s:sulu-sultanate|Sulu Sultanate]], created the Moro Province in 1903 to govern the Muslim regions of Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago, including the former [[s:lanao-sultanates|Lanao sultanates]] and [[s:maguindanao-sultanate|Maguindanao]]. Its capital was Zamboanga, and its governors were army generals.
moro-province.r: Governors [[e:leonard-wood|Leonard Wood]], [[e:tasker-h-bliss|Tasker Bliss]] and John J. Pershing ruled with a legislative council, abolishing [[e:slavery|slavery]], imposing a head tax and courts, and building schools and roads. Resistance was met with force, culminating in the killing of hundreds of Moro men, women and children at Bud Dajo in 1906 and the battle of Bud Bagsak in 1913.
moro-province.e: In 1913 the province was replaced by the civilian-run [[e:departement|Department]] of Mindanao and Sulu under Frank Carpenter, beginning the integration of Muslim areas into the Philippine state, a process whose tensions have continued to the present.

mamprugu.t: The senior kingdom of the Mole-Dagbani peoples of northern Ghana, from whose royal house the Dagbon and Mossi dynasties claim descent.
mamprugu.o: Mole-Dagbani tradition traces Mamprugu to [[e:na-gbewaa|Na Gbewaa]], a chief who settled at Pusiga in the far north of present-day [[e:ghana|Ghana]], probably in the 14th or 15th century. His sons and grandsons are said to have founded [[s:kingdom-of-dagbon|Dagbon]], Nanumba and, through the princess Yennenga, the [[e:mossi|Mossi]] kingdoms, so the Nayiri of Mamprugu is regarded as their senior.
mamprugu.r: A ruling class of horse-owning chiefs governed farming peoples whose earth-priests kept authority over land and shrines. The capital moved from Gambaga to Nalerigu under [[e:na-atabia|Na Atabia]] around 1700. Muslim traders and scholars settled at Gambaga, linking the kingdom to routes between [[s:hausa-kingdoms|Hausaland]] and the [[e:akan|Akan]] forest.
mamprugu.e: Mamprugu was divided in 1898 between the British [[s:northern-territories-of-the-gold-coast|Northern Territories of the Gold Coast]] and [[s:german-togoland|German Togoland]], with a smaller part in French territory. The Nayiri still reigns at Nalerigu as paramount chief of the Mamprusi in [[e:ghana|Ghana]].

mongolian-peoples-republic.t: The world's second communist state, a Soviet ally for nearly seventy years, which made Mongolia a modern state with recognised independence.
mongolian-peoples-republic.o: The Mongolian People's Party took power with [[e:red-army|Red Army]] help in 1921 under the limited monarchy of the [[s:bogd-khanate-of-mongolia|Bogd Khanate of Mongolia]]. When the [[e:bogd-khan|Bogd Khan]] died in 1924, the party abolished the monarchy and proclaimed the Mongolian People's Republic, renaming the capital Ulaanbaatar ('Red Hero').
mongolian-peoples-republic.r: The country followed the Soviet model closely. Forced collectivisation provoked a revolt in 1932, and under [[e:khorloogiin-choibalsan|Khorloogiin Choibalsan]] the purges of 1937 to 1939 killed many thousands of lamas, nobles and officials and destroyed most monasteries. Soviet and Mongolian forces defeated [[e:japan|Japan]] at Khalkhin Gol in 1939. The Cyrillic alphabet was adopted in the 1940s, and under Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal from 1952 [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]] industrialised and joined the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] in 1961.
mongolian-peoples-republic.e: Inspired by reform in the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], peaceful protests in the winter of 1989 to 1990 led to multi-party elections in 1990, and the 1992 constitution created the democratic state of [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]], ending the people's republic. Soviet troops had left by 1992.

mexico.t: The Mexican republic since the defeat of Maximilian in 1867, shaped by the Porfiriato, the Revolution of 1910 and seven decades of one-party rule.
mexico.o: [[e:benito-juarez|Benito Juárez]] re-entered [[e:mexico-city|Mexico City]] in July 1867 after the execution of Maximilian, restoring the republic under the Constitution of 1857. This Restored Republic, under Juárez and then Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada, sought to rebuild the state and enforce the liberal Reform laws.
mexico.r: [[e:porfirio-diaz|Porfirio Díaz]] seized power in 1876 and ruled almost continuously until 1911, attracting foreign investment in railways, mines and oil while peasants lost their land. The Revolution that began in 1910 produced the Constitution of 1917, land reform and the party later called the PRI, which ruled from 1929 to 2000. [[e:lazaro-cardenas|Lázaro Cárdenas]] expropriated foreign oil in 1938. Rapid growth was followed by the [[s:tlatelolco|Tlatelolco]] massacre of 1968 and debt crises.
mexico.e: Mexico joined NAFTA in 1994, the year of the Zapatista rising. Vicente Fox's victory in 2000 ended PRI dominance. Since 2018 the Morena party has governed, and Claudia Sheinbaum became the first woman president in 2024. Mexico is now a federal republic of 32 entities.

cr.a: Omar Alejandro Covarrubias Neri, 9 April 2006. Based on the 1968 arms by Francisco Eppens Helguera and Juan Manuel Ga...

mohammadgarh-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state of the Bhopal Agency in central India, a branch of the Pathan family of Kurwai.
mohammadgarh-state.o: Mohammadgarh was separated from the lands of the Pathan Nawabs of [[s:kurwai-state|Kurwai]] and [[s:basoda-state|Basoda]] in the early 19th century and recognised as a distinct holding under British supervision around 1818.
mohammadgarh-state.r: Its Nawab ruled a few villages within the [[e:bhopal-agency|Bhopal Agency]]. Little else is recorded of its history.
mohammadgarh-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Mohammadgarh was merged into [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and joined Madhya Pradesh in 1956.

medri-bahri.t: The highland kingdom of the 'sea land' in today's Eritrea, ruled by the Bahr Negash as a semi-independent vassal of the Ethiopian emperors.
medri-bahri.o: The region north of the Mareb river was known as Medri Bahri, the land of the sea, and from the 14th century its ruler bore the title Bahr Negash, king of the sea, under the Solomonic emperors of the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]]. The office gained strength in the 15th century under [[e:zara-yaqob|Zara Yaqob]], and its seat became Debarwa.
medri-bahri.r: The Bahr Negash governed the Tigrinya-speaking highlands, collecting tribute and guarding the approaches to the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]] coast. Society was organised around [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Christian villages, monasteries and landholding kin groups with customary codes. In the 1560s and 1570s Bahr Negash Yeshaq allied with the Ottoman [[s:habesh-eyalet|Habesh Eyalet]] against the emperor [[e:sarsa-dengel|Sarsa Dengel]], showing the province's frequent independence.
medri-bahri.e: The office continued under various local dynasties, contested by [[s:tigray|Tigray]] lords, Egyptian forces and the Ethiopian state. After the Italians occupied the highlands, the territory became part of [[s:italian-eritrea|Italian Eritrea]] in 1890, and the old title lapsed.

mongnai-state.t: One of the most senior of the southern Shan states in Myanmar, whose ruler led Shan resistance to the British in the 1880s.
mongnai-state.o: Mongnai, Shan Mong Nai, was one of the older Shan principalities of the southern plateau, with a ruling house traced in Shan tradition to the early 14th century. It was regarded as among the leading states of the southern Shan region.
mongnai-state.r: Its saopha ruled [[e:rice|rice]] valleys and hill country populated by Shan, Pa-O and other peoples, paying tribute to Burmese kings in Ava and later Mandalay, and sending daughters to the royal court. Rivalries with neighbouring [[s:kengtung-state|Kengtung]] and [[s:yawnghwe-state|Yawnghwe]] often turned violent, and Konbaung kings intervened in its successions.
mongnai-state.e: In the 1880s the Mongnai saopha joined the Limbin [[s:confederate-states-of-america|Confederacy]] against [[e:thibaw-min|King Thibaw]] and then the British, but submitted in 1887. Mongnai became part of the British protected Shan states and the [[s:federated-shan-states|Federated Shan States]], and its ruler gave up his powers in 1959.

marca-geronis.t: The vast eastern march of Margrave Gero, from which Otto I's frontier against the Slavs between the Elbe and the Oder was controlled.
marca-geronis.o: In 937 [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] appointed Gero as margrave on the eastern frontier of Saxony, over the Slavic lands between the Saale and the Elbe and beyond. Gero extended German control in campaigns against the [[s:principality-of-the-hevelli|Hevelli]], the Lusatians and other [[e:slavs|Slavs]]. [[e:widukind-of-corvey|Widukind of Corvey]] reports that he killed some thirty Slavic chiefs at a banquet.
marca-geronis.r: The march was a military command over tribute-paying Slavic peoples, the [[s:sorbs|Sorbs]] among them, rather than a settled principality. Gero campaigned as far as the Oder and in 963 forced the Polish ruler Mieszko I to pay tribute for land up to the Warta. He founded the convent of Gernrode, where he was buried.
marca-geronis.e: When Gero died in 965 [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] divided his march into smaller units: the [[s:northern-march|Northern March]], the [[s:margraviate-of-meissen|Margraviate of Meissen]], the [[s:margraviate-of-lower-lusatia|March of Lusatia]] (later Margraviate of [[e:lower-lusatia|Lower Lusatia]]), and the marches of Merseburg and Zeitz. Bishoprics founded in 968 under the [[s:archbishopric-of-magdeburg|Archbishopric of Magdeburg]] completed the new frontier order.

malava-republic.t: A warrior republic that fought Alexander in the Punjab, migrated to Rajasthan and gave its name to the region of Malwa.
malava-republic.o: The Malavas first appear as the Malloi of Greek historians, a republican people of the lower [[e:punjab|Punjab]] who resisted Alexander in 326 to 325 BCE; Alexander was badly wounded storming one of their towns. In the following centuries they moved south-east into Rajasthan, where they were established near [[s:nagar|Nagar]] in the Tonk district by the 2nd century BCE.
malava-republic.r: The Malavas were a gana, governed by an assembly of clan leaders rather than a king. Thousands of small [[e:copper|copper]] coins found at [[s:nagar|Nagar]] carry the legend Malavanam jaya, victory of the Malavas. An era beginning in 57 BCE, later known as the Vikrama Samvat, was long called the era of the Malava gana, and it is still used in [[e:india|India]].
malava-republic.e: The Malavas fought the [[s:western-satraps|Western Satraps]] and in the 4th century acknowledged the overlordship of [[e:samudragupta|Samudragupta]], whose Allahabad pillar inscription lists them among subject peoples. They then disappear as an independent power, but the region of [[e:malwa|Malwa]] preserves their name.

motya.t: Phoenician island city in the Stagnone lagoon of western Sicily, a major Punic trading base until Dionysius I of Syracuse destroyed it in 397 BCE.
motya.o: Motya was founded by [[e:phoenicians|Phoenicians]] in the late 8th century BCE on the small island of San Pantaleo, off the western tip of [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. Like other Phoenician sites, it chose an offshore island with sheltered anchorage close to a native hinterland, here the Elymian towns of [[s:segesta|Segesta]] and Eryx. It soon came within [[e:carthage|Carthage's]] sphere.
motya.r: Motya was a busy port and craft centre, with dye works, potteries and a small artificial basin. A causeway linked it to the mainland, and walls with towers enclosed the island in the 6th century BCE. Its [[e:tophet|tophet]], a sacred precinct for child burials, and its temples show Phoenician religion; the marble Motya Charioteer, a Greek masterpiece of about 470 BCE, was found there in 1979.
motya.e: In 397 BCE [[e:dionysius-i-of-syracuse|Dionysius I of Syracuse]] besieged Motya, building a mole across the lagoon and using [[e:siege-tower|siege towers]] and [[e:catapult|catapults]]; the city fell after fierce street fighting. [[e:carthage|Carthage]] did not rebuild it and moved the survivors to [[s:lilybaeum|Lilybaeum]] on the mainland. The island was bought by Joseph Whitaker, who began its excavation in the early 20th century.

montenegro.t: Present-day Montenegro, independent again since 2006 after nearly nine decades within Yugoslav states, and a NATO member seeking to join the EU.
montenegro.o: Under [[e:milo-dukanovic|Milo Đukanović]], Montenegro distanced itself from [[s:serbia|Serbia]] in the late 1990s and adopted the [[e:deutsche-mark|Deutsche Mark]] and later the euro. Within [[s:serbia-and-montenegro|Serbia and Montenegro]], it used its right to hold an independence referendum, and on 21 May 2006 a narrow majority voted to leave. Independence was declared on 3 June 2006, restoring the statehood lost in 1918 by the [[s:kingdom-of-montenegro|Kingdom of Montenegro]].
montenegro.r: Montenegro is a parliamentary republic with its capital at Podgorica, while Cetinje, the old royal capital, keeps the official residence of the president. A constitution adopted in 2007 made Montenegrin the official language. Đukanović's Democratic Party of Socialists dominated politics for three decades, and tourism along the Adriatic coast is the mainstay of the economy.
montenegro.e: Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 despite Russian opposition and an alleged coup plot in 2016. A dispute over a law on church property brought the opposition to power in 2020, ending thirty years of rule by the Democratic Party of Socialists. It is among the most advanced candidates for EU membership.

margraviate-of-baden-durlach.t: The Protestant half of the divided margraviate of Baden, which founded Karlsruhe in 1715 and reunited Baden in 1771.
margraviate-of-baden-durlach.o: In 1535 the brothers [[e:bernhard-iii-margrave-of-baden-baden|Bernhard III]] and Ernest divided the [[s:margraviate-of-baden|Margraviate of Baden]]. Ernest received the northern lands around Pforzheim and the southern Upper Margraviate around [[s:margraviate-of-hachberg|Hochberg]] and Rötteln; his line moved its residence to Durlach in 1565 and became known as Baden-Durlach.
margraviate-of-baden-durlach.r: Margrave [[e:charles-ii-margrave-of-baden-durlach|Charles II]] introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1556. In the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]] George Frederick was defeated at Wimpfen in 1622, and in 1689 French troops burned Durlach. [[e:charles-iii-william-margrave-of-baden-durlach|Charles III William]] founded Karlsruhe in 1715 as a new residence laid out in a fan around the palace. [[e:charles-frederick-grand-duke-of-baden|Charles Frederick]], ruling from 1738, was a model enlightened prince who abolished [[e:serfdom|serfdom]] in 1783.
margraviate-of-baden-durlach.e: When the Catholic line died out in 1771, [[e:charles-frederick-grand-duke-of-baden|Charles Frederick]] inherited the [[s:margraviate-of-baden-baden|Margraviate of Baden-Baden]] and reunited Baden. Allied with [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], he became elector in 1803 and grand duke in 1806, creating the [[s:grand-duchy-of-baden|Grand Duchy of Baden]].

middle-francia.t: Central share of the Carolingian empire, stretching from Frisia to Rome, given to the emperor Lothair I in 843.
middle-francia.o: The [[e:treaty-of-verdun|Treaty of Verdun]] in 843 ended the war between the sons of [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious]]. The eldest, [[e:lothair-i|Lothair I]], kept the imperial title and received a long strip of land between [[s:west-francia|West Francia]] and [[s:east-francia|East Francia]], including the imperial cities of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-aachen|Aachen]] and [[e:rome|Rome]].
middle-francia.r: The kingdom reached from the [[e:north-sea|North Sea]] through the [[e:low-countries|Low Countries]], the Rhineland, [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] and [[s:county-of-provence|Provence]] to [[e:italy|Italy]]. It held the richest heartlands of the Carolingian dynasty but had no common identity, language or natural frontiers, and suffered [[e:vikings|Viking]] attacks in Frisia and Arab raids in the south.
middle-francia.e: Shortly before his death in 855 [[e:lothair-i|Lothair]] retired to the abbey of Prüm and, by the Treaty of Prüm, divided the kingdom among his three sons: [[e:louis-ii-of-italy|Louis II]] received [[e:italy|Italy]], [[e:lothair-ii|Lothair II]] the north, which became the [[s:kingdom-of-lotharingia|Kingdom of Lotharingia]], and Charles the [[s:kingdom-of-provence|Kingdom of Provence]].
