mosquito-reserve.t: Autonomous Miskito territory on Nicaragua's Caribbean coast, created by a British-Nicaraguan treaty in 1860 and annexed by Nicaragua in 1894.
mosquito-reserve.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] had long protected the [[s:mosquito-kingdom|Miskito Kingdom]] on the [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]] coast of [[e:central-america|Central America]], but under American pressure it agreed to withdraw. The Treaty of Managua of 1860 recognised Nicaraguan [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] while creating a self-governing reserve for the Miskito people, with its seat at Bluefields.
mosquito-reserve.r: The reserve was run by a hereditary chief, as the former king was now styled, and a council and assembly whose officials were often [[e:criollo-people|Creoles]] of African descent from Bluefields. English was the language of government, and Moravian missionaries, active since 1849, spread Protestant [[e:christianity|Christianity]] and schooling. An Austrian imperial arbitration in 1881 upheld the reserve's autonomy. American banana, [[e:timber|timber]] and [[e:rubber|rubber]] firms grew powerful in Bluefields in the 1880s.
mosquito-reserve.e: In 1894 President [[e:jose-santos-zelaya|José Santos Zelaya]] sent troops under General Rigoberto Cabezas to occupy Bluefields, and the territory was reincorporated as the [[e:departement|department]] of Zelaya. The last chief, [[e:robert-henry-clarence|Robert Henry Clarence]], went into exile in [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]]. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] recognised Nicaraguan [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] in 1905, and coastal autonomy remains a live issue.

malgium.t: A small Amorite-era kingdom on the Tigris, caught between Eshnunna, Elam and Babylon, that ended in Hammurabi's conquests.
malgium.o: Malgium lay on the [[e:tigris|Tigris]] south of the Diyala confluence, in the borderland between [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]] and [[e:elam|Elam]]; its exact site is unknown. It emerged as an independent kingdom in the 19th century BCE, after the end of the [[s:neo-sumerian-empire|Neo-Sumerian Empire]].
malgium.r: Its kings, such as Ipiq-Ishtar and Takil-ilissu, left Akkadian building inscriptions recording temples for Ea and Damkina. Malgium's position made it a pawn and occasional ally of greater powers: the [[s:mari|Mari]] letters show its rulers negotiating with [[s:eshnunna|Eshnunna]], [[e:elam|Elam]] and [[e:babylon|Babylon]] and providing troops to coalitions. [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi's]] tenth year name records the destruction of the army of Malgium, but the kingdom survived as a client.
malgium.e: In 1764 BCE Malgium joined [[e:babylon|Babylon's]] coalition against the [[s:sukkalmah-dynasty|Sukkalmah dynasty]] of [[e:elam|Elam]], but soon afterwards [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi]] annexed it, and it disappears from the record as part of the [[s:babylonian-empire|Babylonian Empire]].

mihranid-principality-of-albania.t: A dynasty of Persian origin that revived local rule in Caucasian Albania and steered it from Sasanian control through the Arab conquest.
mihranid-principality-of-albania.o: The Mihranids, a branch of a great Parthian noble family, came to [[s:caucasian-albania|Caucasian Albania]] in the late 6th century and held the canton of Gardman. Around 630, with the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] in crisis, [[e:varaz-grigor|Varaz Grigor]] became ruler of all [[s:albania|Albania]], taking the title of prince and ruling from Partav, modern Barda.
mihranid-principality-of-albania.r: Javanshir, the best-known prince, fought the [[e:arabs|Arabs]], allied with [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and then submitted to the [[e:caliphate|caliphate]] in 667, while repelling [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazar]] raids. The Mihranids patronised the Albanian church and Christian scholarship; the History of the [[e:albanians|Albanians]] attributed to Movses Kaghankatvatsi praises Javanshir. Partav grew as a trading city on the Kura.
mihranid-principality-of-albania.e: Javanshir was murdered in 680, and the princes became tributaries of the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] and [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]]. The line ended in 822 when the last prince, Varaz-Tiridates II, was killed, and his lands passed to Armenian princely houses such as [[s:principality-of-khachen|Khachen]].

mamdot-state.t: A Pathan Nawabi state on the Sutlej, granted by Ranjit Singh to the Kasur family and taken over by the British in 1855.
mamdot-state.o: After [[e:ranjit-singh|Ranjit Singh]] annexed Kasur around 1807, he compensated its Pathan ruling family with the lands of Mamdot on the south bank of the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]]. [[e:qutb-ud-din-khan-of-kasur|Qutb-ud-din Khan]] and his descendants ruled there as Nawabs.
mamdot-state.r: Mamdot later passed under British protection. Nawab Jamal-ud-din Khan supported the British in the [[e:first-anglo-sikh-war|First Anglo-Sikh War]] in 1845, but was deprived of ruling powers in 1855 for misgovernment, after which the family held Mamdot as a large estate.
mamdot-state.e: After 1855 Mamdot was part of British Ferozepur district. The family stayed prominent: Iftikhar Hussain Khan Mamdot became the first Chief Minister of West [[e:punjab|Punjab]] in [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] in 1947.

medang-kingdom.t: The Javanese kingdom of Mataram that built Prambanan and shared Central Java with the Buddhist Sailendras before moving its court to East Java.
medang-kingdom.o: The Canggal inscription of 732 records King Sanjaya erecting a Shiva lingam in Central [[e:java|Java]], and later kings traced their line to him. The kingdom, called Medang i Bhumi [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram]], grew on the [[e:rice|rice]] plains of the Kedu and Kewu basins around Mount Merapi, where the [[s:sailendra-kingdom|Sailendra Kingdom]] also held power in the late 8th century.
medang-kingdom.r: Kings ruled through rakai, regional lords, and drew revenue from wet-[[e:rice|rice]] farming recorded in hundreds of land-grant charters in [[e:old-javanese|Old Javanese]]. [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Buddhist shrines stood side by side: the Shaivite Prambanan complex was consecrated in 856 under [[e:rakai-pikatan|Rakai Pikatan]]. Balitung, around 900, ruled a wide realm. In 929 [[e:mpu-sindok|Mpu Sindok]] moved the court to East [[e:java|Java]], perhaps after eruptions of Merapi.
medang-kingdom.e: In 1016 the palace of King Dharmawangsa Teguh was sacked by Haji Wurawari, a [[e:vassal|vassal]] allied with [[e:srivijaya|Srivijaya]], an event remembered as the pralaya, the great destruction. Dharmawangsa's son-in-law Airlangga survived and founded [[s:kahuripan|Kahuripan]], carrying the Javanese royal tradition forward.

middle-elamite-kingdom.t: The classic age of Elam, when its kings built the ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil and carried off the law code of Hammurabi as plunder to Susa.
middle-elamite-kingdom.o: After the obscure end of the [[s:sukkalmah-dynasty|Sukkalmah dynasty]], a new line, the Kidinuids, ruled [[e:susa|Susa]] and [[s:kingdom-of-anshan|Anshan]] from about 1500 BCE with the title 'king of Susa and [[e:anshan|Anshan]]'. From around 1400 BCE the Igihalkid dynasty consolidated the kingdom, using Elamite rather than Akkadian for royal inscriptions and marrying into the Kassite royal house.
middle-elamite-kingdom.r: [[e:untash-napirisha|Untash-Napirisha]] built a new religious capital, Dur-Untash, with the great [[e:ziggurat|ziggurat]] of [[e:chogha-zanbil|Chogha Zanbil]], dedicated to Inshushinak and Napirisha. In the 12th century the Shutrukid kings made [[e:elam|Elam]] a military power: [[e:shutruk-nahhunte|Shutruk-Nahhunte]] I raided [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]] in 1158 BCE and brought monuments including the stele of [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi]] and [[e:naram-sin|Naram-Sin's]] victory stele to [[e:susa|Susa]], where French excavators found them. [[e:shilhak-inshushinak|Shilhak-Inshushinak]] campaigned widely and left many glazed-brick inscriptions.
middle-elamite-kingdom.e: Around 1110 BCE [[e:nebuchadnezzar-i|Nebuchadnezzar I]] of the [[s:second-dynasty-of-isin|Second Dynasty of Isin]] defeated Hutelutush-Inshushinak and recovered the statue of [[e:marduk|Marduk]]. [[e:elam|Elam]] then entered a poorly documented period until the rise of the [[s:neo-elamite-kingdom|Neo-Elamite kingdom]].

merina-kingdom.t: The highland kingdom that unified most of Madagascar in the 19th century, modernised with British help and fell to France in 1895.
merina-kingdom.o: Merina chiefdoms in the central highlands around Antananarivo were consolidated in the 16th century, traditionally by Andriamanelo, and later divided into rival realms. Around 1787 Andrianampoinimerina began reuniting Imerina from Ambohimanga, made Antananarivo his capital and declared that the sea would be the border of his [[e:rice|rice]] field.
merina-kingdom.r: The Merina state rested on irrigated [[e:rice|rice]] farming, forced labour (fanompoana) and [[e:slavery|slavery]]. Radama I, allied with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] from 1817, built a standing army, conquered much of the island and welcomed missionaries who wrote Malagasy in the [[e:latin|Latin]] alphabet. Ranavalona I persecuted Christians and expelled foreigners, but Ranavalona II converted in 1869, and the prime minister Rainilaiarivony governed through three queens.
merina-kingdom.e: [[e:france|France]] invaded in 1883–85 and again in 1895, capturing Antananarivo. The monarchy was abolished in 1897 and [[e:ranavalona-iii|Ranavalona III]] exiled. The kingdom's palace, the Rova of Antananarivo, and its administrative legacy shaped modern Madagascar.

metztitlan.t: A highland lordship in the Sierra Alta of Hidalgo that, like Tlaxcala, kept its independence from the Aztec Empire.
metztitlan.o: Metztitlan arose in the fertile Vega de Metztitlan, a long valley north-east of the [[e:valley-of-mexico|Valley of Mexico]], in the Postclassic period, probably by the 13th century. Its people were mainly Otomí and Nahua.
metztitlan.r: The lordship was ruled from Metztitlan by a hereditary lord and controlled numerous towns in the rugged Sierra Alta. Its mountains and fortified frontier allowed it to repel Aztec campaigns, including one under Tizoc in the 1480s, and it remained an independent enclave, trading with the Huasteca. Irrigated valley farming supported its population.
metztitlan.e: After the fall of [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]], Metztitlan submitted to the Spanish around 1522. Augustinian friars built a large monastery there, and it became a colonial town.

mysore-state.t: The Wodeyar kingdom restored by the British after Tipu Sultan's fall, later celebrated as a model princely state for its dams, universities and electricity.
mysore-state.o: After [[e:tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]] was killed at Seringapatam in 1799, the British restored the [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] Wodeyar dynasty, which [[e:hyder-ali|Hyder Ali]] had sidelined, and placed the five-year-old [[e:krishnaraja-wodeyar-iii|Krishnaraja Wodeyar III]] on the throne under the [[e:diwan|diwan]] Purnaiah. The new state was smaller than Tipu's realm and bound by a subsidiary alliance.
mysore-state.r: After a revolt in 1830–31 the British took over direct administration for fifty years, restoring the dynasty in 1881. Under Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV (ruled 1894–1940, with full powers from 1902) and [[e:diwan|diwans]] such as M. Visvesvaraya, Mysore built the Shivanasamudra hydroelectric plant, the Krishna Raja Sagara dam, the University of Mysore and industries in Bangalore, which also hosted the Indian Institute of Science. Kannada culture and Carnatic music flourished at court.
mysore-state.e: [[e:jayachamarajendra-wodeyar|Jayachamarajendra Wodeyar]] acceded to [[e:india|India]] and became Rajpramukh when Mysore became a state of the Indian Union in 1950. It was enlarged in 1956 and renamed Karnataka in 1973.

makanjira-chiefdom.t: A Muslim Yao chiefdom on the southeastern shore of Lake Malawi, a centre of the slave trade that fought the early British protectorate.
makanjira-chiefdom.o: The Makanjira chiefdom was founded by Yao who moved to the southeastern shore of [[e:lake-malawi|Lake Malawi]] in the mid-19th century. Successive chiefs bore the title Makanjira.
makanjira-chiefdom.r: Its power came from the trade in [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and slaves: dhows carried captives across the lake towards the coast and [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]]. The chiefs adopted [[e:islam|Islam]] and [[e:swahili|Swahili]] culture, employing coastal scribes and teachers.
makanjira-chiefdom.e: Makanjira resisted the [[s:british-central-africa-protectorate|British Central Africa Protectorate]] under [[e:harry-johnston|Harry Johnston]]; his towns were attacked from 1891, Fort Maguire was built on his land, and by 1895 he had been driven out and the chiefdom brought under colonial rule.

mirambos-state.t: A powerful Nyamwezi state built by the warlord Mirambo, who challenged the Arab traders of Tabora for control of the caravan routes.
mirambos-state.o: Mirambo, a Nyamwezi chief's son from the small chiefdom of Uyowa, built a military following in the 1860s from ruga-ruga, armed young men often of captive or uprooted origin. From his capital at Iselamagazi he conquered neighbouring chiefdoms and created a large state known as Urambo, west of Tabora.
mirambos-state.r: Mirambo's power rested on firearms, ruga-ruga warriors and control of trade. From 1871 to 1875 he fought the Arab and [[e:swahili|Swahili]] traders of [[s:unyanyembe|Unyanyembe]], closing the routes to the lake and Ujiji. [[e:henry-morton-stanley|Henry Morton Stanley]], who met him in 1876, compared him to [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]]. He later made peace and dealt with missionaries and the [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Sultanate of Zanzibar]].
mirambos-state.e: Mirambo died in 1884, and without his leadership the state fragmented among subordinate chiefs. Its lands passed under [[s:german-east-africa|German East Africa]] within a few years. The town and district of Urambo keep his name.

mohu.t: Small ancient Estonian county between Ugandi and Järvamaa, known only from Henry of Livonia's chronicle.
mohu.o: Mõhu, called Mocha by [[e:henry-of-livonia|Henry of Livonia]], was a minor Estonian district in the east-central part of the country, between [[s:ugandi|Ugandi]], [[s:vaiga|Vaiga]] and [[s:jarvamaa|Järvamaa]]. It appears only briefly in the chronicle of the Livonian [[e:crusade|crusade]] in the early 13th century.
mohu.r: Like other Estonian lands, it was probably a union of a few parishes led by elders, with a hillfort for refuge. Nothing specific is recorded of its leaders or customs.
mohu.e: Mõhu was subdued with neighbouring districts during the conquest of [[s:republic-of-estonia|Estonia]], completed in 1224, and passed into the [[s:bishopric-of-dorpat|Bishopric of Dorpat]].

menabe.t: The first great Sakalava kingdom of western Madagascar, whose Maroserana kings built power on cattle, warfare and the cult of royal relics.
menabe.o: Menabe was founded in the mid-17th century by the Maroserana dynasty, which moved north from the south-west into the plains between the Mangoky and Tsiribihina rivers. Under Andriandahifotsy, remembered as a great conqueror, the Sakalava defeated local rulers with firearms obtained from European traders.
menabe.r: Sakalava kingship was sacred: relics of dead kings (dady) were kept and honoured in shrines, and royal ancestor cults bound subjects to the dynasty. The economy was based on [[e:cattle|cattle]], and slaves and cattle were traded with Europeans at the coast. Royal princes went north to found [[s:boina|Boina]], extending Sakalava power along the west coast.
menabe.e: In the 19th century the [[s:merina-kingdom|Merina Kingdom]] took parts of Menabe, though much of the kingdom resisted. The French occupied it after 1895, and the last king, Toera, was killed in 1897. Sakalava royal rituals continue in western Madagascar.

montserrat.t: Small volcanic island in the Leewards, settled by Irish Catholics in the 17th century and still a British Overseas Territory, partly buried by its volcano.
montserrat.o: English and Irish settlers, many of them Catholics from [[s:colony-of-saint-christopher|Saint Kitts]] and [[e:virginia|Virginia]], were sent to Montserrat in 1632 under Sir [[e:thomas-warner|Thomas Warner]]. The island soon had an unusually large Irish population, and later arrivals included Irish prisoners transported after Cromwell's campaigns. The French captured it twice, in 1667 and 1782, but each time it returned to [[e:england|England]] or [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]].
montserrat.r: Governed by a governor with an assembly and council, Montserrat grew tobacco, then [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[e:cotton|cotton]] and limes on estates worked by enslaved Africans. The Irish legacy survives in place names, surnames and a public holiday on Saint Patrick's Day, which also marks a slave uprising planned for 17 March 1768. From 1871 to 1956 it formed part of the [[s:leeward-islands-colony|Leeward Islands colony]].
montserrat.e: Montserrat chose to remain a British dependency when its neighbours became independent. The Soufrière Hills volcano erupted from 1995, destroying the capital Plymouth in 1997 and forcing two thirds of the people to leave. It continues as a [[e:british-overseas-territories|British Overseas Territory]] with a new administrative centre at Brades in the north.

muri-emirate.t: A Fulani emirate on the upper Benue in north-east Nigeria, founded as an offshoot of Gombe and long at war with the Jukun of Wukari.
muri-emirate.o: Muri was founded around 1817 by [[e:hamman-ruwa|Hamman Ruwa]], a kinsman of [[e:buba-yero|Buba Yero]] of the [[s:gombe-emirate|Gombe Emirate]], who led [[e:fula|Fulani]] forces south into the Benue valley. He established a separate [[e:emirate|emirate]], centred first on Muri, among the Jukun, Mumuye and other peoples, and it was later recognised directly by [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]].
muri-emirate.r: The [[e:emirate|emirate]] controlled stretches of the Benue river, a growing route for trade in [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], slaves and later palm produce. Its rulers were frequently at war with the [[s:kingdom-of-wukari|Kingdom of Wukari]] and with hill peoples who resisted conquest, and succession disputes among [[e:hamman-ruwa|Hamman Ruwa's]] descendants divided it. In the 1890s the capital moved to Jalingo.
muri-emirate.e: The [[s:royal-niger-company-territories|Royal Niger Company]] signed treaties with Muri in the 1880s, and British forces occupied it after 1900. It became part of the [[s:protectorate-of-northern-nigeria|Protectorate of Northern Nigeria]], and the [[e:emir|Emir]] of Muri still reigns at Jalingo in Taraba State.

mosquito-shore.t: British protectorate on the Caribbean coast of Honduras and Nicaragua, built on an alliance with the Miskito kings and given up to Spain in 1787.
mosquito-shore.o: English traders and buccaneers had been allied with the Miskito people since the 17th century, and Jamaican governors crowned Miskito kings. During the War of Jenkins' Ear [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] sent [[e:robert-hodgson-mosquito-shore|Robert Hodgson]] to the coast, and in 1749 a superintendency was formally established, with its headquarters at [[e:black-river-honduras|Black River]] on the Honduran coast.
mosquito-shore.r: A British superintendent, appointed by the governor of [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]], oversaw a few hundred settlers and their enslaved workers, who cut mahogany, traded turtle shell, sarsaparilla and hides and smuggled goods into Spanish [[e:central-america|Central America]]. Miskito kings and chiefs remained powerful allies, raiding Spanish settlements and capturing other indigenous people for sale. Settlers sat in a council but quarrelled with the superintendents.
mosquito-shore.e: Under the Convention of [[e:london|London]] of 1786 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] agreed to evacuate the Mosquito Shore in exchange for an enlarged logging area in [[s:belize|Belize]]. In 1787 about 2,000 settlers and enslaved people moved to the [[s:belize-settlement|Belize Settlement]]. British influence on the coast revived in the 19th century and led to the [[s:mosquito-reserve|Mosquito Reserve]].

mandi-state.t: A Sen dynasty hill state on the Beas, known for its rock-salt mines, its temples and the Shanan hydroelectric scheme built under its last Rajas.
mandi-state.o: Mandi was founded by a junior branch of the Sen dynasty of [[s:suket-state|Suket State]]; tradition places the split around 1290. In 1527 Raja Ajbar Sen founded the town of Mandi on the [[e:beas|Beas]] as his capital.
mandi-state.r: The state's revenue came largely from its rock-salt mines at Guma and Drang. Raja Sidh Sen (r. about 1684–1727) expanded its territory, and the town's many temples earned it the name 'Varanasi of the hills'. Mandi became a tributary of the [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]] and passed under British protection in 1846. Under Raja Joginder Sen, the Shanan power station opened in 1932.
mandi-state.e: Mandi merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now a district of Himachal Pradesh. The International Shivratri fair at Mandi continues the old royal festival.

megara.t: City-state on the Isthmus between Athens and Corinth that founded Byzantium and Chalcedon and whose trade ban by Athens helped spark the Peloponnesian War.
megara.o: Megara occupied the small plain of the Megarid between Attica and [[s:corinth|Corinth]]. Dorian settlers formed the city in the early [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]], and it may once have been subject to Corinth before becoming independent. Its limited farmland pushed it to the sea, and from the 8th century BCE it founded colonies.
megara.r: Megarians founded [[s:megara-hyblaea|Megara Hyblaea]] in [[e:sicily|Sicily]], [[s:chalcedon|Chalcedon]], [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and later [[s:heraclea-pontica|Heraclea Pontica]]. Theagenes ruled as tyrant c. 640 BCE and backed his son-in-law Cylon's failed coup at [[s:athens|Athens]]. Megara lost the island of Salamis to [[e:athens|Athens]] in the 6th century BCE. The poet Theognis and the philosopher [[e:euclid|Euclid]] of Megara were citizens. It belonged to the [[s:peloponnesian-league|Peloponnesian League]].
megara.e: The Megarian Decree of c. 432 BCE barred it from Athenian markets and helped start the [[e:peloponnesian-war|Peloponnesian War]]. Megara joined the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]] in 243 BCE and passed under Roman control in 146 BCE.

marquisate-of-bodonitsa.t: Frankish frontier march guarding the pass of Thermopylae, which outlived most crusader states in Greece until the Ottomans took it in 1414.
marquisate-of-bodonitsa.o: In 1204 [[e:boniface-i-marquis-of-montferrat|Boniface of Montferrat]] granted the strategic castle of Bodonitsa, above the [[e:battle-of-thermopylae|Thermopylae]] pass, to the Italian knight [[e:guido-pallavicini|Guido Pallavicini]]. The marquisate was intended as a buffer protecting the Frankish lands of southern [[e:greece|Greece]] from attack from the north.
marquisate-of-bodonitsa.r: Bodonitsa was a small feudal state centred on its hill fortress, whose ruins still stand. Its marquesses were [[e:vassal|vassals]] first of the [[s:kingdom-of-thessalonica|Kingdom of Thessalonica]] and later of the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]], with some ties to the [[s:latin-empire|Latin Empire]]. The Pallavicini line was followed in 1335 by the Venetian Zorzi family through marriage, which brought Venetian protection.
marquisate-of-bodonitsa.e: Catalan, Byzantine and Turkish pressure reduced the marquisate. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] briefly took it in 1393 and finally captured Bodonitsa in 1414, ending the state. The Zorzi family kept the title in exile.

mycenaean-kingdom-of-orchomenos.t: Rich Mycenaean centre of Boeotia, home of the legendary Minyans, which drained Lake Copais in one of the great engineering feats of the Bronze Age.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-orchomenos.o: [[s:orchomenus-boeotia|Orchomenos]], on the north-west edge of [[e:lake-copais|Lake Copais]] in Boeotia, was an important settlement from the [[e:early-bronze-age|Early Bronze Age]] and gave its name to the grey 'Minyan ware' pottery. By c. 1600 BCE it was home to a Mycenaean elite, and its wealth later became proverbial: Homer compared it with Egyptian [[s:thebes|Thebes]].
mycenaean-kingdom-of-orchomenos.r: The so-called Treasury of Minyas, a great tholos tomb with a carved stone ceiling, shows the power of its rulers in the 13th century BCE. Remains of a palace with frescoes have been found. [[s:orchomenus-boeotia|Orchomenos]] is usually credited with draining the Copais basin by dykes and canals, protected by the huge fortress of Gla, creating rich farmland and rivalling [[s:thebes|Thebes]].
mycenaean-kingdom-of-orchomenos.e: The drainage works and Gla were abandoned c. 1200 BCE, when the lake flooded again, and the palace system collapsed. [[s:orchomenus-boeotia|Orchomenos]] survived as a Boeotian city, later a rival of [[s:thebes|Thebes]] within the [[s:boeotian-league|Boeotian League]], and is described separately as Orchomenus (Boeotia).

matsue-domain.t: The domain of Izumo, ruled from the lakeside castle of Matsue, whose lord Matsudaira Harusato was one of Japan's great tea masters.
matsue-domain.o: After [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]], [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] gave Izumo and Oki to [[e:horio-yoshiharu|Horio Yoshiharu]] in 1600. The Horio first used the old Amago fortress of Gassan-Toda, then built Matsue castle on Lake Shinji, finished in 1611.
matsue-domain.r: The Horio line died out in 1633 and the Kyogoku held the domain briefly before [[e:matsudaira-naomasa|Matsudaira Naomasa]], a grandson of [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Ieyasu]], received it in 1638 with about 186,000 koku. His descendants ruled until 1871. [[e:matsudaira-harusato|Matsudaira Harusato]], known as Fumai, restored the domain's finances in the late 18th century and became a leading [[e:tea|tea]] master and collector. The domain produced iron by the tatara method, ginseng and wax.
matsue-domain.e: The domain submitted to the Meiji government and was abolished in 1871, becoming part of Shimane Prefecture. Matsue castle's original keep survives as a national treasure.

mohnyin.t: A northern Shan state on the upper Irrawaddy whose saophas raided and finally conquered the Ava Kingdom in the 16th century.
mohnyin.o: Mohnyin, Shan Mong Yang, lay in the upper Irrawaddy basin in what is now Kachin State. It emerged as a Shan principality in the 14th century, within the sphere of [[s:mong-mao|Mong Mao]], and was later recognised by [[e:ming-empire|Ming China]] as a pacification commission called Mengyang.
mohnyin.r: Its saophas ruled a mix of Shan, Kachin and Burman subjects and were among the most aggressive of the Shan rulers. Under [[e:sawlon|Sawlon]] in the early 16th century Mohnyin led a coalition of Shan states against Ava, and in 1527 they took Ava, killing its king. Sawlon's son [[e:thohanbwa|Thohanbwa]] then reigned at Ava, notorious for attacking monasteries.
mohnyin.e: The Shan hold on Ava was broken by Bayinnaung of the [[s:first-toungoo-empire|First Toungoo Empire]], who conquered Mohnyin and the other northern Shan states in the 1550s. Mohnyin later lost its hereditary rulers and became part of the Burmese provincial order; the town survives in Kachin State.

margraviate-of-styria.t: The Carantanian March on the Mur that grew into Styria, elevated to a duchy in 1180 and later inherited by the Babenbergs and Habsburgs.
margraviate-of-styria.o: The Carantanian March arose around 970 on the south-eastern border of the [[s:duchy-of-carinthia|Duchy of Carinthia]], along the Mur, as a frontier against the [[e:magyars|Magyars]]. From 1056 it was ruled by the Otakar family of Steyr, and the territory took its name, Styria (Steiermark), from their castle of Steyr in [[e:upper-austria|Upper Austria]].
margraviate-of-styria.r: The Otakar margraves gradually made the march independent of Carinthia, adding lands around Graz and in the Enns valley. They founded monasteries such as Rein and Vorau and encouraged colonisation of the hill country. Iron mining at the Erzberg near Eisenerz became a lasting source of wealth.
margraviate-of-styria.e: In 1180 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] raised Styria to a duchy under [[e:ottokar-iv-of-styria|Ottokar IV]]. Having no heir, he concluded the Georgenberg Pact in 1186, leaving Styria to the Babenberg dukes of [[e:austria|Austria]], who inherited in 1192. Styria remained part of the [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] lands until 1918.

marwanids.t: A Kurdish dynasty that ruled Diyar Bakr from Mayyafariqin and Amid, with a long, prosperous reign under Nasr al-Dawla in the 11th century.
marwanids.o: In the 980s the Kurdish chief Badh took advantage of Buyid weakness to seize Mayyafariqin, Amid and much of [[e:diyar-bakr|Diyar Bakr]]. After his death in 990 his nephew Abu Ali ibn Marwan took over the domain, founding the dynasty that bears his father's name.
marwanids.r: Nasr al-Dawla Ahmad ibn Marwan ruled for about fifty years (1011-1061), keeping peace with [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] and the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]] by diplomacy and gifts. His capital Mayyafariqin gained mosques, a hospital and bridges, and attracted scholars, including the [[e:vizier|vizier]] Ibn Jahir and refugees from [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]]. The population mixed [[e:kurds|Kurds]], [[e:arabs|Arabs]], [[e:armenians|Armenians]] and [[e:syriac-christians|Syriac Christians]], and the dynasty was [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]].
marwanids.e: After Nasr al-Dawla's death the [[e:emirate|emirate]] became a Seljuk [[e:vassal|vassal]]. Around 1085 Malik-Shah sent its former [[e:vizier|vizier]] Fakhr al-Dawla ibn Jahir to conquer it, and [[e:diyar-bakr|Diyar Bakr]] passed to Seljuk governors and later to the [[s:inalids|Inalids]] and [[s:artuqids-of-mardin|Artuqids]].

mandubii.t: Small Gallic people of Burgundy whose hilltop town Alesia was the scene of Vercingetorix's last stand against Caesar in 52 BCE.
mandubii.o: The Mandubii lived in the Auxois district of northern [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]], between the [[s:aedui|Aedui]], [[s:lingones|Lingones]] and [[s:sequani|Sequani]], and were probably clients of the Aedui. Their oppidum Alesia stood on Mont Auxois, above modern Alise-Sainte-Reine.
mandubii.r: Almost nothing is known of their society before the siege that made their town famous.
mandubii.e: In 52 BCE [[e:vercingetorix|Vercingetorix]] took refuge in Alesia, and Caesar surrounded it with double lines of siege works. To save food, the defenders expelled the Mandubii with their wives and children, but Caesar would not let them pass, and they were left to starve between the lines. After the surrender Alesia lived on as a Gallo-Roman town.

mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes.t: Mycenaean palace kingdom on the Kadmeia hill in Boeotia, whose Linear B archive and Near Eastern treasures mark it as one of the major Bronze Age Greek powers.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes.o: [[s:thebes|Thebes]] occupies the Kadmeia, a low plateau between fertile plains in southern Boeotia. A palace centre emerged there by c. 1600 BCE, and by the 14th century BCE its rulers controlled much of Boeotia and perhaps Euboea. Greek myth gave the citadel its name from Cadmus, its legendary Phoenician founder.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes.r: Excavations under the modern town have uncovered parts of the palace, workshops for jewellery and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], and a hoard of Near Eastern cylinder seals of lapis lazuli. Several hundred Linear B tablets record offerings to gods, wool, food rations and places as far as Euboea. Some scholars argue that [[s:thebes|Thebes]] was the centre of the [[s:ahhiyawa|Ahhiyawa]] named in Hittite texts.
mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes.e: The palace was destroyed by fire in the 13th century BCE, the setting later remembered in the myths of Oedipus and the Seven against [[s:thebes|Thebes]]. The city remained inhabited and became the leading Boeotian city-state, described separately as [[e:thebes|Thebes]].

melayu-kingdom.t: A Buddhist kingdom on the Batang Hari River in Jambi, Sumatra, which gave its name to the Malay people before being absorbed by Srivijaya.
melayu-kingdom.o: Chinese records note an embassy from Mo-lo-yu in 644 or 645. The kingdom lay on the [[e:batang-hari-river|Batang Hari River]], centred near modern Jambi, where the Muara Jambi temple complex later grew up. It controlled gold from the Minangkabau highlands and access to the [[e:strait-of-malacca|Strait of Malacca]].
melayu-kingdom.r: The Chinese pilgrim [[e:yijing|Yijing]] stopped at Malayu on his voyage to [[e:india|India]] in 671, staying two months on his way from [[e:srivijaya|Srivijaya]] before sailing on to [[s:kedah-sultanate|Kedah]]. Little else is known of its rulers or institutions.
melayu-kingdom.e: When [[e:yijing|Yijing]] returned in the 680s he wrote that Malayu had become part of [[e:srivijaya|Srivijaya]]. The undated Karang Brahi inscription, found upriver in Jambi and usually placed close to the Kota Kapur inscription of 686, records Srivijaya's authority in the area. The name Malayu revived later in the [[s:dharmasraya|Dharmasraya]] kingdom and spread to the [[e:malay-language|Malay language]] and people.

mozambique-company.t: The chartered company that ruled central Mozambique from Beira, built around the railway to Rhodesia.
mozambique-company.o: In 1891 Portugal granted a royal charter to the Companhia de Moçambique for the territories of Manica and [[e:sofala|Sofala]] in central [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]], a region also coveted by [[e:cecil-rhodes|Cecil Rhodes's]] [[e:british-south-africa-company|British South Africa Company]]. The company made the new port of Beira its capital, and the Anglo-Portuguese treaty of 1891 fixed the border with [[s:rhodesia|Rhodesia]].
mozambique-company.r: With sovereign rights to tax, grant land and issue its own stamps and currency, the company built Beira into the main port for the landlocked Rhodesias, linked by the Beira railway, which reached Umtali in 1898 and Salisbury in 1899. [[e:sugar-plantation|Sugar]], [[e:cotton|cotton]] and sisal plantations relied on forced and contract labour, and hut tax provided much of its revenue.
mozambique-company.e: The company's charter expired in 1942 and was not renewed. Manica and [[e:sofala|Sofala]] came under the direct rule of the colonial government of [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Portuguese Mozambique]], and Beira remained the outlet for [[e:zimbabwe|Zimbabwe's]] trade.

malpur-state.t: A small Rajput princely state in north-eastern Gujarat, one of the minor states of the Mahi Kantha Agency.
malpur-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family's settlement at Malpur to 1466, but little is reliably known of its origins.
malpur-state.r: Malpur was a small agricultural state in the hills of the [[e:mahi-kantha-agency|Mahi Kantha]]. It paid tribute to [[s:baroda-state|Baroda State]] and was supervised by the British through the Mahi Kantha Agency. Its history is poorly recorded.
malpur-state.e: Malpur merged into [[e:bombay-state|Bombay State]] in 1948 and is now in Aravalli district, [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

munster-rebellion.t: The radical Anabaptist regime that seized Münster in 1534 and proclaimed a 'New Jerusalem' before being crushed in 1535.
munster-rebellion.o: Münster, capital of the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-munster|Prince-Bishopric of Münster]], had turned Lutheran under the preacher Bernhard Rothmann. Early in 1534 radical Anabaptists, many from the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]], won control of the council. Led by the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] baker [[e:jan-matthys|Jan Matthys]], they expelled those who refused rebaptism and declared Münster the New [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]].
munster-rebellion.r: [[e:franz-von-waldeck|Bishop Franz von Waldeck]] laid siege to the city. After Matthys was killed in a sortie at Easter 1534, the tailor [[e:john-of-leiden|Jan of Leiden]] proclaimed himself king. The regime abolished private property, introduced polygamy and ruled through prophecy and terror, while hunger spread within the walls.
munster-rebellion.e: In June 1535 the besiegers, helped by deserters, stormed the city. The leaders were tortured and executed in January 1536, and their bodies were hung in iron cages from the tower of Saint Lambert's church, where the cages still hang. The episode discredited Anabaptism for generations.

mountainous-republic-of-the-northern-cau.t: A short-lived state of the North Caucasus mountain peoples, declared in 1918 amid the collapse of the Russian Empire.
mountainous-republic-of-the-northern-cau.o: After the [[e:february-revolution|February Revolution]] of 1917, a congress at Vladikavkaz founded the Union of United Mountaineers of the [[e:north-caucasus|North Caucasus]] and [[e:dagestan|Dagestan]], bringing together Chechens, Ingush, Ossetians, Kabardians, Dagestanis and others. In May 1918 it declared independence from [[e:russia|Russia]] with the support of the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]].
mountainous-republic-of-the-northern-cau.r: The republic was led by a government of the mountaineer elite under [[e:tapa-chermoev|Tapa Chermoev]] and later [[e:pshemakho-kotsev|Pshemakho Kotsev]], and aimed at a federal, democratic state. It never controlled its territory firmly: Bolsheviks, [[s:terek-cossack-host|Terek Cossacks]] and local leaders contested it, and its seat moved from Vladikavkaz to Temir-Khan-Shura and elsewhere. It had a constitution and envoys abroad.
mountainous-republic-of-the-northern-cau.e: In 1919 the White army of Denikin occupied much of the [[e:north-caucasus|North Caucasus]] and dissolved the government. After the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]]'s victory in 1920, the Soviets created the Mountain Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic in 1921.

massalia.t: Greek colony at Marseille, the oldest city in France, through which Greek wine, coinage and writing reached the peoples of Gaul for five centuries.
massalia.o: Settlers from [[s:phocaea|Phocaea]] in [[e:asia-minor|Asia Minor]] founded the city around 600 BCE on the sheltered harbour of the Lacydon, east of the Rhône delta. Tradition says their leader Protis married Gyptis, daughter of Nannus, king of the local Segobrigii. Refugees arrived after [[e:phocaea|Phocaea]] fell to [[e:persia|Persia]] in 545 BCE, and Massalia planted daughter towns such as Nikaia (Nice), Antipolis (Antibes) and [[s:emporion|Emporion]] in [[e:spain|Spain]].
massalia.r: The city was an aristocratic republic governed by a council of six hundred timouchoi, praised by [[e:aristotle|Aristotle]] and Strabo for its stability. It traded wine, oil and fine pottery up the Rhône for [[e:tin|tin]], metals and slaves, and its [[e:silver|silver]] coins were widely copied by Gallic peoples. Artemis of [[s:ephesus|Ephesus]] and [[e:apollo-delphinios|Apollo Delphinios]] were its chief cults, and around 325 BCE its navigator Pytheas sailed to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and the [[e:north-sea|North Sea]].
massalia.e: A steady ally of the [[s:roman-republic|Roman Republic]], Massalia called in Roman armies against the [[s:salyes|Salyes]] from 125 BCE, opening the way to the province of [[e:gallia-narbonensis|Gallia Narbonensis]]. Having sided with [[e:pompey|Pompey]], it was besieged and taken by Caesar's forces in 49 BCE and lost its fleet and most of its territory, yet it lived on as a free Greek city under the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]].

mauretania-tingitana.t: The Roman province of northern Morocco, ruled from Tangier and later attached to Roman Spain.
mauretania-tingitana.o: After the execution of [[e:ptolemy-of-mauretania|King Ptolemy]] and the suppression of Aedemon's revolt, Claudius divided the [[s:kingdom-of-mauretania|Kingdom of Mauretania]] in 42 CE. The western part became Mauretania Tingitana, named after its capital Tingis (Tangier), and was governed by an equestrian procurator.
mauretania-tingitana.r: Roman control covered the north of [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], with towns such as Volubilis, Sala, [[s:lixus|Lixus]] and Banasa linked by roads and protected by forts. The economy produced [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]], grain, fish sauce and wild animals for the arena. [[e:berbers|Berber]] tribes such as the Baquates negotiated treaties with [[e:rome|Rome]], recorded on altars at Volubilis. Under [[e:diocletian|Diocletian]] the province was attached to the Diocese of the [[e:spain|Spains]].
mauretania-tingitana.e: Around 285 [[e:rome|Rome]] withdrew from the south, keeping only the region around Tingis and the coast. In 429 the [[e:vandals|Vandals]] crossed from [[e:spain|Spain]] into [[e:africa|Africa]], and Roman rule ended; the strongpoint of [[s:septem|Septem]] later became a Byzantine outpost, while [[e:berbers|Berber]] principalities rose inland.

macae.t: A Libyan people of the Cinyps valley in Tripolitania who helped Carthage drive out a Spartan attempt to settle in Africa.
macae.o: The Macae are known only from Greek and Roman writers. [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] places them in the 5th century BCE along the river Cinyps (Wadi Caam), near [[s:leptis-magna|Leptis Magna]], as neighbours of the [[s:nasamones|Nasamones]]. They lived as pastoralists in the coastal plain and desert edge.
macae.r: [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] notes their distinctive hairstyle, shaved except for a crest, and their use of ostrich-skin shields. Around 515 BCE, together with the [[e:carthage|Carthaginians]], they expelled the Spartan prince Dorieus, who had tried to found a colony on the Cinyps. They stayed within the orbit of the [[s:punic-empire|Punic Empire]] as tributaries and allies.
macae.e: Later writers mention the Macae as a Libyan people of [[s:tripolitania|Tripolitania]] into Roman times, and they were gradually absorbed into the provincial and tribal society of the region. No rulers of theirs are known by name.

marsi.t: Warlike Sabellic people of the Fucine Lake basin, famed as snake charmers, who led the Italian revolt against Rome in 91 BCE.
marsi.o: The Marsi lived around the [[e:fucine-lake|Fucine Lake]] in the central Apennines of Abruzzo from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers linked their name to Marsyas or to Mars and considered them part of the Sabellian peoples. They spoke Marsian, an Italic dialect related to Umbrian and Oscan.
marsi.r: Their main centre was Marruvium on the lake shore. [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] regarded the Marsi as experts in magic, healing and snake-charming, linked to the goddess Angitia, whose grove stood by the lake. They were renowned as soldiers; a Roman saying held that no one had ever triumphed over the Marsi or without them. They lived from farming, fishing and herding.
marsi.e: The Marsi allied with [[e:rome|Rome]] in 304 BCE and served loyally for two centuries. In 91 BCE, led by [[e:quintus-poppaedius-silo|Quintus Poppaedius Silo]], they were among the first to rise in the [[e:social-war-91-87-bce|Social War]], sometimes called the Marsic War. They received citizenship afterwards, and the [[e:fucine-lake|Fucine Lake]] was drained in the 19th century.

mantinea.t: Democratic Arcadian city that twice gave its name to great battles and was twice destroyed for opposing Sparta and Macedon.
mantinea.o: Mantinea grew from the union of several villages on the high plain of eastern Arcadia, a synoecism usually dated to around 500 BCE or soon after. Its constant rival was [[s:tegea|Tegea]], which shared the same plain and its scarce water. Mantinea was normally a member of [[e:sparta|Sparta's]] [[s:peloponnesian-league|Peloponnesian League]] but resented Spartan control.
mantinea.r: Unusually for Arcadia, Mantinea had a moderate democracy, admired by [[e:aristotle|Aristotle]], in which farmers voted but elected officials did the governing. It was famous for its well-drilled [[e:hoplite|hoplites]]. In 418 BCE it joined [[s:argos|Argos]] and [[s:athens|Athens]] against [[s:sparta|Sparta]] and was defeated at the first [[e:battle-of-mantinea-418-bce|Battle of Mantinea]]; in 385 BCE [[e:sparta|Sparta]] broke the city into villages by damming the river Ophis against its walls.
mantinea.e: Refounded in 370 BCE, Mantinea helped create the [[s:arcadian-league|Arcadian League]], and in 362 BCE [[e:epaminondas|Epaminondas]] died winning the second [[e:battle-of-mantinea-418-bce|Battle of Mantinea]]. After it joined [[e:cleomenes-iii|Cleomenes III of Sparta]], the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]] and [[e:antigonus-iii-doson|Antigonus Doson]] destroyed it in 223 BCE and renamed it Antigoneia. Hadrian later restored the old name.

middle-juz.t: The central division of the Kazakhs, whose khan Ablai unified much of the steppe before Russia absorbed it in 1822.
middle-juz.o: After [[e:tauke-khan|Tauke Khan's]] death around 1718 the [[s:kazakh-khanate|Kazakh Khanate]] split into three hordes, with the Middle Juz holding the central and north-eastern steppe from the [[e:syr-darya|Syr Darya]] to the Irtysh. Its main tribes included the Argyn, Naiman, Kerei and Kypchak.
middle-juz.r: The Middle Juz fought the [[e:dzungars|Dzungars]], and in the 1740s its khan Abilmambet and the sultan Ablai accepted Russian protection while balancing ties with the Qing. Ablai, who became khan in 1771, defeated rivals and dominated much of the Kazakh steppe. The biy Kazybek Bi was among its noted judges and diplomats.
middle-juz.e: After Ablai's death in 1781 and the death of his son [[e:vali-khan|Vali Khan]] in 1819, [[e:russia|Russia's]] Speransky reforms of 1822 abolished the khanship and organised the territory into Russian districts. Ablai's grandson Kenesary Kasymov later led a revolt against Russian rule.

mahdist-state.t: The Islamic state founded by the Sudanese Mahdi after his followers took Khartoum and killed Gordon, ruled from Omdurman until the British reconquest.
mahdist-state.o: In 1881 [[e:muhammad-ahmad|Muhammad Ahmad]], a [[e:sufism|Sufi]] teacher on Aba Island, declared himself the [[e:mahdi|Mahdi]] and called for holy war against [[s:turco-egyptian-sudan|Turco-Egyptian Sudan]]. His followers, the Ansar, destroyed Hicks Pasha's army at Shaykan in 1883 and stormed Khartoum in January 1885, killing [[e:charles-george-gordon|Charles Gordon]].
mahdist-state.r: The [[e:mahdi|Mahdi]] died in June 1885, and his successor, the [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]] Abdallahi ibn Muhammad, ruled from Omdurman. He built a centralised state with a treasury, courts and a large army. The Mahdists killed the Ethiopian emperor [[e:yohannes-iv|Yohannes IV]] at Gallabat in 1889 but were defeated invading [[e:egypt|Egypt]] at Toshki the same year. Famine in 1888 to 1892 killed many.
mahdist-state.e: An Anglo-Egyptian army under [[e:herbert-kitchener|Herbert Kitchener]] destroyed the Mahdist army at Omdurman in September 1898, and the [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]] was killed at Umm Diwaykarat in 1899, leading to [[s:anglo-egyptian-sudan|Anglo-Egyptian Sudan]].

makanga.t: A warlord state north of the Zambezi founded by the Goan-Portuguese Pereira family and its Chikunda slave armies.
makanga.o: Makanga grew from the estates of the Pereira family, Goan-Portuguese settlers of the [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]] valley. In the mid-19th century, as the Portuguese prazo system collapsed, Gonçalo Caetano Pereira and his son [[e:pedro-caetano-pereira|Pedro Caetano Pereira]] built an autonomous state north of the river near Tete, ruled from fortified stockades called aringas.
makanga.r: Power rested on armies of Chikunda, enslaved and freed soldier-hunters armed with [[e:musket|muskets]], who raided neighbouring [[e:chewa|Chewa]] and Nsenga lands for [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and captives. The rulers acted like African chiefs, taking African titles and wives, while nominally recognising Portugal and often supplying it with troops against rival states such as [[s:massangano|Massangano]].
makanga.e: Makanga remained effectively independent until the Portuguese, reasserting control over the [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]] valley, conquered it in 1902 and incorporated it into [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Portuguese Mozambique]]. Chikunda communities descended from its soldiers survive in the region.

mengjiang.t: The Japanese-sponsored Mongol autonomous state in Inner Mongolia under Prince Demchugdongrub, which ruled from Kalgan until 1945.
mengjiang.o: Prince Demchugdongrub (De Wang) led an Inner Mongolian movement for autonomy from [[e:china|China]] and turned to the [[e:kwantung-army|Kwantung Army]] for support. A Mongol Military Government was formed in 1936. After Japanese forces occupied Chahar, Suiyuan and northern [[e:shanxi|Shanxi]] in 1937, three client governments were set up, and in 1939 they merged as the Mengjiang United Autonomous Government at Kalgan (Zhangjiakou).
mengjiang.r: Japanese advisers controlled policy, but the state allowed [[e:mongols|Mongols]] a voice in their own affairs and promoted Mongolian language, schools and [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] alongside a much larger Chinese farming population. Its economy supplied [[e:coal|coal]], iron ore and other resources to [[e:japan|Japan]]. From 1940 it was nominally part of the [[s:wang-jingwei-regime|Wang Jingwei regime]] while remaining autonomous, and in 1941 it was restyled the Mongolian Autonomous Federation.
mengjiang.e: Soviet and Mongolian forces invaded in August 1945, and the state collapsed; the region later became part of [[e:inner-mongolia|Inner Mongolia]] in the [[s:peoples-republic-of-china|People's Republic of China]]. Demchugdongrub later fled to the [[s:mongolian-peoples-republic|Mongolian People's Republic]], was handed to [[e:china|China]] and imprisoned until 1963.

march-of-turin.t: March of the Arduinici in Piedmont whose heiress Adelaide of Susa brought its lands to the house of Savoy.
march-of-turin.o: Around 941 King [[e:hugh-of-arles|Hugh of Arles]] or his successor reorganised the western [[e:alps|Alps]] and Piedmont, giving [[e:arduin-glaber|Arduin Glaber]] control of Turin and the [[e:susa|Susa]] valley. Arduin drove out Arab raiders based at Fraxinetum from the passes, and his family, the Arduinici, held the march for 150 years.
march-of-turin.r: The margraves controlled the routes over the Mont Cenis and [[e:montgenevre-pass|Mont Genèvre]] passes, a source of wealth and strategic weight. [[e:ulric-manfred-ii|Ulric Manfred II]] (died 1034) extended the march and founded monasteries. His daughter [[e:adelaide-of-susa|Adelaide of Susa]] ruled for over half a century, married Otto of [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]], and was one of the most powerful figures in northern [[e:italy|Italy]], the mother-in-law of [[e:henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Henry IV]].
march-of-turin.e: When Adelaide died in 1091, the march broke up among her heirs, local lords and the growing commune of Turin. Her Savoyard descendants eventually inherited Turin and Piedmont, the foundation of the later [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] state.

muscogee-confederacy.t: A league of self-governing towns in Georgia and Alabama, heirs of the Mississippian chiefdoms, which balanced rival empires for a century before removal west.
muscogee-confederacy.o: The confederacy grew out of the survivors of Mississippian chiefdoms such as [[s:coosa-chiefdom|Coosa]], along with refugees from other peoples, who regrouped in towns along the Coosa, Tallapoosa, Chattahoochee and Flint rivers in the 17th century. The English called them Creeks after Ochese Creek, where many lived, and by around 1700 they formed a recognised alliance of Upper and Lower Towns.
muscogee-confederacy.r: Each town, or talwa, had its own square ground, council and chief, the mico, and towns were classed as white (peace) or red (war). The annual [[e:green-corn-ceremony|Green Corn]] ceremony renewed community life. Leaders such as Brims of Coweta played British, French and Spanish colonies against each other, and the deerskin trade brought wealth. [[e:alexander-mcgillivray|Alexander McGillivray]], the leading Muscogee diplomat from the 1780s, negotiated the Treaty of [[e:new-york|New York]] with the [[s:united-states|United States]] in 1790.
muscogee-confederacy.e: The Creek War of 1813 to 1814 ended with defeat at Horseshoe Bend and huge land cessions. Most Muscogee were forcibly removed to [[e:indian-territory|Indian Territory]] in the 1830s, where they set up a government at Okmulgee in 1867. It was suppressed by 1907 but revived later.

moravian-serbia.t: Prince Lazar's Serbian state on the Morava, which led the resistance to the Ottomans at Kosovo in 1389 and founded a rich school of church art.
moravian-serbia.o: After the [[s:serbian-empire|Serbian Empire]] broke up, Prince [[e:lazar-of-serbia|Lazar Hrebeljanović]], a court official under Dušan, built the strongest of the successor states in the Morava valley. With Tvrtko I he destroyed [[e:nikola-altomanovic|Nikola Altomanović]] in 1373, and by 1379 he was the leading Serbian ruler, with Kruševac as his capital.
moravian-serbia.r: Lazar ruled with nobles bound by family ties, including his son-in-law [[e:vuk-brankovic|Vuk Branković]]. The [[e:silver|silver]] mines of [[e:novo-brdo|Novo Brdo]] and Rudnik paid for the state, and Lazar reconciled the Serbian church with [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] in 1375. Churches such as Ravanica and Lazarica gave their name to the Morava school of architecture.
moravian-serbia.e: Lazar died at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. His widow Milica and son [[e:stefan-lazarevic|Stefan Lazarević]] became Ottoman [[e:vassal|vassals]]. After fighting at Ankara in 1402, Stefan received the title of despot from [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], and the state became the [[s:serbian-despotate|Serbian Despotate]].

moundville-chiefdom.t: One of the largest Mississippian chiefdoms, centred on a planned town of 29 mounds on the Black Warrior River in Alabama.
moundville-chiefdom.o: Around 1120 farming communities along the Black Warrior River in west-central Alabama began building small mounds at Moundville. By around 1200 the site had been laid out to a deliberate plan: a broad plaza ringed by large platform mounds, the whole enclosed by a wooden palisade, making it the capital of a chiefdom controlling the valley.
moundville-chiefdom.r: Mound pairs around the plaza likely belonged to ranked kin groups, with the paramount chief living on Mound B, some 17 metres high. Only around a thousand people lived inside the town; most farmed [[e:maize|maize]] in the valley and sent food to the centre. Elite graves contain [[e:copper|copper]] axes, engraved black pottery with hand-and-eye and winged-serpent motifs, and stone palettes such as the Rattlesnake Disk. After about 1300 most residents left and Moundville became chiefly a burial and ceremonial centre.
moundville-chiefdom.e: The centre lost its regional authority by about 1450, and smaller chiefdoms took its place; [[e:hernando-de-soto|Hernando de Soto]] met their descendants in 1540. The site is now Moundville Archaeological Park.

myinsaing-kingdom.t: The regency of three Shan-Burmese brothers who repelled the Mongols and ruled central Myanmar after the fall of Pagan.
myinsaing-kingdom.o: Athinkhaya, Yazathingyan and [[e:thihathu|Thihathu]], sons of a Shan chief and commanders under the last Pagan kings, built up power in the Kyaukse district from bases at Myinsaing, Mekkaya and Pinle. In 1297 they overthrew King Kyawswa of Pagan, who had accepted Mongol [[e:vassal|vassalage]], and took control of the Kyaukse [[e:rice|rice]] granary.
myinsaing-kingdom.r: The brothers ruled jointly, maintaining the irrigated [[e:rice|rice]] lands of Kyaukse that fed central [[s:myanmar|Myanmar]]. In 1300 to 1301 they withstood a Yuan Mongol army at Myinsaing, which withdrew after receiving gifts, and the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] soon left [[e:upper-burma|Upper Burma]] altogether. They placed a puppet king, Saw Hnit, on the throne at Pagan.
myinsaing-kingdom.e: Athinkhaya died in 1310 and Yazathingyan around 1312, leaving [[e:thihathu|Thihathu]] sole ruler. In 1313 he founded a new capital at [[s:pinya-kingdom|Pinya]], opening the Pinya Kingdom. The Myinsaing period marks the transition from Pagan to the later Burmese kingdoms of Ava.

motul-de-san-jose.t: The seat of the Ik' kingdom near Lake Petén Itzá, famed for the elegant 'Ik'-style' painted vases that portray its courtly life.
motul-de-san-jose.o: Motul de San José lies on the northern side of [[e:lake-peten-itza|Lake Petén Itzá]]. Settlement there is older, but the Ik' emblem glyph and its royal court are best known from the [[e:late-classic-period|Late Classic]], from about 600 CE, when the kingdom flourished in the shadow of [[s:tikal|Tikal]].
motul-de-san-jose.r: The Ik' court is known chiefly through polychrome vases painted in a distinctive style with pink and red tones, showing kings, dancers, tribute presentations and court scenes, some signed by named artists. Its lords were sometimes subordinate to [[s:tikal|Tikal]] and sometimes rivals. Excavations indicate a modest city with outlying settlements engaged in farming and craft production.
motul-de-san-jose.e: The Ik' kingdom declined during the Terminal Classic, and the city was largely abandoned by about 850 CE. Its vases, scattered in museums worldwide, remain a vital source for Maya court life.

malla-dynasty-nepal.t: The dynasty that ruled the Kathmandu Valley from the 13th century, shaping its Newar culture before dividing into the three Malla kingdoms.
malla-dynasty-nepal.o: The Malla period in the [[e:kathmandu-valley|Kathmandu Valley]] begins with [[e:ari-malla|Ari Malla]], who took the throne in 1201. The early centuries were marked by raids from the [[s:khasa-malla-kingdom|Khasa Malla kingdom]] and the [[s:karnat-dynasty|Karnat dynasty]], and by rivalries between noble houses based at Bhaktapur, Patan and Kathmandu.
malla-dynasty-nepal.r: [[e:jayasthiti-malla|Jayasthiti Malla]], ruling from Bhaktapur in the late 14th century, is remembered for codifying [[e:caste|caste]] and social rules and patronising [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and Newari learning. [[e:yaksha-malla|Yaksha Malla]] extended the kingdom and built temples in Bhaktapur. Newar artisans produced metalwork, painting and architecture for [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Buddhist patrons, and the valley profited from trade between [[e:india|India]] and [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]].
malla-dynasty-nepal.e: On [[e:yaksha-malla|Yaksha Malla's]] death in 1482 the realm was divided among his sons, producing the [[s:kingdom-of-bhaktapur|Kingdom of Bhaktapur]], the [[s:kingdom-of-kantipur|Kingdom of Kantipur]] and later the [[s:kingdom-of-lalitpur|Kingdom of Lalitpur]]. These Malla states lasted until the [[s:gorkha-kingdom|Gorkha]] conquest of 1768 to 1769.
